/-- A subgroup of a finite group whose index is the smallest prime factor is normal.

Note : if `G` is infinite, then `Nat.card G = 0` and `(Nat.card G).minFac = 2` -/
theorem normal_of_index_eq_minFac_card (hHp : H.index = (Nat.card G).minFac) :
    H.Normal := by
  by_cases hG0 : Nat.card G = 0
  · rw [hG0, minFac_zero] at hHp
    exact normal_of_index_eq_two hHp
  by_cases hG1 : Nat.card G = 1
  · rw [hG1, minFac_one] at hHp
    exact normal_of_index_eq_one hHp
  suffices H.normalCore.relIndex H = 1 by
    convert H.normalCore_normal
    exact le_antisymm (relIndex_eq_one.mp this) (normalCore_le H)
  have : Finite G := finite_of_card_ne_zero hG0
  have index_ne_zero : H.index ≠ 0 := index_ne_zero_of_finite
  rw [← mul_left_inj' index_ne_zero, one_mul, relIndex_mul_index H.normalCore_le]
  have hp : Nat.Prime H.index := hHp ▸ minFac_prime hG1
  have h : H.normalCore.index ∣ H.index ! := by
    rw [normalCore_eq_ker, index_ker, index_eq_card, ← Nat.card_perm]
    exact card_subgroup_dvd_card (toPermHom G (G ⧸ H)).range
  apply dvd_antisymm _ (index_dvd_of_le H.normalCore_le)
  rwa [← Coprime.dvd_mul_right, mul_factorial_pred hp.ne_zero]
  have hr1 : H.normalCore.index ≠ 1 := fun hr1 ↦ hp.ne_one <|
    Nat.eq_one_of_dvd_one (hr1 ▸ H.normalCore.index_dvd_of_le H.normalCore_le)
  rw [Nat.coprime_factorial_iff hr1]
  exact lt_of_lt_of_le (Nat.sub_one_lt hp.ne_zero) <|
    hHp ▸ minFac_le_of_dvd (Nat.minFac_prime hr1).two_le
      (dvd_trans (minFac_dvd H.normalCore.index) (H.normalCore.index_dvd_card))

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Let X = G/H be the set of left cosets. It has p elements. The group G acts on X by left multiplication. This action gives a group homomorphism ρ : G → Sym(X) ≅ S_p.
Let K = ker ρ. Then K is a normal subgroup of G. If g is in K, then g fixes the coset H, so gH = H and g is in H. So K ⊆ H.
The first isomorphism theorem gives G/K ≅ ρ(G), a subgroup of S_p. By Lagrange, m = |G/K| divides |S_p| = p!.
Also m = [G:K] divides |G|, because |G| = [G:K]·|K|. So every prime divisor of m divides |G|, hence is at least p by the choice of p.
Every prime divisor of m also divides p! = p·(p−1)!, so it is at most p. Together with step 4, the only prime divisor of m is p. So m = p^a for some a ≥ 0.
The prime p appears in p! exactly once, because the factors 1,…,p each contribute at most one factor p and only p itself does. Since p^a | p!, a ≤ 1. So m is 1 or p.
Now K ⊆ H gives [G:K] = [G:H]·[H:K] = p·[H:K] ≥ p. So m = p and [H:K] = 1. Hence H = K, and H is normal.

Index 2. The same proof with p = 2 uses only that S₂ has order 2. Finiteness of G is used only to say that every prime divisor of m divides |G|. For p = 2 this is not needed, because m divides 2! = 2 already, so the argument works for infinite G.

worked_application.title: Subgroups of index 3 in a group of order 21, and failures for other indices
worked_application.goal: Let G be the group of maps x ↦ ax + b on ℤ/7 with a in {1,2,4}. Find the subgroups of index 3 and check normality. Compare with S₃ and S₄.
hypotheses: |G| = 21 = 3·7, so the smallest prime divisor is 3.
G has 21 elements (a,b), with composition (a,b)(c,d) = (ac, ad+b).
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: A subgroup of order 7 has index 3, which is the smallest prime divisor of 21. So the theorem applies to it.

steps.text: The translations T = {(1,b)} form a subgroup of order 7. Its index is 21/7 = 3. By the theorem T is normal in G.
Direct check. For (a,b) in G and (1,c) in T, the conjugate (a,b)(1,c)(a,b)⁻¹ is the map x ↦ x + ac, which lies in T. So T is normal. A computer check of all 21 conjugations agrees.

Count all subgroups. A computer enumeration of the subgroups generated by one or two elements gives 10 subgroups: the trivial one, 7 subgroups of order 3, one subgroup of order 7 and G. Only the last three are normal.
The 7 subgroups of order 3 have index 7. The smallest prime divisor of 21 is 3, not 7. So the theorem does not apply to them, and indeed none is normal.
Failure for larger index. In S₃ the subgroup H = {id, (1 2)} has index 3. But the smallest prime divisor of 6 is 2, not 3. The subgroup H has 3 conjugates, so it is not normal.
The dihedral group D₄ of order 8 inside S₄ has index 3. The smallest prime divisor of 24 is 2. The subgroup D₄ has 3 conjugates in S₄, so it is not normal.
Consequence for order 21. The unique subgroup of order 7 is normal. This is a quick case of the Sylow theorems that needs no counting of Sylow subgroups.

worked_application.result: In the group of order 21, the subgroup of order 7 (index 3, the smallest prime divisor) is normal. The subgroups of order 3 (index 7) are not. In S₃ and S₄ the index 3 subgroups are not normal.

The theorem does not say that every normal subgroup has such an index. It is only a sufficient test.

/-- Let $F$ be a field. Let $G$ be a finite group acting faithfully on $F$.
Then $[F : F^G] = |G|$. -/
@[stacks 09I3 "second part"]
theorem finrank_eq_card [Fintype G] [FaithfulSMul G F] :
    finrank (FixedPoints.subfield G F) F = Fintype.card G :=
  le_antisymm (FixedPoints.finrank_le_card G F) <|
    calc
      Fintype.card G ≤ Fintype.card (F →ₐ[FixedPoints.subfield G F] F) :=
        Fintype.card_le_of_injective _ (MulSemiringAction.toAlgHom_injective _ F)
      _ ≤ finrank F (F →ₗ[FixedPoints.subfield G F] F) := finrank_algHom (subfield G F) F
      _ = finrank (FixedPoints.subfield G F) F := finrank_linearMap_self _ _ _

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Let K = F^G and n = |G|. Write G = {g₁,…,gₙ}. We show [F:K] ≤ n and [F:K] ≥ n.

Upper bound. Suppose x₁,…,x_m in F are linearly independent over K with m > n. Consider the n equations Σⱼ gᵢ(xⱼ)·yⱼ = 0 for i = 1,…,n, in the m unknowns yⱼ. There are fewer equations than unknowns, so a nonzero solution exists in F.

Choose a nonzero solution with the fewest nonzero entries. Scale it so that one entry equals 1. Apply an element g of G to all equations. Since G permutes the equations, g(y) is again a solution with the same support.
The difference y − g(y) is a solution with fewer nonzero entries, because the entry equal to 1 cancels. By minimality it is zero. So every yⱼ is fixed by G, that is, every yⱼ lies in K.
One equation is the one for the identity element: Σⱼ xⱼ·yⱼ = 0 with yⱼ in K, not all zero. This contradicts the independence of the xⱼ over K. So [F:K] ≤ n.
Lower bound. Suppose [F:K] = m < n, with a K-basis x₁,…,x_m. The m equations Σᵢ gᵢ(xⱼ)·yᵢ = 0 (j = 1,…,m) in n unknowns have a nonzero solution (y₁,…,yₙ) in F.
Every element a of F has the form Σⱼ cⱼxⱼ with cⱼ in K. Each cⱼ is fixed by every gᵢ. So Σᵢ yᵢ·gᵢ(a) = Σⱼ cⱼ·Σᵢ yᵢ·gᵢ(xⱼ) = 0.
So the n distinct automorphisms g₁,…,gₙ satisfy the nontrivial relation Σ yᵢgᵢ = 0 on F. This contradicts the independence of characters. So [F:K] ≥ n, and [F:K] = n.
Consequence. For a subgroup H of G, apply the theorem to H and to G. The degree multiplicativity [F:E][E:K]=[F:K] for a tower K⊆E⊆F gives [F:F^H]·[F^H:F^G] = [F:F^G], so [F^H : F^G] = |G|/|H|.

worked_application.goal: Let F = Q(√2, √3) with basis (1, √2, √3, √6) over Q. Let G be the group generated by the automorphisms σ and τ. Compute the dimension of each fixed field.
hypotheses: σ sends √2 to −√2 and fixes √3. τ sends √3 to −√3 and fixes √2.
On the basis, σ, τ and στ act as diag(1,−1,1,−1), diag(1,1,−1,−1) and diag(1,−1,−1,1).
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The dimension of a fixed field over Q equals the dimension of the common fixed space of the matrices. The theorem predicts 4/|H| for a subgroup H.

steps.text: The trivial subgroup fixes all of F. Its fixed space has dimension 4 = 4/1.
The subgroup ⟨σ⟩ fixes the basis vectors 1 and √3. Its fixed space has dimension 2 = 4/2. This is Q(√3).
The subgroup ⟨τ⟩ fixes 1 and √2. The subgroup ⟨στ⟩ fixes 1 and √6. Both have dimension 2 = 4/2. These are Q(√2) and Q(√6).
The whole group G has order 4. Only the vector 1 is fixed by all three matrices. The fixed space has dimension 1 = 4/4. So F^G = Q.
The numbers agree with the theorem for all five subgroups. Also [F : Q] = 4 = |G|, so F is a Galois extension of Q with group G.

steps.text: Let n₁,…,n_k generate N over A. Since bN ⊆ N, write b·nᵢ = Σⱼ mᵢⱼ·nⱼ with mᵢⱼ in A. Let M be the matrix (mᵢⱼ).
Let v be the column of the nⱼ. Then (b·I − M)·v = 0 in B^k.
Multiply by the adjugate of (b·I − M). Since adj(X)·X = det(X)·I over a commutative ring, we get det(b·I − M)·nⱼ = 0 for every j.
The element 1 lies in N, so it is a combination of the nⱼ. Hence det(b·I − M)·1 = 0, that is, det(b·I − M) = 0.
Expand the determinant. It is a monic polynomial of degree k in b with coefficients in A. It is the characteristic polynomial of M. So b is integral over A.

Sums and products. Let a and b be integral, with monic equations of degrees r and s. The A-module N spanned by aⁱbʲ with i < r and j < s is finitely generated and contains 1. It is stable under multiplication by a and by b. So a + b and ab satisfy the hypothesis, and they are integral.

theorem radical_eq_sInf (I : Ideal R) : radical I = sInf { J : Ideal R | I ≤ J ∧ IsPrime J } :=
  le_antisymm (le_sInf fun _ hJ ↦ hJ.2.radical_le_iff.2 hJ.1) fun r hr ↦
    by_contradiction fun hri ↦
      let ⟨m, hIm, hm⟩ :=
        zorn_le_nonempty₀ { K : Ideal R | r ∉ radical K }
          (fun c hc hcc y hyc =>
            ⟨sSup c, fun ⟨n, hrnc⟩ =>
              let ⟨_, hyc, hrny⟩ := (Submodule.mem_sSup_of_directed ⟨y, hyc⟩ hcc.directedOn).1 hrnc
              hc hyc ⟨n, hrny⟩,
              fun _ => le_sSup⟩)
          I hri
      have hrm : r ∉ radical m := hm.prop
      have : ∀ x ∉ m, r ∈ radical (m ⊔ span {x}) := fun x hxm =>
        by_contradiction fun hrmx => hxm <| by
          rw [hm.eq_of_le hrmx le_sup_left]
          exact Submodule.mem_sup_right <| mem_span_singleton_self x
      have : IsPrime m :=
        ⟨by rintro rfl; rw [radical_top] at hrm; exact hrm trivial, fun {x y} hxym =>
          or_iff_not_imp_left.2 fun hxm =>
            by_contradiction fun hym =>
              let ⟨n, hrn⟩ := this _ hxm
              let ⟨p, hpm, q, hq, hpqrn⟩ := Submodule.mem_sup.1 hrn
              let ⟨c, hcxq⟩ := mem_span_singleton'.1 hq
              let ⟨k, hrk⟩ := this _ hym
              let ⟨f, hfm, g, hg, hfgrk⟩ := Submodule.mem_sup.1 hrk
              let ⟨d, hdyg⟩ := mem_span_singleton'.1 hg
              hrm
                ⟨n + k, by
                  rw [pow_add, ← hpqrn, ← hcxq, ← hfgrk, ← hdyg, add_mul, mul_add (c * x),
                      mul_assoc c x (d * y), mul_left_comm x, ← mul_assoc]
                  refine
                    m.add_mem (m.mul_mem_right _ hpm)
                    (m.add_mem (m.mul_mem_left _ hfm) (m.mul_mem_left _ hxym))⟩⟩
    hrm <|
      this.radical.symm ▸ (sInf_le ⟨hIm, this⟩ : sInf { J : Ideal R | I ≤ J ∧ IsPrime J } ≤ m) hr

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: A nilpotent element lies in every prime ideal. If xⁿ = 0 is in P, then x is in P by repeated use of primality.
Now suppose x is not nilpotent. Let S = {x, x², x³,…}. Then 0 is not in S.
Let Σ be the set of ideals that do not meet S. It is nonempty, because (0) is in it. Order it by inclusion.
A union of a chain of ideals in Σ is an ideal in Σ. By Zorn lemma, Σ has a maximal element P.
We show that P is prime. First, P is proper, because 1 is not in P when x is not in P. Suppose a and b are not in P.
Then P + (a) and P + (b) are bigger than P, so they meet S. We get xᵐ = p + ra and xᵏ = q + sb with p, q in P.
Multiply: xᵐ⁺ᵏ is in P + (ab). If ab were in P, then xᵐ⁺ᵏ would be in P, which contradicts P ∩ S = ∅. So ab is not in P, and P is prime.
Since x is not in P, x is not in the intersection of all primes. So the intersection is contained in the nilradical. For the general form, apply the result to R/I.

results.name: Euler criterion for trails and circuits through all edges
results.statement: Let G be a finite simple graph with at least one edge, such that all vertices of positive degree lie in one connected component. (a) G has a closed trail that uses every edge exactly once, an Euler circuit, if and only if every vertex has even degree. (b) For vertices u≠v, G has a trail from u to v that uses every edge exactly once if and only if u and v are the only vertices of odd degree. In particular, if G has any Euler trail, then the number of vertices of odd degree is 0 or 2.
hypotheses: A trail is a walk with no repeated edge. Vertices may repeat.
Isolated vertices are allowed. They do not affect the criterion.
The graph is simple and finite. For multigraphs the same proof works with edges counted with multiplicity.

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Counting lemma. Let W=(x0,e1,x1,…,ek,xk) be a trail and w a vertex. The number of edges of W at w equals 2·#{i : 0<i<k, xi=w} plus the number of ends of W that are equal to w. Each inner visit to w uses the two distinct edges ei and ei+1. The start x0 uses only e1, and the end xk uses only ek. No edge is counted twice because W has no repeated edge and G has no loops.

Necessity. Let W be an Euler trail. Then the edges of W at w are all the edges at w, so deg(w) is given by the lemma. If W is closed, both ends equal x0, so deg(x0)=2·(inner visits)+2 is even, and every other degree is even. If W is open from u to v, then deg(u) and deg(v) are odd, and every other degree is even. This proves the "only if" parts of (a) and (b). It also proves the last sentence.

Sufficiency in (a): the trail is closed. Assume all degrees are even. Let W be a trail of maximum length. The number of trails is finite, so W exists. G has an edge, so W has length at least 1. Let W go from a to b. Suppose a≠b. By the lemma the number of edges of W at b is odd, but deg(b) is even. So some edge at b is not in W. Appending it gives a longer trail. This is a contradiction, so a=b and W is closed.

Sufficiency in (a): the trail uses every edge. Suppose some edge e is not in W. All vertices of positive degree lie in one component. So there is a walk from a to an endpoint of e. Append e to this walk. The new walk has at least one edge not in W. Let f be the first such edge. Its first vertex x is a, or the end of an earlier edge that is in W. So x lies on W, and f is an unused edge at x.

Rotate W to start at x. A closed trail through x=xi can be rewritten as xi,…,xk=x0,…,xi. It has the same edges. Appending f gives a closed-then-open trail that is longer than W. This contradicts the maximality of W. So W uses every edge, and W is an Euler circuit.

Sufficiency in (b). Let u≠v be the only vertices of odd degree. Add a new vertex z and the edges zu and zv. In the new graph G′ the degrees of u and v are even, deg(z)=2, and all other degrees are unchanged. So all degrees are even. All vertices of positive degree are still in one component, because z is joined to u. By (a), G′ has an Euler circuit. Rotate it to start at z. Its first and last edges are zu and zv in some order. Reverse the circuit if needed so that it starts with zu. Delete z and these two edges. What remains is a trail from u to v that uses every edge of G exactly once.

worked_application.title: Which small graphs have an Euler trail?
worked_application.goal: Decide for K5, K4, the 3×3 grid graph and the house graph whether an Euler circuit or an Euler trail exists. Give the trail when it exists.
hypotheses: K5 and K4 are complete graphs.
The 3×3 grid graph has 9 vertices at the points of a 3×3 grid, joined to horizontal and vertical neighbors. It has 12 edges.
The house graph has a square 0,1,2,3 with edges 01, 12, 23, 30, and a roof vertex 4 with edges 04 and 14.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: Each graph is finite, simple and connected. So the criterion decides the question from the degrees alone.

steps.text: K5: every vertex has degree 4, which is even. By (a) an Euler circuit exists. The circuit 0,4,3,2,4,1,3,0,2,1,0 uses 10 distinct edges. K5 has 10 edges, so it uses all of them.
K4: every vertex has degree 3. There are 4 vertices of odd degree, which is neither 0 nor 2. By the last sentence of the statement, K4 has no Euler trail.
The 3×3 grid: the 4 corners have degree 2, the 4 edge midpoints have degree 3, and the center has degree 4. There are 4 vertices of odd degree. So no Euler trail exists.
The house graph: the degrees are 3 for vertices 0 and 1, and 2 for vertices 2, 3 and 4. The only odd vertices are 0 and 1. By (b) there is an Euler trail from 0 to 1.
Such a trail is 0,4,1,2,3,0,1. Its edges are 04, 41, 12, 23, 30, 01. They are 6 distinct edges, and the house graph has 6 edges. The trail starts at 0 and ends at 1, as (b) requires.
The proof is also an algorithm: take any closed trail, find an unused edge at a vertex of the trail, and splice a new closed trail into it. This is Hierholzer’s method. It found the trails above.

worked_application.result: K5 has an Euler circuit. The house graph has an Euler trail from 0 to 1. K4 and the 3×3 grid have no Euler trail, because each has 4 vertices of odd degree.

results.name: The kernel of the graph Laplacian counts connected components
results.statement: Let G be a finite simple graph on the vertex set V, with adjacency matrix A and degree matrix D. Let L=D−A be the Laplacian. Then for every x∈ℝ^V, xᵀLx=∑_{uv∈E}(x_u−x_v)², where the sum runs over the edges. Hence L is positive semidefinite, and Lx=0 if and only if x is constant on each connected component of G. The dimension of ker L is the number of connected components of G. In particular G is connected if and only if rank L=|V|−1, and the eigenvalue 0 of L has multiplicity equal to the number of components.
hypotheses: G is a finite simple graph. Loops and repeated edges are not allowed.
Vectors are real. The statement over other ordered fields needs only the quadratic identity.
The multiplicity of the eigenvalue 0 is the multiplicity as a root of the characteristic polynomial.

prerequisites.reason: Step 6 uses the spectral theorem to equate algebraic and geometric multiplicity.

results.proof_status: source declaration inspected; authored proof awaits inference review; no local Lean check

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Quadratic form. First, xᵀDx=∑_v d(v)x_v². Each edge uv adds x_u² to the term of u and x_v² to the term of v. So xᵀDx=∑_{uv∈E}(x_u²+x_v²). Next, xᵀAx=∑_{(u,v) adjacent} x_u x_v. Each edge appears twice as an ordered pair, so xᵀAx=2∑_{uv∈E} x_u x_v. Subtract: xᵀLx=∑_{uv∈E}(x_u²−2x_ux_v+x_v²)=∑_{uv∈E}(x_u−x_v)².
Positive semidefinite. By step 1, xᵀLx is a sum of squares, so it is not negative. L is symmetric because A and D are symmetric.
If Lx=0, then xᵀLx=0. By step 1 every term (x_u−x_v)² is 0, so x_u=x_v for every edge uv. Along any walk the value of x does not change. So x is constant on each connected component.
Conversely, let x be constant on each component. For a vertex v, (Lx)_v=d(v)x_v−∑_{w∼v}x_w=∑_{w∼v}(x_v−x_w). Each neighbor w of v lies in the component of v, so x_w=x_v. The sum is 0. Hence Lx=0.

By steps 3 and 4, ker L is the set of vectors constant on each component. This space is spanned by the indicators 1_C. They have disjoint supports and are nonzero, so they are linearly independent. Every vector x constant on components equals ∑_C x_C·1_C. Hence dim ker L equals the number c of components, and rank L=|V|−c by rank-nullity.

L is real symmetric, so by the spectral theorem it has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors. For a symmetric matrix the multiplicity of the eigenvalue 0 as a root of the characteristic polynomial equals dim ker L. So the eigenvalue 0 has multiplicity c.
The case c=1 gives the last claim: G is connected if and only if dim ker L=1, which holds if and only if rank L=|V|−1.

steps.text: The degrees are 1,2,2,1 on the path, 2,2,2 on the triangle and 0 on vertex 7. The trace of L is 12, which equals 2·6, twice the edge count.
Exact elimination gives rank L=5. The nullity is 8−5=3. This equals the number of components: the path, the triangle and the isolated vertex.
The three indicators 1_{0,1,2,3}, 1_{4,5,6} and 1_{7} satisfy L·1_C=0. A direct multiplication confirms it.

Quadratic form at x=(3,1,4,1,5,9,2,6): the path gives (3−1)²+(1−4)²+(4−1)²=4+9+9=22. The triangle gives (5−9)²+(9−2)²+(5−2)²=16+49+9=74. The isolated vertex gives 0. The total is 96. The matrix product xᵀLx also gives 96.

Spectrum. The path P4 has Laplacian eigenvalues 0, 2−√2, 2 and 2+√2. The triangle has 0, 3 and 3. The isolated vertex has 0. The eigenvalue 0 appears 3 times, as predicted. The sum of all eigenvalues is 6+6+0=12, which equals the trace. A determinant test confirms that each of the four P4 values makes L−λI singular.
Join the pieces with the edges 34 and 67. The graph is now connected, and exact elimination gives rank L=7=8−1. The nullity is 1, as the theorem predicts for a connected graph.

worked_application.result: The nullity of L is 3 for the disjoint union and 1 after the two joining edges. In both cases the nullity equals the number of connected components.

limitations: The result is for the combinatorial Laplacian D−A. The normalized Laplacian has the same kernel dimension, but its kernel vectors are different.
Over a field of positive characteristic, the kernel can be larger, because a sum of squares can vanish without each square vanishing. The proof needs an ordered field.
The count of components says nothing about how well connected each component is. That is the job of the smallest nonzero eigenvalue.

results.name: Parameter identity and spectrum of strongly regular graphs
results.statement: Let G be a finite simple graph with n vertices. Assume G is regular of degree k, any two adjacent vertices have exactly λ common neighbors, and any two distinct non-adjacent vertices have exactly μ common neighbors. Let A be the adjacency matrix, I the identity and J the all-ones matrix. Then (a) A²=kI+λA+μ(J−I−A); (b) k(k−λ−1)=(n−k−1)μ; (c) every eigenvalue θ of A that has an eigenvector orthogonal to the all-ones vector satisfies θ²−(λ−μ)θ−(k−μ)=0.
hypotheses: G is finite and simple.
The three conditions (regular, λ, μ) hold for all vertices and all pairs. G is called SRG(n,k,λ,μ).
For (c) the eigenvector is a real vector orthogonal to the all-ones vector.

prerequisites.reason: Step 5 uses the spectral theorem on the invariant space W.

definitions.name: strongly regular graph
definitions.text: A graph that is k-regular with every adjacent pair having λ common neighbors and every non-adjacent pair having μ common neighbors.

definitions.name: common neighbors
definitions.text: The common neighbors of v and w are the vertices adjacent to both v and w.

/-- The parameters of a strongly regular graph with at least one vertex satisfy
`k * (k - ℓ - 1) = (n - k - 1) * μ`. -/
theorem IsSRGWith.param_eq
    {V : Type u} [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    (h : G.IsSRGWith n k ℓ μ) (hn : 0 < n) :
    k * (k - ℓ - 1) = (n - k - 1) * μ := by
  let := Classical.decEq V
  rw [← h.card, Fintype.card_pos_iff] at hn
  obtain ⟨v⟩ := hn
  convert card_mul_eq_card_mul G.Adj (s := G.neighborFinset v) (t := Gᶜ.neighborFinset v) _ _
  · simp [h.regular v]
  · simp [h.compl.regular v]
  · intro w hw
    rw [mem_neighborFinset] at hw
    simp_rw [bipartiteAbove, ← mem_neighborFinset, filter_mem_eq_inter]
    have s : {v} ⊆ G.neighborFinset w \ G.neighborFinset v := by
      rw [singleton_subset_iff, mem_sdiff, mem_neighborFinset]
      exact ⟨hw.symm, G.notMem_neighborFinset_self v⟩
    rw [inter_comm, neighborFinset_compl, ← inter_sdiff_assoc, ← sdiff_eq_inter_compl,
      card_sdiff_of_subset s, card_singleton, ← sdiff_inter_self_left,
      card_sdiff_of_subset inter_subset_left]
    congr
    · simp [h.regular w]
    · simp_rw [inter_comm, neighborFinset_def, ← Set.toFinset_inter, ← h.of_adj v w hw,
        ← Set.toFinset_card]
      congr!
  · intro w hw
    simp_rw [neighborFinset_compl, mem_sdiff, mem_compl, mem_singleton, mem_neighborFinset,
      ← Ne.eq_def] at hw
    simp_rw [bipartiteBelow, adj_comm, ← mem_neighborFinset, filter_mem_eq_inter,
      neighborFinset_def, ← Set.toFinset_inter, ← h.of_not_adj hw.2.symm hw.1,
      ← Set.toFinset_card]
    congr!

/-- Let `A` and `C` be the adjacency matrices of a strongly regular graph with parameters `n k ℓ μ`
and its complement respectively and `I` be the identity matrix,
then `A ^ 2 = k • I + ℓ • A + μ • C`. `C` is equivalent to the expression `J - I - A`
more often found in the literature, where `J` is the all-ones matrix. -/
theorem IsSRGWith.matrix_eq {α : Type*} [Semiring α] (h : G.IsSRGWith n k ℓ μ) :
    G.adjMatrix α ^ 2 = k • (1 : Matrix V V α) + ℓ • G.adjMatrix α + μ • Gᶜ.adjMatrix α := by
  ext v w
  simp only [adjMatrix_pow_apply_eq_card_walk, Matrix.add_apply, Matrix.smul_apply,
    adjMatrix_apply, compl_adj]
  rw [@Fintype.card_congr _ _ (G.fintypeSetWalkLength v w 2) _
    (G.walkLengthTwoEquivCommonNeighbors v w)]
  obtain rfl | hn := eq_or_ne v w
  · rw [← Set.toFinset_card]
    simp [commonNeighbors, ← neighborFinset_def, h.regular v]
  · simp only [Matrix.one_apply_ne' hn.symm, ne_eq, hn]
    by_cases ha : G.Adj v w <;>
      simp only [ha, ite_true, ite_false, add_zero, zero_add, nsmul_eq_mul, smul_zero, mul_one,
        not_true_eq_false, not_false_eq_true, and_false, and_self]
    · rw [h.of_adj v w ha]
    · rw [h.of_not_adj hn ha]

steps.text: Walks of length 2. The entry (A²)_{vw} is the number of walks v,x,w of length 2. This is the number of common neighbors of v and w. For v=w it is the degree k. For adjacent v,w it is λ. For distinct non-adjacent v,w it is μ.
The matrix J−I−A has entry 1 exactly at the pairs of distinct non-adjacent vertices, and 0 elsewhere. So the three cases of step 1 say A²=kI+λA+μ(J−I−A). This proves (a).

Apply (a) to the all-ones vector 1. We have A1=k1 and J1=n1. So the left side is A²1=k²1. The right side is (k+λk+μ(n−1−k))1. Hence k²=k+λk+μ(n−k−1). Rearranged, this is k(k−λ−1)=μ(n−k−1). This proves (b).
Rewrite (a) as A²−(λ−μ)A−(k−μ)I=μJ. This follows because μ(J−I−A)=μJ−μI−μA.

Let W be the set of vectors orthogonal to 1. For w∈W, 1ᵀ(Aw)=(A1)ᵀw=k·1ᵀw=0, because A is symmetric. So A maps W to W. On W we have Jw=0. A restricted to W is symmetric, so by the spectral theorem W has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors of A.
Let Aw=θw with w∈W and w≠0. Apply the identity of step 4 to w. The left side is (θ²−(λ−μ)θ−(k−μ))w and the right side is μJw=0. So θ²−(λ−μ)θ−(k−μ)=0. This proves (c).

Multiplicities. All eigenvalues of A are k, for the vector 1, together with those on W. Let the two roots of the quadratic be r and s with multiplicities f and g on W. Then f+g=n−1. The trace of A is 0, because G has no loops, so k+fr+gs=0. These two equations determine f and g when r≠s.

worked_application.title: The Petersen graph and the test for SRG(10,4,1,1)
worked_application.goal: Take the Petersen graph: the vertices are the 2-subsets of {0,1,2,3,4}, and two vertices are adjacent when the subsets are disjoint. Check (a), (b) and find the spectrum. Then test other parameter sets.
hypotheses: n=10. Each vertex has 3 neighbors: the 2-subsets of the 3 remaining numbers.
Two adjacent vertices share no neighbor: λ=0. Two non-adjacent vertices (subsets that meet in one number) share exactly one neighbor: μ=1.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The graph is regular of degree k=3 with λ=0 and μ=1, so it is SRG(10,3,0,1). The theorem applies.

steps.text: Identity (b): k(k−λ−1)=3·(3−0−1)=6 and (n−k−1)μ=(10−3−1)·1=6. The two sides agree.
Identity (a): a direct matrix computation gives A²=3I+0·A+1·(J−I−A) for the 10×10 matrix A. The trace of A² is 30, which equals 10·3, the sum of the degrees.
Spectrum: the quadratic is θ²−(0−1)θ−(3−1)=θ²+θ−2=(θ−1)(θ+2). The roots are r=1 and s=−2.
Multiplicities: f+g=9 and 3+f−2g=0. Substitute f=9−g. Then 3+9−g−2g=0, so g=4 and f=5. The spectrum of the Petersen graph is 3 with multiplicity 1, 1 with multiplicity 5, and −2 with multiplicity 4.
A rank computation confirms it: the nullity of A−I is 5, the nullity of A+2I is 4 and the nullity of A−3I is 1.

Other parameter sets. For (10,4,1,1) we get 4·(4−1−1)=8 on the left and (10−4−1)·1=5 on the right. They differ, so no SRG(10,4,1,1) exists. For (50,7,0,1) we get 7·6=42 and 42·1=42. For (15,6,1,3) we get 6·4=24 and 8·3=24. For (9,4,1,2) we get 4·2=8 and 4·2=8. These pass the test.

worked_application.result: The Petersen graph satisfies A²+A−2I=J with eigenvalues 3, 1, −2 of multiplicities 1, 5, 4. No SRG(10,4,1,1) exists.

limitations: Identity (b) is necessary and not sufficient. Parameter sets that pass it can still fail integrality of the multiplicities or other conditions.
The spectrum part needs the quadratic to have two different roots. If k=μ, then the quadratic has the root 0 twice only in degenerate cases such as complete multipartite graphs.
The Mathlib source covers (a) and (b). Part (c) and the multiplicity argument are authored here.

/-- An integer Hadamard matrix of order greater than two has order divisible by four.

This is the standard divisibility obstruction in [Section 2.3][deLauneyFlannery2011]. -/
theorem IsHadamard.four_dvd_card {A : Matrix n n ℤ}
    (hA : A.IsHadamard) (hcard : 2 < Fintype.card n) : 4 ∣ Fintype.card n := by
  have hpm : ∀ i j, A i j = 1 ∨ A i j = -1 := fun i j =>
    Unitary.mem_iff_eq_one_or_eq_neg_one.mp (hA.apply_mem i j)
  obtain ⟨r, s, t, hrs, hrt, hst⟩ := Fintype.two_lt_card_iff.mp hcard
  have horth ⦃i k : n⦄ (hik : i ≠ k) : ∑ j, A i j * A k j = 0 := by
    simpa [Matrix.mul_apply, hik] using congr($hA.mul_conjTranspose i k)
  have hexpand : ∀ j, (1 + A s j * A r j) * (1 + A t j * A r j) =
      1 + A s j * A r j + A t j * A r j + A s j * A t j := fun j => by
    obtain hr | hr := hpm r j <;> simp [hr] <;> ring
  have hdvd : ∀ j, (4 : ℤ) ∣ (1 + A s j * A r j) * (1 + A t j * A r j) := fun j => by
    obtain hs | hs := hpm s j <;> obtain hr | hr := hpm r j <;>
      obtain ht | ht := hpm t j <;> simp [hs, hr, ht]
  have hsum : ∑ j, (1 + A s j * A r j) * (1 + A t j * A r j) = (Fintype.card n : ℤ) := by
    simp_rw [hexpand]
    simp [Finset.sum_add_distrib, horth hrs.symm, horth hrt.symm, horth hst]
  rw [← Int.ofNat_dvd, ← hsum]
  exact Finset.dvd_sum fun j _ => hdvd j

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Normalization. Multiply column j by −1 if the first entry of the first row in column j is −1. This changes no product of two rows, because each column enters the product with a square factor. After this step, the first row has only entries equal to 1.
Row sums. Every other row is orthogonal to the first row. So its entries add up to 0. Hence each other row has the same number of entries 1 and −1. This shows that n is even.

Choose three different rows r1 (the first row), r2 and r3. Such rows exist because n>2. Sort the columns into four classes by the pair (r2 entry, r3 entry). Let a, b, c, d be the sizes of the classes (+,+), (+,−), (−,+), (−,−). Then a+b+c+d=n.
Row r2 has zero sum, so a+b=c+d. Row r3 has zero sum, so a+c=b+d. The rows r2 and r3 are orthogonal, so a+d=b+c. These are the three equations of the proof.
Subtract the second equation from the first. We get b−c=c−b, so b=c. Then the second equation gives a=d. The third equation now reads 2a=2b, so a=b. All four class sizes are equal.
Hence n=a+b+c+d=4a. So n is divisible by 4.

worked_application.title: Which orders up to 12 admit a Hadamard matrix?
worked_application.goal: Use the theorem to rule out orders. Then build a Hadamard matrix of order 12 from the quadratic residues modulo 11. Check it by exact multiplication.
hypotheses: The orders are n=1,…,12.
Q is the 11×11 matrix with entry χ(i−j), where χ(x) is 1 for a nonzero square mod 11, −1 for a non-square, and 0 for x=0.
The squares mod 11 are 1, 3, 4, 5, 9.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The theorem excludes every order above 2 that is not divisible by 4. So only n=1, 2, 4, 8, 12 can occur up to 12.

steps.text: Orders 3, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10 and 11 are not divisible by 4 and are above 2. By the theorem, none of them admits a Hadamard matrix.

Order 4 and order 8 exist. The Kronecker product of [[1,1],[1,−1]] with itself gives order 4. A third factor gives order 8. A direct check of all 28 pairs of rows of the order-8 matrix gives inner product 0.
Order 12 is divisible by 4, so the theorem does not exclude it. Build the matrix S with S[0][j]=1 and S[j][0]=−1 for j≥1, S[0][0]=0, and S[i+1][j+1]=χ(i−j) for i, j in 0,…,10. Put H=I+S.
Since 11≡3 (mod 4), χ(−1)=−1. Hence Q is skew-symmetric, and S is skew-symmetric. So H has entries 1 and −1 only: the diagonal of S is 0, and every other entry of S is 1 or −1.
Exact integer computation of HHᵀ for all 144 entries gives 12 on the diagonal and 0 off the diagonal. So H is a Hadamard matrix of order 12.
Therefore the orders up to 12 that occur are exactly 1, 2, 4, 8 and 12. Order 12 is the first case where divisibility by 4 holds and a direct power-of-two construction does not give the matrix.

worked_application.result: No Hadamard matrix exists for the orders 3, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10 and 11. Orders 1, 2, 4, 8 and 12 occur. The order-12 matrix built from the squares mod 11 passes the check HHᵀ=12I.

limitations: The converse is open. It is the Hadamard conjecture: a Hadamard matrix of order 4k exists for every k. Order 668 is the smallest unresolved case.
The first proof step assumes real or integer entries. For complex Hadamard matrices the argument does not apply.
The Mathlib statement is for integer matrices with entries 1 or −1.

results.statement: Let F be a field. Let f∈F[x1,…,xn] have total degree t1+…+tn. Assume the coefficient of the monomial x1^{t1}⋯xn^{tn} in f is not 0. Let S1,…,Sn be finite subsets of F with |Si|>ti for all i. Then there is a point s=(s1,…,sn) in S1×⋯×Sn with f(s)≠0.

/-- The **Combinatorial Nullstellensatz**.

Given a multi-index `t : σ →₀ ℕ` such that `t s < (S s).card` for all `s`,
`f.totalDegree = t.degree` and `f.coeff t ≠ 0`,
there exists a point `x : σ → R` such that `x s ∈ S s` for all `s` and `f.eval s ≠ 0`.

[Alon_1999], theorem 2 -/
theorem combinatorial_nullstellensatz_exists_eval_nonzero [IsDomain R]
    (f : MvPolynomial σ R)
    (t : σ →₀ ℕ) (ht : f.coeff t ≠ 0) (ht' : f.totalDegree = t.degree)
    (S : σ → Finset R) (htS : ∀ i, t i < #(S i)) :
    ∃ s : σ → R, (∀ i, s i ∈ S i) ∧ eval s f ≠ 0 := by
  let _ : LinearOrder σ := WellOrderingRel.isWellOrder.linearOrder
  by_contra! Heval
  apply ht
  obtain ⟨h, hh, hf⟩ := combinatorial_nullstellensatz_exists_linearCombination S
    (fun i ↦ by rw [← Finset.card_pos]; exact Nat.zero_lt_of_lt (htS i)) f Heval
  rw [hf]
  rw [linearCombination_apply, Finsupp.sum, coeff_sum]
  apply Finset.sum_eq_zero
  intro i _
  set g := h i * Alon.P (S i) i with hg
  by_cases hi : h i = 0
  · simp [hi]
  have : g.totalDegree ≤ f.totalDegree := by
    rw [hg, mul_comm]
    exact hh i
  -- one could simplify this by proving `totalDegree_mul_eq` (at least in a domain)
  rw [hg, ← degree_degLexDegree,
    degree_mul_of_isRegular_right hi (by simp only [(Alon.monic_P ..).leadingCoeff_eq_one,
      isRegular_one]),
    Alon.degree_P, map_add, degree_degLexDegree, degree_single, ht'] at this
  rw [smul_eq_mul, coeff_mul, Finset.sum_eq_zero]
  rintro ⟨p, q⟩ hpq
  simp only [Finset.mem_antidiagonal] at hpq
  simp only [mul_eq_zero, Classical.or_iff_not_imp_right]
  rw [← ne_eq, ← mem_support_iff]
  intro hq
  obtain ⟨e, hq', hq⟩ := Alon.of_mem_P_support _ _ _ hq
  apply coeff_eq_zero_of_totalDegree_lt
  rw [← Finsupp.degree_apply]
  apply lt_of_add_lt_add_right (lt_of_le_of_lt this _)
  rw [← hpq, map_add, add_lt_add_iff_left, hq, degree_single]
  apply lt_of_le_of_lt _ (htS i)
  simp [← hpq, hq]

/-- The **Combinatorial Nullstellensatz**.

If `f` vanishes at every point `x : σ → R` such that `x s ∈ S s` for all `s`,
then it can be written as a linear combination
`f = linearCombination (MvPolynomial σ R) (fun i ↦ (∏ r ∈ S i, (X i - C r))) h`,
for some `h : σ →₀ MvPolynomial σ R` such that
`((∏ r ∈ S s, (X i - C r)) * h i).totalDegree ≤ f.totalDegree` for all `s`.

[Alon_1999], theorem 1. -/
theorem combinatorial_nullstellensatz_exists_linearCombination
    [IsDomain R] (S : σ → Finset R) (Sne : ∀ i, (S i).Nonempty)
    (f : MvPolynomial σ R) (Heval : ∀ (x : σ → R), (∀ i, x i ∈ S i) → eval x f = 0) :
    ∃ (h : σ →₀ MvPolynomial σ R),
      (∀ i, ((∏ s ∈ S i, (X i - C s)) * h i).totalDegree ≤ f.totalDegree) ∧
      f = linearCombination (MvPolynomial σ R) (fun i ↦ ∏ r ∈ S i, (X i - C r)) h := by
  let : LinearOrder σ := WellOrderingRel.isWellOrder.linearOrder
  obtain ⟨h, r, hf, hh, hr⟩ := degLex.div (b := fun i ↦ Alon.P (S i) i)
      (fun i ↦ by simp only [(Alon.monic_P ..).leadingCoeff_eq_one, isUnit_one]) f
  use h
  suffices r = 0 by
    rw [this, add_zero] at hf
    exact ⟨fun i ↦ degLex_totalDegree_monotone (hh i), hf⟩
  apply eq_zero_of_eval_zero_at_prod_finset r S
  · intro i
    rw [degreeOf_eq_sup, Finset.sup_lt_iff (by simp [Sne i])]
    aesop (add simp [Alon.degree_P])
  · intro x hx
    rw [Iff.symm sub_eq_iff_eq_add'] at hf
    rw [← hf, map_sub, Heval x hx, zero_sub, neg_eq_zero,
      linearCombination_apply, map_finsuppSum, Finsupp.sum, Finset.sum_eq_zero]
    intro i _
    rw [smul_eq_mul, map_mul]
    convert mul_zero _
    rw [Alon.P, _root_.map_prod]
    apply Finset.prod_eq_zero (hx i)
    simp

/-- A multivariate polynomial that vanishes on a large product finset is the zero polynomial. -/
theorem eq_zero_of_eval_zero_at_prod_finset {σ : Type*} [Finite σ] [IsDomain R]
    (P : MvPolynomial σ R) (S : σ → Finset R)
    (Hdeg : ∀ i, P.degreeOf i < #(S i))
    (Heval : ∀ (x : σ → R), (∀ i, x i ∈ S i) → eval x P = 0) :
    P = 0 := by
  induction σ using Finite.induction_empty_option with
  | @of_equiv σ τ e h =>
    suffices MvPolynomial.rename e.symm P = 0 by
      have that := MvPolynomial.rename_injective (R := R) e.symm (e.symm.injective)

steps.text: Reduce to |Si|=ti+1. Replace each Si by a subset of size ti+1. A point found in the smaller grid lies in the larger grid. So assume |Si|=ti+1 for all i.
Define gi(xi)=∏_{s∈Si}(xi−s). It is monic of degree ti+1 and it vanishes on Si. Suppose, for contradiction, that f vanishes at every point of the grid.

Division. Divide f by g1 in the variable x1: f=h1g1+f1, where f1 has degree at most t1 in x1. Do the same for x2, …, xn, one after the other. The result is f=Σ hi gi + r, where r has degree at most ti in xi for every i. Each division keeps the total degree at most deg f, and the quotient hi has total degree at most deg f−(ti+1).

The coefficient is unchanged. The part of degree t1+…+tn in the product hi gi is (top part of hi)·xi^{ti+1}. Every monomial in it has xi exponent at least ti+1. The target monomial x^t has xi exponent ti. So it does not occur in hi gi. Hence r has the same coefficient at x^t as f, and this coefficient is not 0.
Vanishing. At each grid point, f is 0 by assumption, and each gi is 0. So r is 0 at each grid point.

Zero lemma. A polynomial r with degree at most ti in xi, and with ti<|Si|, that vanishes on S1×⋯×Sn, is the zero polynomial. Proof by induction on n. Write r=Σ_k ck(x1,…,x_{n−1}) xn^k with k≤tn. For a fixed point of the smaller grid, the one-variable polynomial in xn has degree at most tn and at least tn+1 roots. So it is 0. Hence each ck vanishes on the smaller grid. By induction each ck=0.
By steps 5 and 6, r=0. This contradicts step 4, where the coefficient of x^t in r is nonzero. Hence f does not vanish on the whole grid.

worked_application.title: Cauchy-Davenport over a prime field
worked_application.goal: Show that for sets A, B in Z/p with A+B the set of sums, |A+B| is at least min(p, |A|+|B|−1). Check the claim for three explicit pairs of sets.
hypotheses: p is prime. F=Z/p.
Let a=|A| and b=|B|. Assume a+b−1≤p, since otherwise the bound is p.
Suppose |A+B|≤a+b−2. Take C⊇A+B with |C|=a+b−2. This needs a+b−2≤p.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The polynomial f(x,y)=∏_{c∈C}(x+y−c) vanishes on A×B and has degree a+b−2. Its top monomial coefficient is a binomial. The theorem gives a contradiction when this binomial is nonzero mod p.

steps.text: f has total degree m=a+b−2, because each factor has degree 1. Its top part is (x+y)^m.
Let t1=a−1 and t2=b−1. Then t1+t2=m. The coefficient of x^{a−1}y^{b−1} in (x+y)^m is the binomial coefficient C(m, a−1).
Since m=a+b−2<p, the number C(m, a−1) has no factor p. So it is nonzero in Z/p.
Take S1=A and S2=B. Then |S1|=a>t1 and |S2|=b>t2. The theorem gives (x,y) in A×B with f(x,y)≠0. But x+y∈A+B⊆C, so one factor is 0. This is a contradiction. Hence |A+B|≥a+b−1.
Check 1: p=11, A={0,1,3}, B={0,2,3,7}. Here A+B has 10 elements, and the bound is min(11, 6)=6. The claim holds. The coefficient C(5,2)=10 is nonzero mod 11.
Check 2: p=11, A={0,1,2}, B={0,1,2,3}. Then A+B={0,1,2,3,4,5}, which has 6 elements. This equals the bound a+b−1=6. So the bound is sharp for arithmetic progressions.
Check 3: p=5, A={0,1,2}, B={0,1,2,3}. Here a+b−1=6>5. The proof does not apply, since C(5,2)=10 is 0 mod 5. The true size is |A+B|=5=p, which agrees with min(p, a+b−1).

worked_application.result: The three checks give |A+B|=10, 6 and 5. These are at least 6, 6 and 5, as the Cauchy-Davenport bound states. The bound is sharp for arithmetic progressions.

results.name: The gauge of a convex absorbing set is sublinear
results.statement: Let C be a convex subset of a real vector space E. Assume 0∈C and C is absorbing: for each x there is r>0 with x∈rC. Define the gauge g(x)=inf{r>0 : x∈rC}. Then (a) 0≤g(x)<∞ for all x; (b) g(tx)=t·g(x) for t≥0; (c) g(x+y)≤g(x)+g(y); (d) {g<1}⊆C⊆{g≤1}. If C is also balanced (for |s|≤1, sC⊆C), then g is a seminorm.
hypotheses: E is a real vector space with no topology.
C is convex, contains 0, and is absorbing.
For the seminorm claim, C is also balanced.

/-- Gauge is subadditive. -/
theorem gauge_add_le (hs : Convex ℝ s) (absorbs : Absorbent ℝ s) (x y : E) :
    gauge s (x + y) ≤ gauge s x + gauge s y := by
  refine le_of_forall_pos_lt_add fun ε hε => ?_
  obtain ⟨a, ha, ha', x, hx, rfl⟩ :=
    exists_lt_of_gauge_lt absorbs (lt_add_of_pos_right (gauge s x) (half_pos hε))
  obtain ⟨b, hb, hb', y, hy, rfl⟩ :=
    exists_lt_of_gauge_lt absorbs (lt_add_of_pos_right (gauge s y) (half_pos hε))
  calc
    gauge s (a • x + b • y) ≤ a + b := gauge_le_of_mem (by positivity) <| by
      rw [hs.add_smul ha.le hb.le]
      exact add_mem_add (smul_mem_smul_set hx) (smul_mem_smul_set hy)
    _ < gauge s (a • x) + gauge s (b • y) + ε := by linarith

steps.text: Monotone scaling. If x∈aC and a<a′, then x∈a′C. Proof: a⁻¹x∈C. Then a′⁻¹x=(a/a′)(a⁻¹x)+(1−a/a′)·0 is a convex combination of two points of C. So a′⁻¹x∈C.
Part (a). Because C is absorbing, the set {r>0 : x∈rC} is not empty, so g(x) is finite. It consists of positive numbers, so g(x)≥0.
Part (b). For t>0, tx∈rC if and only if x∈(r/t)C. So {r : tx∈rC}=t·{r : x∈rC}, and g(tx)=t·g(x). For t=0: 0∈rC for all r>0, because 0∈C. So g(0)=0.

Part (c). Let a>g(x) and b>g(y). By step 1, x∈aC and y∈bC. Write x+y=(a+b)[(a/(a+b))·(x/a)+(b/(a+b))·(y/b)]. The point in square brackets is a convex combination of two points of C, so it lies in C. Hence x+y∈(a+b)C and g(x+y)≤a+b.
Let a decrease to g(x) and b decrease to g(y). We get g(x+y)≤g(x)+g(y).
Part (d). If g(x)<1, there is r<1 with x∈rC. By step 1, x∈1·C=C. If x∈C, then 1 belongs to the set {r : x∈rC}, so g(x)≤1.
Balanced case. If |s|=1, then sC⊆C and s⁻¹C⊆C, so sC=C. Then g(sx)=g(x). With part (b) this gives g(sx)=|s|·g(x) for all real s. Together with part (c), g is a seminorm.

worked_application.goal: Let C be the triangle with vertices (−1,−1), (2,−1), (−1,2) in the plane. Compute g exactly. Check the three properties on test points and on random rational points.
hypotheses: The origin is inside C. C is convex and absorbing.

steps.text: A point v=(x,y) lies in rC if and only if x≥−r, y≥−r and x+y≤r. The smallest such r is g(v)=max(0, −x, −y, x+y).
Asymmetry: g(1,1)=2 but g(−1,−1)=1. So g(−v)≠g(v) and g is not a seminorm. This agrees with C not being balanced.

Part (d): the vertex (2,−1) has g=1, and (−1,1/2) has g=1. They lie on the boundary of C. A point inside, such as (1/2,1/2), has g=1 and also lies on the edge x+y=1. A point such as (0,0) has g=0<1 and lies in C.
Subadditivity example: v=(1,1), w=(−3,0). Then g(v)=2, g(w)=3, and v+w=(−2,1) has g=2. We have 2≤2+3.
Random test: 20000 pairs of rational points with exact arithmetic satisfy g(v+w)≤g(v)+g(w). The same number of tests satisfy g(tv)=t·g(v) for t≥0.

worked_application.result: The gauge of the triangle is g(x,y)=max(0,−x,−y,x+y). It is sublinear, equal to 1 on the boundary of C, and not symmetric. All tests pass.

results.name: Birkhoff-von Neumann theorem
results.statement: Let M be an n×n real matrix with nonnegative entries and with every row sum and every column sum equal to 1. Then M is a convex combination of permutation matrices: M=Σ θk Pσk with θk>0 and Σθk=1. Conversely, every such convex combination is doubly stochastic. /--
**Birkhoff's theorem**
The set of doubly stochastic matrices is the convex hull of the permutation matrices.  Note
`exists_eq_sum_perm_of_mem_doublyStochastic` gives a convex weighting of each permutation matrix
directly.  To show `doublyStochastic n` is convex, use `convex_doublyStochastic`.
-/
theorem doublyStochastic_eq_convexHull_permMatrix :
    doublyStochastic R n = convexHull R {σ.permMatrix R | σ : Equiv.Perm n} := by
  refine (convexHull_min ?g1 convex_doublyStochastic).antisymm' fun M hM => ?g2
  case g1 =>
    rintro x ⟨h, rfl⟩
    exact permMatrix_mem_doublyStochastic
  case g2 =>

    exact mem_convexHull_of_exists_fintype w (·.permMatrix R) hw1 hw2 (by simp) hw3

steps.text: Converse. A permutation matrix has one entry 1 in each row and column, so it is doubly stochastic. A convex combination of nonnegative matrices with all row and column sums 1 is nonnegative with all row and column sums Σθk=1.
Plan. Induction on the number N of positive entries of M. Each row has a positive entry, so N≥n. We show that M is a convex combination of permutation matrices.

Hall condition on the support. Make a bipartite graph with rows on one side and columns on the other. Join row i to column j if Mij>0. Let R be a set of rows and N(R) the set of columns joined to a row of R. The entries of the rows in R add up to |R|, and all of them lie in columns of N(R). So |R|=Σ_{i∈R,j∈N(R)}Mij≤Σ_{j∈N(R)}Σ_i Mij=|N(R)|. Thus |N(R)|≥|R| for every R. By Hall’s marriage theorem there is a perfect matching: a permutation σ with Mi,σ(i)>0 for all i.
Peeling. Let θ=min_i Mi,σ(i)>0 and let P be the permutation matrix of σ. If θ=1, then each row i has Mi,σ(i)=1. The row sum is 1, so all other entries of row i are 0. So M=P and we are done.

If θ<1, define M′=(M−θP)/(1−θ). The entries of M−θP are not negative, because we subtract θ only at the positions (i,σ(i)) and θ is at most the entry there. Each row sum and column sum of M−θP is 1−θ. So M′ is doubly stochastic.

M′ has fewer positive entries than M. The position (i,σ(i)) where the minimum is attained is positive in M and zero in M′. Entries that are zero in M stay zero in M′. By the induction hypothesis M′ is a convex combination of permutation matrices. Then M=θP+(1−θ)M′ is also one. This proves the first claim.

Extreme points. A permutation matrix P is extreme: if P=tA+(1−t)B with 0<t<1 and A, B doubly stochastic, then at a position where P is 0, both A and B are 0 since entries are nonnegative. At a position where P is 1, both entries are at most 1 and their weighted mean is 1, so both are 1. So A=B=P. Conversely, an extreme point M is a convex combination of permutation matrices, so it equals one of them.

steps.text: Inverse. The inverse of I+cEij is I−cEij. So the set of products of transvections is closed under inverse, and the claim M=L D R is the same as L⁻¹ M R⁻¹=D.
Induction on n. For n=1, M is already diagonal. Let n≥2 and M≠0. We show that row and column operations by transvections turn M into diag(p, N) with p≠0 and N of size n−1.
Make the corner nonzero. Choose Mij≠0. If M1j=0, add row i to row 1 (this needs i≠1, and if i=1 then M1j≠0 already). Now M1j≠0. If M11=0 and j≠1, add column j to column 1. Now M11≠0. Call it p.
Clear the first column. Let p=M11≠0. For each i>1 add −(Mi1/p) times row 1 to row i. These are transvections and they give zeros in column 1 below p.
Clear the first row. For each j>1 add −(M1j/p) times column 1 to column j. This does not change column 1, which is now (p,0,…,0). The first row becomes (p,0,…,0). The result is diag(p, N).

Induction. N is an (n−1)×(n−1) matrix, so N=L′D′R′ with transvections in dimension n−1. A transvection of size n−1 extends to a transvection of size n by adding a 1 on the first diagonal position. Hence diag(p,N)=diag(1,L′)·diag(p,D′)·diag(1,R′), and diag(p,D′) is diagonal. Combining with step 2 gives M=L D R. If M=0, take D=0 and empty lists.

Invertible case. Let w(a)=T12(a)·T21(−a⁻¹)·T12(a). A product of the three matrices gives w(a)=[[0,a],[−a⁻¹,0]]. Then w(a)·w(−1)=diag(a,a⁻¹), so diag(a,a⁻¹) is a product of six transvections. Also diag(a,b)=diag(a,a⁻¹)·diag(1,ab). Let M be invertible. Then every di is not 0 and det D=det M, because transvections have determinant 1. Apply the identity to the pairs (d1,d2), then (d1d2,d3), and so on. We get D=Q·diag(1,…,1,d1⋯dn), where Q is a product of transvections. Hence M=L·Q·diag(1,…,1,det M)·R.
SL_n. If det M=1, then D=diag(1,…,1,1)=I, so M is a product of transvections.

Step 2. Subtract 2 times row 1 from row 3. Row 3 becomes (0,−8,−5). The first column is now (1,0,0).
Step 3. Subtract 5 times column 1 from column 2. Subtract 6 times column 1 from column 3. The first row is now (1,0,0). The matrix is diag(1, N) with N=[[−2,−1],[−8,−5]].
Step 4. Subtract 4 times row 2 from row 3. Row 3 becomes (0,0,−1). Then add −1/2 times column 2 to column 3. Column 3 becomes (0,0,−1). The result is D=diag(1,−2,−1).
Check the determinant: det D=1·(−2)·(−1)=2=det M. This is consistent, because transvections have determinant 1.
Exact rational multiplication of the inverses in reverse order gives back M. So M=L D R with 4 left transvections, 3 right transvections and D=diag(1,−2,−1).

results.name: Cycle lemma and the Catalan number formula
results.statement: Let s be a sequence of n steps +1 and n+1 steps −1, in any order. Among its 2n+1 cyclic rotations, exactly one has all partial sums negative. Consequently the number of such sequences with this property is C(2n+1,n)/(2n+1). This number is the Catalan number Cn=C(2n,n)/(n+1), and it is also the number of Dyck words of semilength n.
hypotheses: The sequence has exactly n steps +1 and n+1 steps −1.
A partial sum is the sum of the first k steps for 1≤k≤2n+1.
A Dyck word of semilength n is a sequence of n steps +1 and n steps −1 whose partial sums are never negative.

theorem catalan_eq_centralBinom_div (n : ℕ) : catalan n = n.centralBinom / (n + 1) := by
  suffices (catalan n : ℚ) = Nat.centralBinom n / (n + 1) by
    have h := Nat.succ_dvd_centralBinom n
    exact mod_cast this
  induction n using Nat.caseStrongRecOn with
  | zero => simp
  | ind d hd =>
    simp_rw [catalan_succ, Nat.cast_sum, Nat.cast_mul]
    trans (∑ i : Fin d.succ, Nat.centralBinom i / (i + 1) *
                            (Nat.centralBinom (d - i) / (d - i + 1)) : ℚ)
    · congr
      ext1 x
      have m_le_d : x.val ≤ d := by lia
      have d_minus_x_le_d : (d - x.val) ≤ d := tsub_le_self
      rw [hd _ m_le_d, hd _ d_minus_x_le_d]
      norm_cast
    · trans (∑ i : Fin d.succ, (gosperCatalan (d + 1) (i + 1) - gosperCatalan (d + 1) i))
      · refine sum_congr rfl fun i _ => ?_
        rw [gosper_trick i.is_le, mul_div]
      · rw [← sum_range fun i => gosperCatalan (d + 1) (i + 1) - gosperCatalan (d + 1) i,
            sum_range_sub, Nat.succ_eq_add_one]
        rw [gosper_catalan_sub_eq_central_binom_div d]
        norm_cast

steps.text: Setup. Let Sk be the k-th partial sum of s for k=0,…,2n+1, with S0=0 and S_{2n+1}=−1. Extend s periodically. Then S_{k+2n+1}=S_k−1 for all k≥0.
The rotation that starts after position m has partial sums S_{m+j}−S_m for j=1,…,2n+1. It has all partial sums negative if and only if S_k<S_m for all k with m<k≤m+2n+1.

Existence. Among 0,…,2n let m be the last index at which S attains its maximum. For m<k≤2n we have S_k<S_m by the choice of m. For 2n+1≤k≤m+2n+1 write k=k′+2n+1 with 0≤k′≤m. Then S_k=S_{k′}−1≤S_m−1<S_m. So the rotation after m has all partial sums negative.

Uniqueness. Suppose that the rotation after m (with 0≤m≤2n) has all partial sums negative. For k′ with 0≤k′≤m, the index k=k′+2n+1 lies in the range (m, m+2n+1], so S_{k′}−1=S_k<S_m. Hence S_{k′}≤S_m. For m<k≤2n we have S_k<S_m by step 2. So m is the last index of the maximum on 0,…,2n, which is a single index.

Counting. A sequence has period dividing 2n+1 only if both counts, n and n+1, are divisible by the number of repeats. Since gcd(n,n+1)=1, a sequence cannot be a repeat of a shorter block, so its 2n+1 rotations are distinct. The set of C(2n+1,n) sequences splits into groups of 2n+1 rotations, and each group has exactly one good member by steps 3 and 4. So the number of good sequences is C(2n+1,n)/(2n+1).
Simplification. C(2n+1,n)/(2n+1)=(2n)!/(n!(n+1)!)=C(2n,n)/(n+1)=Cn.

Dyck words. A good sequence has first step −1 and partial sums S_k<0. Remove the first step. The remaining 2n steps have partial sums S_k+1≤0 and total 0. Negating these steps gives a Dyck word. The map is reversible: a Dyck word, negated and preceded by a step −1, is a good sequence. So the number of Dyck words of semilength n is also Cn.

steps.text: Equivalent form. If two different vertices a and b had two common neighbors u and v, then a,u,b,v would form a 4-cycle. So G is C4-free if and only if every pair {a,b} has at most one common neighbor.
Double count. Count the cherries (v;{a,b}), where v is a vertex and {a,b} is a pair of neighbors of v. For a fixed v there are C(d(v),2) choices. So the number of cherries is Σ_v C(d(v),2).
Count the same cherries by the pair {a,b}. Each pair {a,b} has at most one common neighbor v. So the number of cherries is at most the number of pairs, C(n,2). Hence Σ_v C(d(v),2)≤C(n,2).

Jensen. The function φ(d)=d(d−1)/2 is convex on the real line. By Jensen’s inequality, with mean degree d̄=2e/n, Σ_v φ(d(v))≥n·φ(d̄)=n·d̄(d̄−1)/2. Here we used the degree sum formula to get Σ_v d(v)=2e.
Combine steps 3 and 4. n·d̄(d̄−1)/2≤n(n−1)/2. So d̄²−d̄−(n−1)≤0.
The quadratic in d̄ has roots (1±√(4n−3))/2. So d̄≤(1+√(4n−3))/2. Using e=n·d̄/2 we get e≤(n/4)(1+√(4n−3)).

Bipartite version. In the bipartite graph count the cherries (y;{x,x′}), with y∈Y and x, x′∈X neighbors of y. The count by y is Σ_y C(d(y),2). The count by the pair {x,x′} gives at most C(m,2). This is the inequality in the statement.

steps.text: Lifting. The quotient map ℝ→ℝ/ℤ is a covering map with fiber ℤ. By path lifting, each loop γ at x0 has a unique lift γ̃ starting at 0. By homotopy lifting, a homotopy of paths with fixed ends lifts to a homotopy with a fixed starting point.
Integer values. The end point γ̃(1) lies in the fiber over x0, which is ℤ. So w(γ)∈ℤ.

Invariance. Let H be a homotopy of loops at x0 from γ to γ′. Lift H to H̃ with H̃(0,0)=0. The end points H̃(s,1) lie in ℤ and depend continuously on s. A continuous map from [0,1] into the discrete set ℤ is constant. So γ̃(1)=γ̃′(1). Equal winding number follows from homotopy, and w is well defined on π1.
Homomorphism. Let γ and δ be loops with w(γ)=a and w(δ)=b. The lift of the concatenation γ·δ is γ̃ followed by the path δ̃ shifted by a. This path starts at 0 and ends at a+b. So w(γ·δ)=a+b.
Surjective. The loop ωn(t)=nt mod 1 has the lift t↦nt. Its end point is n. So w(ωn)=n.

Injective. Let w(γ)=w(γ′). Their lifts γ̃ and γ̃′ are paths in ℝ from 0 to the same integer. The straight-line homotopy (1−s)γ̃+sγ̃′ fixes both ends. Composing with the quotient map gives a homotopy from γ to γ′ at the base point. Hence w is injective.
So w is a bijective homomorphism, which is the isomorphism π1(S¹,x0)≅ℤ.

worked_application.title: Count the zeros of z⁴+2z+1 with winding numbers
worked_application.goal: Let p(z)=z⁴+2z+1. For a radius r, let wr be the winding number of the loop t↦p(re^{2πit}) around 0. Compute wr for r=0.4, 0.8, 1.2 and 2, and compare with the zeros of p.
hypotheses: The map z↦z/|z| identifies loops in ℂ minus 0 with loops in S¹, up to homotopy.
The winding number around 0 of a loop in ℂ minus 0 is the integer of the theorem for the normalized loop.
p(−1)=1−2+1=0. The other zeros come from the cubic z³−z²+z+1.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The homotopy invariance of the winding number lets us replace p by a simpler polynomial on the circle, as long as no zero of the family lies on the circle.

steps.text: r=2. For s in [0,1] let ps(z)=z⁴+s(2z+1). On |z|=2 we have |z⁴|=16 and |s(2z+1)|≤5. So ps has no zero on the circle. The loops for s=0 and s=1 are homotopic in ℂ minus 0. The loop of z⁴ winds 4 times. So w2=4.
r=0.4. For s in [0,1] let ps(z)=1+s(z⁴+2z). On |z|=0.4 we have |z⁴+2z|≤0.0256+0.8=0.8256<1. So ps has no zero on the circle. The loop for s=0 is constant at 1. So w0.4=0.

r=0.8 and r=1.2. No such simple comparison works, so we sum the changes of argument numerically with 200000 steps. The sums are 1.000000 and 2.000000 in units of 2π, to six places. So w0.8=1 and w1.2=2.

Compare with the zeros. The real zero of the cubic z³−z²+z+1 is about −0.5437. The product of the four zeros is the constant term 1. The two real zeros −1 and −0.5437 have product 0.5437. So the two complex zeros have product 1/0.5437=1.839. They are conjugate, so each has modulus √1.839=1.356.
The zero moduli are 0.5437, 1, 1.356 and 1.356. The counts of zeros inside the circles are 0 for r=0.4, 1 for r=0.8, 2 for r=1.2 and 4 for r=2. These match w0.4, w0.8, w1.2 and w2.
The circle r=1 passes through the zero −1, so the winding number around 0 is not defined there. The jump from 1 to 2 between r=0.8 and r=1.2 comes from that zero.

worked_application.result: The winding numbers are 0, 1, 2 and 4 for r=0.4, 0.8, 1.2 and 2. They equal the number of zeros of p inside each circle.

limitations: The statement is for the circle. For the torus the group is ℤ², and for the wedge of circles the group is free and not abelian.
The application uses the identification of loops in ℂ minus 0 with loops in S¹. This is a homotopy equivalence and it is not part of the Mathlib source cited.

steps.text: Convergence. By submultiplicativity, ‖tᵏAᵏ/k!‖≤(|t|‖A‖)ᵏ/k!. The series ∑(|t|‖A‖)ᵏ/k! converges to e^{|t|‖A‖}. So the matrix series converges absolutely for every t, and the partial sums converge uniformly for t in any bounded interval [−T,T].
Termwise derivative. The k-th term has derivative tᵏ⁻¹Aᵏ/(k−1)! for k≥1. The derivative series equals A·∑_{j≥0} tʲAʲ/j! and its norm is bounded by ‖A‖e^{T‖A‖} on [−T,T]. It converges uniformly there.

A series of C¹ functions whose derivative series converges uniformly, and which converges at one point, can be differentiated termwise. So d/dt e^{tA}=A e^{tA}. The factor A can also be taken out on the right, so d/dt e^{tA}=e^{tA}A. Both forms hold because A commutes with every power of A.
Existence. Put x(t)=e^{tA}x₀. Then x′(t)=Ae^{tA}x₀=Ax(t). Also x(0)=I·x₀=x₀, because every term with k≥1 vanishes at t=0.

Inverse. Put h(t)=e^{tA}e^{−tA}. By the product rule and step 3, h′(t)=Ae^{tA}e^{−tA}−e^{tA}Ae^{−tA}=0, because A commutes with e^{tA}. So h is constant, and h(0)=I. Hence e^{tA}e^{−tA}=I for all t, and e^{−tA} is the inverse of e^{tA}.
Uniqueness. Let y be any differentiable solution with y(0)=x₀. Put z(t)=e^{−tA}y(t). By the product rule z′(t)=−Ae^{−tA}y(t)+e^{−tA}Ay(t)=0, again because A commutes with e^{−tA}.
A differentiable function with zero derivative on an interval is constant. So z(t)=z(0)=x₀. Multiply by e^{tA} and use step 5: y(t)=e^{tA}x₀=x(t).

worked_application.title: Damped oscillator x″+2x′+5x=0 as a first order system
worked_application.goal: Compute the solution with x(0)=1 and x′(0)=0 at time t=1, in closed form and by series.
hypotheses: Write the unknown as the vector (x,x′). Then the system is v′=Av with A=[[0,1],[−5,−2]] and v(0)=(1,0).
Use t=1.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The system is linear with a constant matrix, so the theorem gives v(t)=e^{tA}v(0) and no other solution exists.

steps.text: Since A=B−I and I commutes with B, e^{tA}=e^{−t}e^{tB}. The even and odd powers of B are Bᵏ=(−4)^{k/2}I and (−4)^{(k−1)/2}B. So e^{tB}=cos(2t)I+(sin(2t)/2)B.
Hence e^{tA}=e^{−t}(cos(2t)I+(sin(2t)/2)B). At t=1 the first column is e^{−1}(cos 2+(sin 2)/2, −(5/2)sin 2). Numerically, x(1)=e^{−1}(cos 2+sin(2)/2)=0.014164 and x′(1)=−(5/2)e^{−1}sin 2=−0.836280.

Check with the series. The partial sums ∑_{k≤K}Aᵏ/k! have first-row entries (0.375, 0.3333) for K=4, (0.011533, 0.167857) for K=8, and (0.014161, 0.167253) for K=12. The exact entries are (0.014164, 0.167256). The partial sums converge to the closed form.
Check the ODE. The vector Av(1)=(x′(1), −5x(1)−2x′(1))=(−0.836280, 1.601739). A central difference of v(t) at t=1 with step 10⁻¹⁰ gives the second component 1.601739 as well. So v′=Av holds.
Check the group law. The matrix product e^{0.4A}e^{0.6A} equals e^{A}. This follows from step 5 of the proof with exp(sA)exp(tA)=exp((s+t)A), and the numeric product agrees to 25 digits.

worked_application.result: x(1)=0.014164 and x′(1)=−0.836280. The solution is x(t)=e^{−t}(cos 2t+(1/2)sin 2t), and it is the only solution.

limitations: The theorem needs a constant A. For x′=A(t)x with varying A, the formula e^{∫A} is false in general unless A(s) and A(t) commute for all s,t.
Computing e^{tA} by the series is slow and can lose accuracy when ‖tA‖ is large. In practice one uses diagonalization, Jordan form, or scaling and squaring.
The uniqueness proof needs a solution that is differentiable at each point. It does not need a bound on growth. The result does not extend to infinite dimensions unless A is bounded.

results.proof_status: source declaration inspected; authored proof awaits inference review; no local Lean check

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Notation. Put L=inf_{n≥1} u(n)/n∈[−∞,∞). For every N, u(N)/N≥L by definition of L. So liminf u(N)/N≥L. It remains to show limsup u(N)/N≤L.
Block decomposition. Fix n≥1. By induction on k, u(kn+r)≤k·u(n)+u(r) for all k≥0 and r≥1. The case k=0 is trivial. For the step, u((k+1)n+r)=u(n+(kn+r))≤u(n)+u(kn+r).
Let M_n=max{u(r): 1≤r≤n}. Any N≥n can be written N=kn+r with k≥0 and 1≤r≤n. By step 2, u(N)≤k·u(n)+M_n.
Divide by N. Then u(N)/N≤(kn/N)·(u(n)/n)+M_n/N. As N→∞ with n fixed, k=(N−r)/n, so kn/N=(N−r)/N→1, and M_n/N→0.
Take limsup in step 4. Since kn/N→1 and u(n)/n is a fixed real number, limsup_{N→∞} u(N)/N≤u(n)/n. This holds for each n.
Take the infimum over n in step 5. limsup u(N)/N≤inf_n u(n)/n=L. Combined with step 1, limsup≤L≤liminf, so the limit exists and equals L.
If L=−∞, then limsup u(N)/N≤u(n)/n for every n, and u(n)/n takes arbitrarily negative values. So u(N)/N→−∞. If L is finite, the limit is the real number L.

/-- A function `f : α → ℝ` which is `K`-Lipschitz on a subset `s` admits a `K`-Lipschitz extension
to the whole space. -/
theorem LipschitzOnWith.extend_real {f : α → ℝ} {s : Set α} {K : ℝ≥0} (hf : LipschitzOnWith K f s) :
    ∃ g : α → ℝ, LipschitzWith K g ∧ EqOn f g s := by
  /- An extension is given by `g y = Inf {f x + K * dist y x | x ∈ s}`. Taking `x = y`, one has
    `g y ≤ f y` for `y ∈ s`, and the other inequality holds because `f` is `K`-Lipschitz, so that it
    cannot counterbalance the growth of `K * dist y x`. One readily checks from the formula that
    the extended function is also `K`-Lipschitz. -/
  rcases eq_empty_or_nonempty s with (rfl | hs)
  · exact ⟨fun _ => 0, (LipschitzWith.const _).weaken zero_le, eqOn_empty _ _⟩
  have : Nonempty s := by simp only [hs, nonempty_coe_sort]
  let g := fun y : α => iInf fun x : s => f x + K * dist y x
  have B : ∀ y : α, BddBelow (range fun x : s => f x + K * dist y x) := fun y => by
    rcases hs with ⟨z, hz⟩
    refine ⟨f z - K * dist y z, ?_⟩
    rintro w ⟨t, rfl⟩
    dsimp
    rw [sub_le_iff_le_add, add_assoc, ← mul_add, add_comm (dist y t)]
    calc
      f z ≤ f t + K * dist z t := hf.le_add_mul hz t.2
      _ ≤ f t + K * (dist y z + dist y t) := by gcongr; apply dist_triangle_left
  have E : EqOn f g s := fun x hx => by
    refine le_antisymm (le_ciInf fun y => hf.le_add_mul hx y.2) ?_
    simpa only [add_zero, Subtype.coe_mk, mul_zero, dist_self] using ciInf_le (B x) ⟨x, hx⟩
  refine ⟨g, LipschitzWith.of_le_add_mul K fun x y => ?_, E⟩
  rw [← sub_le_iff_le_add]
  refine le_ciInf fun z => ?_
  rw [sub_le_iff_le_add]
  calc
    g x ≤ f z + K * dist x z := ciInf_le (B x) _
    _ ≤ f z + K * dist y z + K * dist x y := by
      rw [add_assoc, ← mul_add, add_comm (dist y z)]
      gcongr
      apply dist_triangle

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: F is finite. Fix s₀∈S and x∈X. For every s∈S, f(s)≥f(s₀)−K d(s,s₀)≥f(s₀)−K d(s,x)−K d(x,s₀), by the Lipschitz property and the triangle inequality. So f(s)+K d(x,s)≥f(s₀)−K d(x,s₀). The set of values is bounded below, and non-empty, so the infimum is a real number.
F extends f. Let x∈S. Taking s=x in the infimum gives F(x)≤f(x). Conversely, for any s∈S, f(x)−f(s)≤K d(x,s), so f(s)+K d(x,s)≥f(x). Take the infimum over s: F(x)≥f(x). Hence F(x)=f(x).
Key inequality. Let x,y∈X and s∈S. By the triangle inequality, d(x,s)≤d(y,s)+d(x,y). Since K≥0, f(s)+K d(x,s)≤f(s)+K d(y,s)+K d(x,y).
Since F(x) is at most the left side for each s, F(x)≤f(s)+K d(y,s)+K d(x,y) for every s∈S. Take the infimum over s on the right: F(x)≤F(y)+K d(x,y).
Swap x and y in step 4 to get F(y)≤F(x)+K d(x,y). Together, |F(x)−F(y)|≤K d(x,y). So F is K-Lipschitz on X.
For the order statement: if H is any K-Lipschitz extension of f, then for s∈S, H(x)≤H(s)+K d(x,s)=f(s)+K d(x,s). Take the infimum over s to get H≤F. The symmetric argument gives G≤H.

worked_application.goal: Extend f on S={0,1,3,4} with f=(0,1,0.5,2) to ℝ, with the best Lipschitz constant. Evaluate the largest and the smallest extension at several points.

steps.text: Compute the slopes. Between neighbours: (1−0)/1=1, (0.5−1)/2=−0.25 and (2−0.5)/1=1.5. For non-neighbours the slopes are 0.5/3≈0.167, 2/4=0.5 and (2−1)/3≈0.333. The largest absolute value is K=1.5.

The largest extension is F(x)=min_s (f(s)+1.5|x−s|). At x=2 the four values are 3, 2.5, 2 and 5, so F(2)=2. At x=2.5 the best s is 3, so F(2.5)=0.5+1.5·0.5=1.25. At x=3.5 the best s is 3, so F(3.5)=1.25.
Outside S the values are F(5)=3.5 and F(−1)=1.5. At every point of S the value equals f. A check on a grid of step 0.05 over [−2,6.95] gives maximal difference quotient 1.5 for F and also for G.
So any 1.5-Lipschitz extension H has −0.5≤H(2)≤2 and −0.25≤H(2.5)≤1.25. These intervals are the exact range of values that stay consistent with K=1.5.

results.name: Bessel inequality for orthonormal families
results.statement: Let H be a real or complex inner product space. Let (eᵢ)_{i∈I} be an orthonormal family in H. Then for every x∈H, ∑_{i∈I}|⟨eᵢ,x⟩|²≤‖x‖². hypotheses: H need not be complete.

source.excerpt:
/-- Bessel's inequality for finite sums. -/
theorem Orthonormal.sum_inner_products_le {s : Finset ι} (hv : Orthonormal 𝕜 v) :
    ∑ i ∈ s, ‖⟪v i, x⟫‖ ^ 2 ≤ ‖x‖ ^ 2 := by
  have h₂ :
    (∑ i ∈ s, ∑ j ∈ s, ⟪v i, x⟫ * ⟪x, v j⟫ * ⟪v j, v i⟫) = (∑ k ∈ s, ⟪v k, x⟫ * ⟪x, v k⟫ : 𝕜) := by
    exact hv.inner_left_right_finset
  have h₃ : ∀ z : 𝕜, re (z * conj z) = ‖z‖ ^ 2 := by
    intro z
    simp only [mul_conj]
    norm_cast
  suffices hbf : ‖x - ∑ i ∈ s, ⟪v i, x⟫ • v i‖ ^ 2 = ‖x‖ ^ 2 - ∑ i ∈ s, ‖⟪v i, x⟫‖ ^ 2 by
    rw [← sub_nonneg, ← hbf]
    simp only [norm_nonneg, pow_nonneg]
  rw [@norm_sub_sq 𝕜, sub_add]
  simp only [@InnerProductSpace.norm_sq_eq_re_inner 𝕜 E, inner_sum, sum_inner]
  simp only [inner_smul_right, two_mul, inner_smul_left, inner_conj_symm, ← mul_assoc, h₂,
    add_sub_cancel_right, sub_right_inj]
  simp only [map_sum, ← inner_conj_symm x, ← h₃]

steps.text: Fix a finite set F⊆I. Put cᵢ=⟨eᵢ,x⟩ and p=∑_{i∈F}cᵢeᵢ. Put r=x−p.
The residual r is orthogonal to each eⱼ with j∈F. Indeed ⟨eⱼ,r⟩=⟨eⱼ,x⟩−∑_{i∈F}cᵢ⟨eⱼ,eᵢ⟩=cⱼ−cⱼ=0.
So r is orthogonal to p, because p is a combination of the eⱼ with j∈F. The Pythagorean identity gives ‖x‖²=‖p‖²+‖r‖².
Compute ‖p‖² with orthonormality: ‖p‖²=∑_{i,j∈F}cᵢ conj(cⱼ)⟨eⱼ,eᵢ⟩=∑_{i∈F}|cᵢ|². Hence ∑_{i∈F}|cᵢ|²=‖x‖²−‖r‖²≤‖x‖².
The partial sums over finite sets are all bounded by ‖x‖². The sum over I of non-negative terms is the supremum of these partial sums. So ∑_{i∈I}|cᵢ|²≤‖x‖².
For each n≥1 the set {i: |cᵢ|²>1/n} has at most n‖x‖² elements, by step 5. So {i: cᵢ≠0} is a countable union of finite sets.
Equality in step 4 holds exactly when ‖r_F‖² tends to 0 along the finite sets, which means x is the limit of its partial Fourier sums. This is the Parseval case.

worked_application.title: Fourier sine coefficients of f(x)=x on (−π,π)
worked_application.goal: Use the functions eₙ(x)=sin(nx)/√π in L²(−π,π). Compute the coefficients of f(x)=x and check Bessel inequality and the Pythagorean gap.
hypotheses: The inner product is ⟨g,h⟩=∫_{−π}^{π} g(x)h(x)dx, with real functions.
The family (eₙ)_{n≥1} is orthonormal. We checked ⟨e₁,e₂⟩=0 and ‖e₂‖²=1 by numerical integration.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: L²(−π,π) is an inner product space and (eₙ) is orthonormal, so the theorem applies to f(x)=x.

steps.text: Integration by parts gives ⟨eₙ,f⟩=(1/√π)∫x sin(nx)dx=2√π(−1)^{n+1}/n. Numerical integration gives 3.5449, −1.7725 and 1.1816 for n=1,2,3, which equal 2√π, −√π and 2√π/3.
So cₙ²=4π/n². The squared norm is ‖f‖²=∫x²dx=2π³/3=20.6709.
Bessel inequality for the first N terms gives ∑_{n≤N}4π/n²≤2π³/3. Dividing by 4π: ∑_{n≤N}1/n²≤π²/6. For N=10 the left side is 1.5498 and π²/6=1.6449. The inequality holds.

The Pythagorean gap ‖f‖²−∑_{n≤N}cₙ² equals ‖f−pₙ‖², the squared distance to the partial sum. We computed both ways: for N=1,2,5,10,100 the gap is 8.1045, 4.9629, 2.2786, 1.1959 and 0.12504, and the integral of (f−p_N)² gives the same numbers to 15 digits.

The gap tends to 0 like 4π/N, so the family is complete for this f. If the sine family is complete for odd functions, then ∑cₙ²=‖f‖² and ∑1/n²=π²/6. The numbers agree with this, and Parseval identity for the full trigonometric system proves it.

worked_application.result: Bessel inequality gives ∑_{n≤N}1/n²≤π²/6 for all N, and the gap ‖f−p_N‖² equals ‖f‖²−∑cₙ² exactly.

The sum over I makes sense without ordering because all terms are non-negative.

/-- Cauchy condensation test for antitone series of nonnegative real numbers. -/
theorem summable_condensed_iff_of_nonneg {f : ℕ → ℝ} (h_nonneg : ∀ n, 0 ≤ f n)

  have h_succ_diff : SuccDiffBounded 2 (2 ^ ·) := by
    intro n
    simp [pow_succ, mul_two, two_mul]
  convert!
    summable_schlomilch_iff_of_nonneg h_nonneg h_mono (pow_pos zero_lt_two)
      (pow_right_strictMono₀ one_lt_two) two_ne_zero h_succ_diff

steps.text: Upper block bound. For 2ᵏ≤n<2^{k+1}, monotonicity gives f(n)≤f(2ᵏ). The block has 2ᵏ terms, so ∑_{2ᵏ≤n<2^{k+1}} f(n)≤2ᵏ f(2ᵏ).
Sum the blocks for k=0,…,K. They partition {1,…,2^{K+1}−1}. So S_{2^{K+1}−1}≤T_K.
Lower block bound. For 2^{k−1}<n≤2ᵏ with k≥1, monotonicity gives f(n)≥f(2ᵏ). This block has 2^{k−1} terms. So ∑_{2^{k−1}<n≤2ᵏ} f(n)≥2^{k−1}f(2ᵏ)=½·2ᵏf(2ᵏ).
Sum these for k=1,…,K and add f(1). Then S_{2^K}≥f(1)+½∑_{k=1}^K 2ᵏf(2ᵏ). Since f(1)≥½f(1), we get S_{2^K}≥½T_K.
Suppose ∑f(n) converges, with sum S. Then S_{2^K}≤S for all K, so T_K≤2S by step 4. The partial sums T_K are non-decreasing and bounded, so the condensed series converges.

Suppose the condensed series converges, with sum T. Then S_{2^{K+1}−1}≤T for all K by step 2. For any N choose K with N<2^{K+1}. Then S_N≤S_{2^{K+1}−1}≤T. The partial sums S_N are non-decreasing and bounded, so ∑f(n) converges.

worked_application.title: Decide ∑1/(n ln n) and ∑1/(n ln²n) and bound the second sum
worked_application.goal: Use condensation to show the first series diverges and the second converges. Give numeric bounds for the sum of the second series from n=2.
hypotheses: f(n)=1/(n ln n) and g(n)=1/(n (ln n)²) for n≥2. Both are positive and decreasing for n≥2.
For the test, define the value at n=1 by f(1)=f(2) and g(1)=g(2). This changes finitely many terms and keeps monotonicity.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The functions are non-negative and non-increasing, so the condensation test applies.

steps.text: For f, 2ᵏf(2ᵏ)=2ᵏ/(2ᵏ·k ln 2)=1/(k ln 2). The condensed series is (1/ln 2)∑1/k. The harmonic series diverges, so ∑1/(n ln n) diverges.
For g, 2ᵏg(2ᵏ)=1/(k² ln²2). The condensed series is (1/ln²2)∑1/k². It converges. So ∑1/(n ln²n) converges.

The block bound in step 1 holds for blocks starting at n=2ᵏ with k≥1. Hence ∑_{n≥2}g(n)≤∑_{k≥1}1/(k ln 2)²=(π²/6)/ln²2=3.4237. The dyadic lower bound ½∑_{k≥2}1/(k ln 2)² gives 0.6712 as a lower bound for the sum from n=2.
A sharper bound uses the tail. Direct summation gives ∑_{2≤n<2²⁰} g(n)=2.03761. The tail ∑_{n≥2²⁰} g(n)≤∑_{k≥20}1/(k ln 2)²≤(1/ln²2)(1/19)=0.10955, since ∑_{k≥20}1/k²≤1/19.
So 2.0376≤∑_{n≥2}g(n)≤2.1472. The integral ∫_N^∞ dx/(x ln²x)=1/ln N gives a tail estimate 1/ln(2²⁰)=0.0721. The estimate 2.0376+0.0721=2.1097 lies inside the interval.

The slow decay is visible: a sum to a million terms is off by about 0.07. The series is a standard example where the partial sums give a poor numeric value, yet condensation gives a certain convergence proof.

/-- General fencing theorem for continuous functions with an estimate on the norm of the derivative.
Let `f` and `B` be continuous functions on `[a, b]` such that

* `‖f a‖ ≤ B a`;
* `f` has right derivative `f'` at every point of `[a, b)`;
* `B` has derivative `B'` everywhere on `ℝ`;
* we have `‖f' x‖ ≤ B x` everywhere on `[a, b)`.

Then `‖f x‖ ≤ B x` everywhere on `[a, b]`. We use one-sided derivatives in the assumptions
to make this theorem work for piecewise differentiable functions.
-/
theorem image_norm_le_of_norm_deriv_right_le_deriv_boundary {f' : ℝ → E}
    (hf : ContinuousOn f (Icc a b)) (hf' : ∀ x ∈ Ico a b, HasDerivWithinAt f (f' x) (Ici x) x)
    {B B' : ℝ → ℝ} (ha : ‖f a‖ ≤ B a) (hB : ∀ x, HasDerivAt B (B' x) x)
    (bound : ∀ x ∈ Ico a b, ‖f' x‖ ≤ B' x) : ∀ ⦃x⦄, x ∈ Icc a b → ‖f x‖ ≤ B x :=
  image_norm_le_of_norm_deriv_right_le_deriv_boundary' hf hf' ha
    (fun x _ => (hB x).continuousAt.continuousWithinAt) (fun x _ => (hB x).hasDerivWithinAt) bound

steps.text: Put v=f(b)−f(a). If v=0, then ‖v‖=0. The claim then needs B(b)−B(a)≥0. This holds because B′≥‖f′‖≥0 on (a,b), so B is non-decreasing by the scalar mean value theorem. So assume v≠0.
By the Hahn-Banach theorem there is a continuous linear φ:E→ℝ with ‖φ‖≤1 and φ(v)=‖v‖.
Define the real function h(t)=φ(f(t))−B(t) on [a,b]. It is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b). Linear continuous maps commute with the derivative, so h′(t)=φ(f′(t))−B′(t).
Estimate h′. Since ‖φ‖≤1, φ(f′(t))≤‖f′(t)‖≤B′(t). So h′(t)≤0 on (a,b).
Apply the scalar mean value theorem: h(b)−h(a)=h′(ξ)(b−a)≤0 for some ξ∈(a,b). So φ(f(b))−φ(f(a))≤B(b)−B(a).
The left side equals φ(v)=‖v‖. Hence ‖f(b)−f(a)‖≤B(b)−B(a).
For a constant bound M, take B(t)=Mt. Then B′=M and B(b)−B(a)=M(b−a).

steps.text: For f₁, f₁′(s)=ie^{is} and ‖f₁′‖=1. Take B(s)=s. Then ‖e^{it}−1‖≤t.
For f₂, f₂′(s)=i(e^{is}−1), so ‖f₂′(s)‖=‖e^{is}−1‖≤s by step 1. Take B(s)=s²/2. Then ‖e^{it}−1−it‖≤t²/2.
For f₃, f₃′(s)=ie^{is}−i+s=i(e^{is}−1−is), so ‖f₃′(s)‖≤s²/2 by step 2. Take B(s)=s³/6. Then ‖e^{it}−1−it+t²/2‖≤t³/6.

Numeric check at t=0.5. The three left sides are |e^{0.5i}−1|=0.4948, |e^{0.5i}−1−0.5i|=0.12413 and |e^{0.5i}−1−0.5i+0.125|=0.020736. The right sides are 0.5, 0.125 and 0.020833. All three inequalities hold, and the last two are tight to within 1 percent.
These bounds give the standard estimate for characteristic functions: |E e^{itX}−1−itE X+t²E X²/2|≤|t|³E|X|³/6, when E|X|³ is finite.

worked_application.result: The three inequalities hold with no series. They follow from the theorem three times, each time with the boundary function from the previous step.

limitations: The equality form of the scalar theorem fails for vector valued f. For f(t)=(cos t, sin t) on [0,2π], f(2π)−f(0)=0, but f′(t) never vanishes. Only the inequality survives.
The proof of step 2 uses the Hahn-Banach theorem. In an infinite dimensional space this needs a form of the axiom of choice, unless E is separable.
Differentiability on the open interval and continuity at the end points are both needed.

results.name: Monotone sandwich for the Euler-Mascheroni constant
results.statement: Let Hₙ=1+1/2+…+1/n. Put aₙ=Hₙ−ln(n+1) and bₙ=Hₙ−ln n for n≥1. Then aₙ is strictly increasing, bₙ is strictly decreasing, aₙ<bₙ, and bₙ−aₙ=ln(1+1/n)→0. Hence both sequences converge to the same limit γ, and aₙ<γ<bₘ for all n,m≥1. In particular 0<bₙ−γ<ln(1+1/n)<1/n.
hypotheses: n and m are positive integers.
ln is the natural logarithm.
No assumption beyond the two bounds 1/(n+1)<ln(1+1/n)<1/n is needed.

steps.text: Key bounds. For n≥1 the mean value theorem gives ln(n+1)−ln n=1/ξ for some ξ∈(n,n+1). So 1/(n+1)<ln(1+1/n)<1/n.
The sequence aₙ increases. aₙ₊₁−aₙ=1/(n+1)−ln((n+2)/(n+1))=1/(n+1)−ln(1+1/(n+1)). By the upper bound in step 1, applied to n+1, this is positive.
The sequence bₙ decreases. bₙ₊₁−bₙ=1/(n+1)−ln((n+1)/n)=1/(n+1)−ln(1+1/n). By the lower bound in step 1, this is negative.
The gap is bₙ−aₙ=ln(n+1)−ln n=ln(1+1/n). It is positive, and it tends to 0 as n→∞.
Bounded monotone sequences converge. We have a₁≤aₙ<bₙ≤b₁, so both sequences are bounded. Let A=lim aₙ and B=lim bₙ. Since bₙ−aₙ→0, A=B. Call it γ.
Strict inequalities. Since aₙ is strictly increasing with limit γ, aₙ<aₙ₊₁≤γ. Since bₙ is strictly decreasing with limit γ, γ≤bₙ₊₁<bₙ. So aₙ<γ<bₘ for all n,m.
Error bound. bₙ−γ<bₙ−aₙ=ln(1+1/n)<1/n, by step 1 and aₙ<γ.

worked_application.title: Bounds for γ and for the coupon collector time with 50 coupons
worked_application.goal: Bound γ from n=6 and n=1000. Bound the mean number of draws needed to collect all of 50 coupon types, which is 50·H₅₀.
hypotheses: The mean time to collect all of m types, drawn uniformly with replacement, is m·H_m. We take this formula as known.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The theorem gives numeric two sided bounds for γ and for Hₙ−ln n at any n.

steps.text: For n=1000 the bounds are a₁₀₀₀=0.576716 and b₁₀₀₀=0.577716. So 0.57671<γ<0.57772. The width is ln(1.001)=0.0009995.
For n=10⁶ the value b_n=0.5772161649 differs from γ=0.5772156649 by 5.0·10⁻⁷. This agrees with the error bound 0<bₙ−γ<1/n=10⁻⁶.
Coupon collector. Since a₅₀>a₁>0, ln 51<H₅₀. Since b₅₀<b₆, H₅₀<ln 50+b₆. Here b₆=0.65824 and ln 50=3.91202.
So 50·ln 51=196.59 < 50·H₅₀ < 50·(ln 50+0.65824)=228.51. The exact value 50·H₅₀=224.96 is inside the interval.
The estimate 50(ln 50+γ)=224.46 is closer. The difference to the exact value is 0.50, which equals 50·(1/(2·50)) to the shown accuracy, the size of the next correction term.

worked_application.result: γ lies in (0.57671, 0.57772). The mean time for 50 coupons lies in (196.59, 228.51) by the theorem alone, and the exact value is 224.96.
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: The sandwich gives a convergent constant, not a closed form. It does not decide whether γ is rational. That question is open.
The error bound 1/n is weak. The true error of bₙ is about 1/(2n). Euler-Maclaurin summation gives better bounds.
The same method works for any pair of a monotone-up and a monotone-down sequence whose gap tends to 0. It needs both monotonicities.
