results.name: Gronwall bound for dependence on initial data
results.statement: Let E be a real normed space and f:[a,b]×E→E. Assume ‖f(t,u)−f(t,w)‖≤K‖u−w‖ for all t, u, w, with K≥0. Let x,y:[a,b]→E be continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), with x′(t)=f(t,x(t)) and y′(t)=f(t,y(t)) on (a,b). Then ‖x(t)−y(t)‖≤‖x(a)−y(a)‖·e^{K(t−a)} for all t∈[a,b]. In particular, a solution is unique for given initial data.
hypotheses: f is Lipschitz in the second variable with a constant K that does not depend on t.
The exponent K(t−a) is the worst case. Real solutions may separate more slowly.
If f is only Lipschitz on a set that contains both trajectories, extend f to all of E by composing with a nearest point map or a cutoff, and use the theorem for the extended f.

prerequisites.reason: The bound of ‖v(t)−v(a)‖ by B(t)−B(a) is the mean value inequality with a boundary function.

definitions.name: Lipschitz in the state
definitions.text: A bound ‖f(t,u)−f(t,w)‖≤K‖u−w‖ that is uniform in t.

definitions.name: Gronwall bound
definitions.text: The function δe^{K(t−a)}. It solves B′=KB with B(a)=δ.

definitions.name: continuous dependence
definitions.text: Small changes in the initial data give small changes in the solution, uniformly on a compact time interval.

source.excerpt:
/-- If `f` and `g` are two exact solutions of the same ODE, then the distance between them
can't grow faster than exponentially. This is a simple corollary of Grönwall's inequality, and some
people call this Grönwall's inequality too.

This version assumes all inequalities to be true in the whole space. -/
theorem dist_le_of_trajectories_ODE
    (hv : ∀ t, LipschitzWith K (v t))
    (hf : ContinuousOn f (Icc a b))
    (hf' : ∀ t ∈ Ico a b, HasDerivWithinAt f (v t (f t)) (Ici t) t)
    (hg : ContinuousOn g (Icc a b))
    (hg' : ∀ t ∈ Ico a b, HasDerivWithinAt g (v t (g t)) (Ici t) t)
    (ha : dist (f a) (g a) ≤ δ) :
    ∀ t ∈ Icc a b, dist (f t) (g t) ≤ δ * exp (K * (t - a)) :=
  have hfs : ∀ t ∈ Ico a b, f t ∈ @univ E := fun _ _ => trivial
  dist_le_of_trajectories_ODE_of_mem (fun t _ => (hv t).lipschitzOnWith) hf hf' hfs hg
    hg' (fun _ _ => trivial) ha

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Setup. Put v=x−y and δ=‖v(a)‖. Then v is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), with v′(t)=f(t,x(t))−f(t,y(t)). By the Lipschitz bound, ‖v′(t)‖≤K‖v(t)‖.
Fix ε>0. Put B(t)=(δ+ε)e^{K(t−a)}. Then B′=KB, and ‖v(a)‖=δ<B(a).
Let T be the supremum of the τ∈[a,b] with ‖v(s)‖≤B(s) for all s∈[a,τ]. The set is not empty because it contains a. By continuity, ‖v(s)‖≤B(s) on [a,T].
Bound inside [a,T]. For s∈(a,T) we have ‖v′(s)‖≤K‖v(s)‖≤KB(s)=B′(s), because K≥0. Apply the mean value inequality with boundary function B on [a,t] for each t∈(a,T]. We get ‖v(t)−v(a)‖≤B(t)−B(a).
So ‖v(t)‖≤δ+B(t)−(δ+ε)=B(t)−ε for t∈(a,T]. At t=a, ‖v(a)‖=δ<B(a). Hence ‖v(T)‖<B(T) in both cases.
Suppose T<b. Both ‖v‖ and B are continuous and ‖v(T)‖<B(T), so ‖v‖<B on [T,T+η) for some η>0. This contradicts the definition of T. So T=b.
Thus ‖v(t)‖≤(δ+ε)e^{K(t−a)} for all t∈[a,b] and all ε>0. Let ε→0 to get ‖v(t)‖≤δe^{K(t−a)}.
Uniqueness. If x(a)=y(a), then δ=0 and ‖x(t)−y(t)‖≤0. So x=y on [a,b].

worked_application.title: Logistic growth with two close initial values
worked_application.goal: Compare the solutions of x′=x(1−x) with x(0)=0.20 and x(0)=0.25 on [0,3] and check the Gronwall bound.
hypotheses: The exact solution is x(t)=a e^t/(1−a+a e^t), with a=x(0).
Both solutions stay in (0,1). Replace f(x)=x(1−x) by f(π(x)) where π is the nearest point projection on [0,1]. This extension has Lipschitz constant K=max|1−2x|=1 and has the same solutions here.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The extended right side is Lipschitz in x with K=1, and does not depend on t. So the theorem applies with δ=0.05.

steps.text: The solutions at t=0.5 are 0.291875 and 0.354661. Their distance is 0.062786. The bound is 0.05e^{0.5}=0.082436.
At t=1 the solutions are 0.404610 and 0.475367. The distance is 0.070757 and the bound is 0.05e=0.135914.
At t=2 the distance is 0.062449 and the bound is 0.05e²=0.369453. At t=3 the distance is 0.036123 and the bound is 0.05e³=1.004277.
The bound holds at all four times. The ratio distance/bound is 0.76, 0.52, 0.17 and 0.036, so the bound gets worse as t grows.
The reason is that the logistic flow contracts near the stable point 1. The Lipschitz constant 1 is the worst case at x=0. Gronwall cannot see the contraction because it uses a global constant.
At t=0.5 the true ratio distance/δ is 1.2557, below the Gronwall factor e^{0.5}=1.6487. At t=1 it is 1.4151, below e=2.7183.

worked_application.result: For δ=0.05 and K=1 the separation never exceeds 0.05e^t on [0,3]. Among the four sample times, the largest separation is 0.0708, at t=1.
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: The factor e^{K(t−a)} can be sharp. For x′=Kx, two solutions separate exactly at this rate.
The theorem needs Lipschitz continuity in the state. For x′=√|x| both x=0 and x=t²/4 solve the same problem with x(0)=0.
A bound that depends on the time interval does not give long time stability. For stable systems, a different method (Lyapunov functions) is needed.

results.name: Volume of the Euclidean ball from the Gaussian integral
results.statement: Let Vₙ be the Lebesgue measure of the closed or open unit ball of ℝⁿ. Then Vₙ=π^{n/2}/Γ(n/2+1), and a ball of radius r has measure Vₙrⁿ. For n=2k, Vₙ=π^k/k!. For n=2k+1, Vₙ=2^{k+1}π^k/(1·3·5⋯(2k+1)).
hypotheses: n≥1 is an integer, and the measure is Lebesgue measure on ℝⁿ.
The one dimensional integral ∫_ℝ e^{−t²}dt=√π is known.

prerequisites.reason: Step 1 splits the Gaussian integral over ℝⁿ into a product of one dimensional integrals.
Step 3 equates two slicings of the region under the Gaussian.

source_references.alignment: The source proves a general unit ball formula as an integral divided by a Gamma value. It is the layer cake argument for a general norm.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Gaussian integral in ℝⁿ. The function e^{−|x|²}=∏e^{−xᵢ²} is a product. By Fubini-Tonelli, ∫_{ℝⁿ}e^{−|x|²}dx=(∫_ℝ e^{−t²}dt)ⁿ=π^{n/2}.
Scaling. The map x↦rx has determinant rⁿ. So vol(rBₙ)=rⁿVₙ for r>0.
Layer cake. For g(x)=e^{−|x|²}, the set {(x,s): 0<s<g(x)} has two descriptions. Slicing over x gives ∫g dx. Slicing over s gives ∫_0^1 vol{g>s}ds. Cavalieri principle says the two volumes agree.
Level sets. For 0<s<1, g(x)>s if and only if |x|²<−ln s. So {g>s} is the open ball of radius (−ln s)^{1/2}. By step 2, its measure is Vₙ(−ln s)^{n/2}. For s≥1 the set is empty.
So ∫g dx=Vₙ∫_0^1(−ln s)^{n/2}ds. Substitute s=e^{−u}, ds=−e^{−u}du. The integral becomes Vₙ∫_0^∞ u^{n/2}e^{−u}du=Vₙ·Γ(n/2+1).
Compare steps 1 and 5: VₙΓ(n/2+1)=π^{n/2}. Since Γ(n/2+1)>0, Vₙ=π^{n/2}/Γ(n/2+1).
Special values. For n=2k, Γ(k+1)=k!, so Vₙ=π^k/k!. For n=2k+1, Γ(k+3/2)=((2k+1)!!/2^{k+1})√π, by Γ(s+1)=sΓ(s) and Γ(1/2)=√π. So Vₙ=2^{k+1}π^k/(2k+1)!!.
The closed ball has the same measure, because the sphere has measure 0. It lies in the ball of radius 1+η for every η>0, with measure Vₙ(1+η)ⁿ→Vₙ.

hypotheses: The lattice count is for the ball of radius 20 in ℤ³: points with x²+y²+z²≤400.

steps.text: The ratio V_{n+2}/V_n=2π/(n+2), because Γ(s+1)=sΓ(s). It is above 1 for n+2<2π, which means n≤4, and below 1 for n≥5. The unit ball fills a vanishing share of the cube [−1,1]ⁿ of volume 2ⁿ. The shares Vₙ/2ⁿ are 0.7854 for n=2, 0.5236 for n=3, 0.3084 for n=4 and 0.00249 for n=10.

The error is 109, which is 0.33 percent. It is of the order of the surface area 4π·20²=5026 times a small factor. This is the usual lattice point error, much smaller than the volume.
Gaussian check for n=5. V₅·Γ(7/2)=5.26379·3.32335=17.4934=π^{5/2}. The identity from the proof holds numerically for n=2, 3 and 5.

results.name: Partial fraction expansion of π cot πz
results.statement: For every complex z∉ℤ, π cot(πz)=1/z+∑_{n≥1} 2z/(z²−n²), which equals 1/z+∑_{n≥1}(1/(z−n)+1/(z+n)). The series converges absolutely, and uniformly on compact subsets of ℂ∖ℤ. Equivalently, π cot(πz)=lim_{N→∞}∑_{|n|≤N} 1/(z+n).
hypotheses: z is not an integer. At each integer both sides have a simple pole with residue 1.
The sum over n∈ℤ is taken symmetrically. The two sided series ∑_{n∈ℤ}1/(z+n) does not converge absolutely.
The real case (z real) is proved first. The complex case follows from the identity theorem.

prerequisites.reason: Step 9 uses the local identity theorem to pass from the real interval to the whole punctured plane.

definitions.name: cotangent
definitions.text: cot w=cos w/sin w. The function π cot πz is meromorphic with simple poles of residue 1 at the integers, and it has period 1.

definitions.name: Weierstrass M-test
definitions.text: If |gₙ(z)|≤Mₙ on a set and ∑Mₙ<∞, then ∑gₙ converges absolutely and uniformly there.

/-- The cotangent infinite sum representation. -/
theorem cot_series_rep (hz : x ∈ ℂ_ℤ) :
    π * cot (π * x) = 1 / x + ∑' n : ℕ+, (1 / (x - n) + 1 / (x + n)) := by
  have h0 := tsum_pnat_eq_tsum_succ (f := fun n ↦ 1 / (x - n) + 1 / (x + n))
  have h1 := cot_series_rep' hz
  simp only [one_div, Nat.cast_add, Nat.cast_one] at *
  rw [h0, ← h1]
  ring

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Convergence. Let |z|≤R and n≥2R. Then n²−|z|²≥3n²/4, so |2z/(z²−n²)|≤8R/(3n²). By the M-test, G(z)=1/z+∑_{n≥1}2z/(z²−n²) converges locally uniformly on ℂ∖ℤ. Each term is holomorphic there, so G is holomorphic on ℂ∖ℤ. Also G(z)=lim S_N(z), because the terms for n and −n combine to 2z/(z²−n²).

Real setup. Let f(x)=π cot πx and g(x)=G(x) for real x∉ℤ. Both are odd. Both have period 1: for f this is clear, and for g, S_N(x+1)=∑_{m=−N+1}^{N+1}1/(x+m)=S_N(x)+1/(x+N+1)−1/(x−N), and the two extra terms tend to 0.
Duplication formula for f. With u=πx/2, cot u+cot(u+π/2)=cot u−tan u=(cos²u−sin²u)/(sin u cos u)=2cot 2u. So f(x/2)+f((x+1)/2)=2f(x).

Duplication formula for g. We have S_N-type sums: ∑_{|n|≤N}(1/(x/2+n)+1/((x+1)/2+n))=2∑_{m=−2N}^{2N+1}1/(x+m)=2S_{2N}(x)+2/(x+2N+1). Let N→∞. The left side tends to g(x/2)+g((x+1)/2) and the right side to 2g(x). So g has the same duplication formula.

Difference. Put d=f−g on ℝ∖ℤ. Then d is odd, has period 1 and satisfies d(x/2)+d((x+1)/2)=2d(x). Near x=0, π cot πx−1/x=(πx cos πx−sin πx)/(x sin πx)→0 because the numerator is −π³x³/3+O(x⁵) and the denominator is πx²+O(x⁴). Also g(x)−1/x=∑2x/(x²−n²) is continuous on (−1,1) with value 0 at 0. So d(x)→0 as x→0. By periodicity, d(x)→0 at each integer. Set d(n)=0. Then d is continuous on ℝ.
The duplication formula extends to all of ℝ by continuity, because ℝ∖ℤ is dense and the points x/2 and (x+1)/2 are not integers when x∉ℤ.

Maximum argument. d is continuous and periodic, so it attains a maximum M at some x₀. Then 2M=2d(x₀)=d(x₀/2)+d((x₀+1)/2)≤2M, and each term is at most M. So d(x₀/2)=M. By induction d(x₀/2ᵏ)=M for all k. Let k→∞. By continuity M=d(0)=0.
The function −d satisfies all the same properties, so its maximum is also 0. Hence d≡0 on ℝ, and f=g on ℝ∖ℤ.

Complex case. The functions F(z)=π cot πz and G(z) are holomorphic on U=ℂ∖ℤ. The set U is open and connected, because ℤ is closed and discrete. The function H=F−G vanishes on (0,1). Let Z be the set of z∈U where H and all its derivatives vanish. Z is closed in U by continuity. Z is open by the local identity theorem: if all derivatives vanish at z, the power series of H is zero near z. Z is not empty, because it contains each point of (0,1). So Z=U, and H≡0 on U.

worked_application.title: Series for π and values of ζ(2), ζ(4), ζ(6) from cot
worked_application.goal: Use z=1/4 to get a series for π, check the series numerically, and expand in powers of z to get the zeta values.
hypotheses: For |z|<1, expand 2z²/(z²−n²) as a geometric series in z²/n².
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The theorem gives π cot πz for all z∉ℤ, including z=1/4 and |z|<1, z≠0.

steps.text: Put z=1/3. The theorem gives π cot(π/3)=π/√3=1.813799. The series 3+∑2(1/3)/(1/9−n²) gives 1.813799 to 25 digits.

For 0<|z|<1, πz cot πz=1+∑_{n≥1}2z²/(z²−n²)=1−2∑_{n≥1}∑_{k≥1}(z/n)^{2k}. All terms of the double series are non-negative for real z, so the order of summation can change. We get πz cot πz=1−2∑_{k≥1}ζ(2k)z^{2k}.

Taylor expansion of u cos u/sin u with u=πz: divide 1−u²/2+u⁴/24 by 1−u²/6+u⁴/120. The quotient is 1−u²/3−u⁴/45+O(u⁶). Check: (1−u²/6+u⁴/120)(1−u²/3−u⁴/45)=1−u²/2+u⁴(1/120+1/18−1/45)+…, and 1/120+1/18−1/45=(3+20−8)/360=1/24.
Compare coefficients. The z² terms give −2ζ(2)z²=−π²z²/3, so ζ(2)=π²/6=1.644934. And −2ζ(4)z⁴=−π⁴z⁴/45, so ζ(4)=π⁴/90=1.082323.
A numeric Taylor expansion of πz cot πz at 0 gives coefficients −3.289868, −2.164646 and −2.034686 for z², z⁴, z⁶. These equal −π²/3, −π⁴/45 and −2ζ(6) with ζ(6)=1.017343=π⁶/945.

worked_application.result: π cot πz=1/z+∑2z/(z²−n²) gives ζ(2)=π²/6, ζ(4)=π⁴/90 and (numerically checked) ζ(6)=π⁶/945.
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: The series must be summed symmetrically. In the order n=1,2,3,… of 1/(z+n) and 1/(z−n) separately, the two parts diverge.
The proof of the real case uses the duplication formula, and it needs continuity at the poles. Without the removable singularity step the maximum principle argument fails.
The expansion is not a power series in z. It is a Mittag-Leffler expansion with poles at all integers.

steps.text: Convergence. On |z|≤R, ∑|z²/n²|≤R²∑1/n²<∞. So the product ∏(1−z²/n²) converges absolutely, and uniformly on compact sets, to a holomorphic function. Hence P(z)=πz∏(1−z²/n²) is entire. Its zeros are exactly the zeros of the factors: the integers.
Take x real with 0<x<1. All factors 1−x²/n² are positive. Put L_N(x)=ln(P_N(x)/(πx))=∑_{n≤N}ln(1−x²/n²). Then L_N(0)=0.
Differentiate: L_N′(x)=∑_{n≤N}(−2x/n²)/(1−x²/n²)=∑_{n≤N}2x/(x²−n²).
By the partial fraction expansion, L_N′(x)→π cot πx−1/x as N→∞, uniformly on [0,r] for each r<1. At x=0 the limit is 0.
Integrate on [0,x]. Uniform convergence of L_N′ allows the limit to pass under the integral: lim L_N(x)=∫_0^x(π cot πt−1/t)dt.
An antiderivative of π cot πt−1/t is ln(sin πt/t). Its limit at t→0 is ln π. So ∫_0^x=ln(sin πx/x)−ln π=ln(sin πx/(πx)).
So P_N(x)/(πx)→sin πx/(πx), which means P(x)=sin πx for x∈(0,1).

Both P and z↦sin πz are entire and they agree on (0,1). Let Z be the set where their difference and all its derivatives vanish. Z is closed. Z is open by the local identity theorem. Z contains (0,1), so Z=ℂ because ℂ is connected. Hence sin πz=P(z) for every complex z.

steps.text: At z=1/4 the partial product with N=10 is π/4·∏_{n≤10}(1−1/(16n²))=0.711326. The exact value is sin(π/4)=0.707107. The ratio is 1.00597.
At z=1/3 and N=10, the partial product is 0.875233 and sin(π/3)=0.866025. The ratio is 1.01063.
The error shrinks slowly. At z=1/4 and N=10⁵ the partial product is 0.7071072 and the error is 4.4·10⁻⁷, which is of order 1/N.
At z=1/2, sin(π/2)=1 gives 1=(π/2)∏(1−1/(4n²)). So π/2=∏(2n)²/((2n−1)(2n+1)). This is Wallis product. For N=10 the partial product is 1.533852, and π/2=1.570796.
The partial products at z=1/2 are P_10(1/2)=1.024086 and P_{10⁵}(1/2)=1.0000025. So the product converges like 1/N to 1.
Thus the sine product gives the infinite product for π without any integral of sin^m. Compare with the Wallis entry, which proves the same product by integration by parts.

results.name: Euler formula for ζ(2k) in terms of Bernoulli numbers
results.statement: Let B_n be the Bernoulli numbers, defined by t/(eᵗ−1)=∑_{n≥0}B_n tⁿ/n! with B₁=−1/2. Then for every integer k≥1, ζ(2k)=∑_{n≥1} n^{−2k}=(−1)^{k+1}(2π)^{2k}B_{2k}/(2·(2k)!). Equivalently ζ(2k)=(−1)^{k+1}2^{2k−1}π^{2k}B_{2k}/(2k)!. In particular ζ(2k)/π^{2k} is rational, and B_{2k} has sign (−1)^{k+1}. The proof also gives πz cot πz=∑_{k≥0}(−1)^k B_{2k}(2πz)^{2k}/(2k)! for |z|<1.
hypotheses: k is an integer with k≥1.
The Bernoulli numbers use the convention B₁=−1/2. With B₁=+1/2 the odd index changes sign, but B_{2k} does not change.
The power series identities hold for |z|<1, the largest disc around 0 that contains no pole of cot πz other than 0.

prerequisites.reason: Step 5 expands π z cot π z using the partial fraction series.

definitions.name: Bernoulli numbers

/-- Explicit formula for `ζ (2 * k)`, for `k ∈ ℕ` with `k ≠ 0`, in terms of the Bernoulli number
`bernoulli (2 * k)`.

Compare `hasSum_zeta_nat` for a version formulated in terms of a sum over `1 / n ^ (2 * k)`, and
`riemannZeta_neg_nat_eq_bernoulli` for values at negative integers (equivalent to the above via
the functional equation). -/
theorem riemannZeta_two_mul_nat {k : ℕ} (hk : k ≠ 0) :
    riemannZeta (2 * k) = (-1) ^ (k + 1) * (2 : ℂ) ^ (2 * k - 1)
      * (π : ℂ) ^ (2 * k) * bernoulli (2 * k) / (2 * k)! := by
  convert congr(($((hasSum_zeta_nat hk).tsum_eq) : ℂ))
  · rw [← Nat.cast_two, ← Nat.cast_mul, zeta_nat_eq_tsum_of_gt_one (by lia)]
    simp [push_cast]
  · norm_cast

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Bernoulli series. The function φ(t)=t/(eᵗ−1) with φ(0)=1 is holomorphic for |t|<2π. The zeros of eᵗ−1 are the points 2πim, and the point t=0 is a removable singularity. So the Taylor series of φ at 0 converges for |t|<2π. Its coefficients are B_n/n!, because they satisfy the same recursion as the formal definition.

Parity. Compute φ(t)+t/2=t(eᵗ+1)/(2(eᵗ−1))=(t/2)coth(t/2). This function is even. So the Taylor series of φ(t)+t/2 has no odd terms. Since the t term of φ is −t/2, we get B₁=−1/2 and B_n=0 for odd n≥3.
Switch to cotangent. Put t=2iu. Then (t/2)coth(t/2)=iu coth(iu)=iu(−i cot u)=u cot u. By step 2, u cot u=∑_{k≥0}B_{2k}(2iu)^{2k}/(2k)!=∑_{k≥0}(−1)^k B_{2k}(2u)^{2k}/(2k)! for |u|<π.
Put u=πz. Then πz cot πz=∑_{k≥0}(−1)^k B_{2k}(2πz)^{2k}/(2k)! for |z|<1.

Zeta expansion. By the partial fraction expansion of π cot πz, πz cot πz=1+∑_{n≥1}2z²/(z²−n²) for z∉ℤ. For |z|<1 write 2z²/(z²−n²)=−2(z/n)²/(1−(z/n)²)=−2∑_{k≥1}(z/n)^{2k}. The double series is absolutely convergent, because ∑_n∑_k|z/n|^{2k}≤∑_n(|z|²/n²)/(1−|z|²)<∞. So we may swap the sums. We get πz cot πz=1−2∑_{k≥1}ζ(2k)z^{2k}.

Compare. The series of steps 4 and 5 are two power series that agree on |z|<1. So their coefficients are equal. For k≥1 this gives −2ζ(2k)=(−1)^k B_{2k}(2π)^{2k}/(2k)!. Solve for ζ(2k) to get ζ(2k)=(−1)^{k+1}(2π)^{2k}B_{2k}/(2(2k)!).

Consequences. Since ζ(2k)>1, we get |B_{2k}|=2(2k)!ζ(2k)/(2π)^{2k}>2(2k)!/(2π)^{2k}. The sign of B_{2k} is (−1)^{k+1}. As ζ(2k)→1, |B_{2k}|∼2(2k)!/(2π)^{2k}. So the Bernoulli numbers grow faster than any geometric sequence, and the Taylor series of t/(eᵗ−1) has radius exactly 2π.

hypotheses: The Bernoulli numbers come from the recursion ∑_{j=0}^{m}C(m+1,j)B_j=0.

steps.text: The recursion gives B₂=1/6, B₄=−1/30, B₆=1/42, B₈=−1/30, B₁₀=5/66, B₁₂=−691/2730 and B₂₀=−174611/330.

The same computation gives ζ(6)/π⁶=1/945, ζ(8)/π⁸=1/9450, ζ(10)/π¹⁰=1/93555 and ζ(12)/π¹²=691/638512875.

Growth test. For k=10 the bound is 2·20!/(2π)²⁰=529.1237377. The exact value is |B₂₀|=174611/330=529.1242424. The ratio is 1.000000954, which equals ζ(20)=1.000000954, as the theorem predicts.
For k=15 the same ratio is 1.000000001. So |B₃₀|=601580873.9 agrees with 2·30!/(2π)³⁰ to nine digits.

results.name: Gauss limit formula for the Gamma function
results.statement: For every complex s that is not a pole of Γ (that is, s∉{0,−1,−2,…}), Γ(s)=lim_{n→∞} nˢ·n!/(s(s+1)⋯(s+n)). When Re s>0, Γ(s)=lim_{n→∞}∫₀ⁿ(1−t/n)ⁿt^{s−1}dt, and the n-th integral equals nˢB(s,n+1). The relative error of the n-th term is of order 1/n.
hypotheses: Γ(s)=∫₀^∞e^{−t}t^{s−1}dt for Re s>0. For other s, Γ is the meromorphic continuation, which obeys Γ(s+1)=sΓ(s).
nˢ means exp(s ln n) for n≥1.
The limit is taken over integers n.

prerequisites.reason: Step 3 passes the limit under the integral sign by dominated convergence.

definitions.name: Gauss sequence
definitions.text: G_n(s)=nˢ n!/∏_{j=0}^{n}(s+j). It is defined when s is not in {0,−1,…,−n}.

definitions.name: Euler Beta integral
definitions.text: B(u,v)=∫₀¹x^{u−1}(1−x)^{v−1}dx for Re u>0 and Re v>0.

definitions.name: dominated convergence
definitions.text: If fₙ→f pointwise and |fₙ|≤g with g integrable, then ∫fₙ→∫f.

/-- Euler's limit formula for the complex Gamma function. -/
theorem GammaSeq_tendsto_Gamma (s : ℂ) : Tendsto (GammaSeq s) atTop (𝓝 <| Gamma s) := by
  suffices ∀ m : ℕ, ⌊1 - s.re⌋₊ = m → Tendsto (GammaSeq s) atTop (𝓝 <| Gamma s) by tauto
  intro m
  induction m generalizing s with intro hs
  | zero => -- Base case: `0 < re s`, so Gamma is given by the integral formula
    rw [Nat.floor_eq_zero, sub_lt_self_iff] at hs
    apply (approx_Gamma_integral_tendsto_Gamma_integral hs).congr'
    filter_upwards [eventually_ne_atTop 0] with n hn using
      (GammaSeq_eq_approx_Gamma_integral hs hn).symm
  | succ m IH => -- Induction step: use recurrence formulae in `s` for Gamma and GammaSeq
    -- Silly case `s = 0`: both sides are zero
    rcases eq_or_ne s 0 with rfl | hsne
    · unfold GammaSeq
      simp [Finset.prod_range_succ']
    specialize IH (s + 1) ?_
    · rw [Nat.floor_eq_iff' (by lia)] at hs
      have : s.re ≤ -m := by grind
      rw [Nat.floor_eq_iff <| by simpa using (show s.re ≤ 0 by grind)]
      grind [add_re, one_re]
    rw [Gamma_add_one _ hsne] at IH
    have := (IH.div_const s).congr' <| by
      filter_upwards [eventually_ne_atTop 0] with n using GammaSeq_add_one_left s
    simp only [mul_comm _ (s.GammaSeq _)] at this
    rwa [mul_div_cancel_left₀ _ hsne, ← mul_one (Gamma s),
      tendsto_mul_iff_of_ne_zero _ (one_ne_zero' ℂ)] at this
    simp_rw [add_assoc]
    exact tendsto_natCast_div_add_atTop (1 + s)

/-- The main technical lemma for `GammaSeq_tendsto_Gamma`, expressing the integral defining the
Gamma function for `0 < re s` as the limit of a sequence of integrals over finite intervals. -/
theorem approx_Gamma_integral_tendsto_Gamma_integral {s : ℂ} (hs : 0 < re s) :
    Tendsto (fun n : ℕ => ∫ x : ℝ in 0..n, ((1 - x / n) ^ n : ℝ) * (x : ℂ) ^ (s - 1)) atTop
      (𝓝 <| Gamma s) := by
  rw [Gamma_eq_integral hs]
  -- We apply dominated convergence to the following function, which we will show is uniformly
  -- bounded above by the Gamma integrand `exp (-x) * x ^ (re s - 1)`.
  let f : ℕ → ℝ → ℂ := fun n =>
    indicator (Ioc 0 (n : ℝ)) fun x : ℝ => ((1 - x / n) ^ n : ℝ) * (x : ℂ) ^ (s - 1)
  -- integrability of f
  have f_ible : ∀ n : ℕ, Integrable (f n) (volume.restrict (Ioi 0)) := by
    intro n
    rw [integrable_indicator_iff (measurableSet_Ioc : MeasurableSet (Ioc (_ : ℝ) _)), IntegrableOn,
      Measure.restrict_restrict_of_subset Ioc_subset_Ioi_self, ← IntegrableOn, ←
      intervalIntegrable_iff_integrableOn_Ioc_of_le (by positivity : (0 : ℝ) ≤ n)]
    apply IntervalIntegrable.continuousOn_mul
    · refine intervalIntegral.intervalIntegrable_cpow' ?_
      rwa [sub_re, one_re, ← zero_sub, sub_lt_sub_iff_right]
    · fun_prop
  -- pointwise limit of f
  have f_tends : ∀ x : ℝ, x ∈ Ioi (0 : ℝ) →
      Tendsto (fun n : ℕ => f n x) atTop (𝓝 <| ↑(Real.exp (-x)) * (x : ℂ) ^ (s - 1)) := by
    intro x hx
    apply Tendsto.congr'
    · change ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop, ↑((1 - x / n) ^ n) * (x : ℂ) ^ (s - 1) = f n x
      filter_upwards [eventually_ge_atTop ⌈x⌉₊] with n hn
      rw [Nat.ceil_le] at hn
      dsimp only [f]
      rw [indicator_of_mem]
      exact ⟨hx, hn⟩
    · simp_rw [mul_comm]
      refine (Tendsto.comp (continuous_ofReal.tendsto _) ?_).const_mul _
      convert Real.tendsto_one_add_div_pow_exp (-x) using 1
      ext1 n
      rw [neg_div, ← sub_eq_add_neg]
  -- let `convert` identify the remaining goals
  convert!
    tendsto_integral_of_dominated_convergence _ (fun n => (f_ible n).1)
      (Real.GammaIntegral_convergent hs) _
      ((ae_restrict_iff' measurableSet_Ioi).mpr (ae_of_all _ f_tends)) using 1
    -- limit of f is the integrand we want

  -- limit of f is the integrand we want
  · ext1 n
    rw [MeasureTheory.integral_indicator (measurableSet_Ioc : MeasurableSet (Ioc (_ : ℝ) _)),
      intervalIntegral.integral_of_le (by positivity : 0 ≤ (n : ℝ)),
      Measure.restrict_restrict_of_subset Ioc_subset_Ioi_self]
  -- f is uniformly bounded by the Gamma integrand
  · intro n
    rw [ae_restrict_iff' measurableSet_Ioi]
    filter_upwards with x hx
    simp only [mem_Ioi, f] at hx ⊢
    rcases lt_or_ge (n : ℝ) x with (hxn | hxn)
    · rw [indicator_of_notMem (notMem_Ioc_of_gt hxn), norm_zero,
        mul_nonneg_iff_right_nonneg_of_pos (exp_pos _)]
      positivity
    · rw [indicator_of_mem (mem_Ioc.mpr ⟨mem_Ioi.mp hx, hxn⟩), norm_mul, Complex.norm_of_nonneg
          (pow_nonneg (sub_nonneg.mpr <| div_le_one_of_le₀ hxn <| by positivity) _),
          norm_cpow_eq_rpow_re_of_pos hx, sub_re, one_re]
      gcongr
      exact one_sub_div_pow_le_exp_neg hxn

steps.text: Truncated integrals. For Re s>0 and n≥1 put fₙ(t)=(1−t/n)ⁿt^{s−1} for 0<t<n, and fₙ(t)=0 for t≥n.
Domination. For 0≤t<n we have 0≤1−t/n≤e^{−t/n}. Raising to the power n gives 0≤(1−t/n)ⁿ≤e^{−t}. So |fₙ(t)|≤e^{−t}t^{Re s−1}, which is integrable on (0,∞).
Limit. For fixed t, (1−t/n)ⁿ→e^{−t}, so fₙ(t)→e^{−t}t^{s−1}. By dominated convergence, ∫₀ⁿ(1−t/n)ⁿt^{s−1}dt=∫₀^∞fₙ→Γ(s).
Scale. Substitute t=nu. Then ∫₀ⁿ(1−t/n)ⁿt^{s−1}dt=nˢ∫₀¹(1−u)ⁿu^{s−1}du=nˢB(s,n+1).

Evaluate B(s,n+1) by parts. For Re s>0 and n≥1, integrate u^{s−1}(1−u)ⁿ: the boundary terms [u^s(1−u)ⁿ/s]₀¹ vanish, and we get B(s,n+1)=(n/s)B(s+1,n). Repeat n times and use B(s+n,1)=1/(s+n). The result is B(s,n+1)=n!/(s(s+1)⋯(s+n)). Hence nˢB(s,n+1)=G_n(s), and G_n(s)→Γ(s) for Re s>0.
Recursion for G_n. Directly from the definition, G_n(s)=G_n(s+1)·(s+n+1)/(sn), valid when s and s+1,…,s+n+1 are nonzero.

Extend to all other s. Let s not be a pole and choose m≥0 with Re(s+m)>0. By step 5, G_n(s+m)→Γ(s+m). Apply step 6 m times. Each time, (s+j+n+1)/n→1, so G_n(s+j)→Γ(s+j+1)/(s+j)=Γ(s+j) by the recursion Γ(w+1)=wΓ(w). Going down from j=m−1 to j=0 gives G_n(s)→Γ(s).

Error size. From G_n(s)=G_n(s+1)(s+n+1)/(sn) and the Beta form one finds G_n(s)/Γ(s)−1=−s(s+1)/(2n)+O(1/n²). This is a numerical observation in the application below. The proof above gives convergence but no rate.

results.name: Euler reflection formula Γ(z)Γ(1−z)=π/sin(πz)
results.statement: For every complex z∉ℤ, Γ(z)Γ(1−z)=π/sin(πz). Consequently Γ has no zeros, Γ(1/2)=√π, and |Γ(1/2+it)|²=π/cosh(πt) for real t. The gauss product satisfies the exact finite identity G_n(z)G_n(1−z)=n/((n+1−z)·z·∏_{j=1}^{n}(1−z²/j²)).
hypotheses: z is complex and not an integer. At integers one factor of Γ(z)Γ(1−z) is at a pole, and sin(πz)=0.
Γ(1/2)>0 is used to fix the sign of the square root.

Step 5 uses the sine product for the limit of the partial products.

/-- Euler's reflection formula for the complex Gamma function. -/
theorem Gamma_mul_Gamma_one_sub (z : ℂ) : Gamma z * Gamma (1 - z) = π / sin (π * z) := by
  have pi_ne : (π : ℂ) ≠ 0 := Complex.ofReal_ne_zero.mpr pi_ne_zero
  by_cases hs : sin (↑π * z) = 0
  · -- first deal with silly case z = integer
    rw [hs, div_zero]
    rw [← neg_eq_zero, ← Complex.sin_neg, ← mul_neg, Complex.sin_eq_zero_iff, mul_comm] at hs
    obtain ⟨k, hk⟩ := hs
    rw [mul_eq_mul_right_iff, eq_false (ofReal_ne_zero.mpr pi_pos.ne'), or_false,
      neg_eq_iff_eq_neg] at hk
    rw [hk]
    cases k
    · rw [Int.ofNat_eq_natCast, Int.cast_natCast, Complex.Gamma_neg_nat_eq_zero, zero_mul]
    · rw [Int.cast_negSucc, neg_neg, Nat.cast_add, Nat.cast_one, add_comm, sub_add_cancel_left,
        Complex.Gamma_neg_nat_eq_zero, mul_zero]
  refine tendsto_nhds_unique ((GammaSeq_tendsto_Gamma z).mul (GammaSeq_tendsto_Gamma <| 1 - z)) ?_
  have : ↑π / sin (↑π * z) = 1 * (π / sin (π * z)) := by rw [one_mul]
  convert
    Tendsto.congr'
      ((eventually_ne_atTop 0).mp (Eventually.of_forall fun n hn => (GammaSeq_mul z hn).symm))
      (Tendsto.mul _ _)
  · convert tendsto_natCast_div_add_atTop (1 - z) using 1; ext1 n; rw [add_sub_assoc]
  · have : ↑π / sin (↑π * z) = 1 / (sin (π * z) / π) := by simp
    convert tendsto_const_nhds.div _ (div_ne_zero hs pi_ne)
    rw [← tendsto_mul_iff_of_ne_zero tendsto_const_nhds pi_ne, div_mul_cancel₀ _ pi_ne]
    convert tendsto_euler_sin_prod z using 1
    ext1 n; rw [mul_comm, ← mul_assoc]

theorem GammaSeq_mul (z : ℂ) {n : ℕ} (hn : n ≠ 0) :
    GammaSeq z n * GammaSeq (1 - z) n =
      n / (n + ↑1 - z) * (↑1 / (z * ∏ j ∈ Finset.range n, (↑1 - z ^ 2 / ((j : ℂ) + 1) ^ 2))) := by
  -- also true for n = 0 but we don't need it
  have aux : ∀ a b c d : ℂ, a * b * (c * d) = a * c * (b * d) := by intros; ring
  rw [GammaSeq, GammaSeq, div_mul_div_comm, aux, ← pow_two]
  have : (n : ℂ) ^ z * (n : ℂ) ^ (1 - z) = n := by
    rw [← cpow_add _ _ (Nat.cast_ne_zero.mpr hn), add_sub_cancel, cpow_one]
  rw [this, Finset.prod_range_succ', Finset.prod_range_succ, aux, ← Finset.prod_mul_distrib,
    Nat.cast_zero, add_zero, add_comm (1 - z) n, ← add_sub_assoc]
  have : ∀ j : ℕ, (z + ↑(j + 1)) * (↑1 - z + ↑j) =
      ((j + 1) ^ 2 :) * (↑1 - z ^ 2 / ((j : ℂ) + 1) ^ 2) := by
    intro j
    push_cast
    have : (j : ℂ) + 1 ≠ 0 := by rw [← Nat.cast_succ, Nat.cast_ne_zero]; exact Nat.succ_ne_zero j
    field
  simp_rw [this]
  rw [Finset.prod_mul_distrib, ← Nat.cast_prod, Finset.prod_pow,
    Finset.prod_range_add_one_eq_factorial, Nat.cast_pow,
    (by intros; ring : ∀ a b c d : ℂ, a * b * (c * d) = a * (d * (b * c))), ← div_div,
    mul_div_cancel_right₀, ← div_div, mul_comm z _, mul_one_div]
  exact pow_ne_zero 2 (Nat.cast_ne_zero.mpr <| by positivity)

steps.text: Fix z∉ℤ. Then neither z nor 1−z is a pole of Γ, and all denominators below are nonzero.
Limits. By the Gauss limit formula, G_n(z)→Γ(z) and G_n(1−z)→Γ(1−z). So G_n(z)G_n(1−z)→Γ(z)Γ(1−z).
Product formula. Write G_n(1−z)=n^{1−z}n!/∏_{j=0}^{n}(1−z+j)=n^{1−z}n!/∏_{j=1}^{n+1}(j−z). The factors nᶻ and n^{1−z} multiply to n. So G_n(z)G_n(1−z)=n·(n!)²/[z·∏_{j=1}^{n}(z+j)·∏_{j=1}^{n+1}(j−z)].

Regroup. Pull out the last factor n+1−z. The remaining product is ∏_{j=1}^{n}(j+z)(j−z)=∏_{j=1}^{n}(j²−z²)=(n!)²∏_{j=1}^{n}(1−z²/j²). So G_n(z)G_n(1−z)=n/((n+1−z)·z·∏_{j=1}^{n}(1−z²/j²)). This is an exact identity for each n.
Pass to the limit. We have n/(n+1−z)→1. By the Euler sine product, ∏_{j=1}^{n}(1−z²/j²)→sin(πz)/(πz), which is nonzero for z∉ℤ. Therefore the limit of the right side is 1/(z·sin(πz)/(πz))=π/sin(πz).
Combine steps 2 and 5: Γ(z)Γ(1−z)=π/sin(πz) for z∉ℤ.

No zeros. Since π/sin(πz) is finite and nonzero for z∉ℤ, both Γ(z) and Γ(1−z) are nonzero for z∉ℤ. At the poles Γ is not zero in the sense of a value, as 1/Γ vanishes there. So 1/Γ is entire with zeros exactly at 0,−1,−2,….

Special values. Put z=1/2: Γ(1/2)²=π/sin(π/2)=π. Since Γ(t)>0 for t>0, Γ(1/2)=√π. For z=1/2+it, we have 1−z=1/2−it=conj(z) and Γ(conj z)=conj(Γ(z)). So |Γ(1/2+it)|²=π/sin(π/2+iπt)=π/cos(iπt)=π/cosh(πt).

theorem Gamma_mul_Gamma_add_half (s : ℂ) :
    Gamma s * Gamma (s + 1 / 2) = Gamma (2 * s) * (2 : ℂ) ^ (1 - 2 * s) * ↑(√π) := by
  suffices (fun z => (Gamma z)⁻¹ * (Gamma (z + 1 / 2))⁻¹) = fun z =>
      (Gamma (2 * z))⁻¹ * (2 : ℂ) ^ (2 * z - 1) / ↑(√π) by
    convert congr_arg Inv.inv (congr_fun this s) using 1
    · rw [mul_inv, inv_inv, inv_inv]
    · rw [div_eq_mul_inv, mul_inv, mul_inv, inv_inv, inv_inv, ← cpow_neg, neg_sub]
  have h1 : AnalyticOnNhd ℂ (fun z : ℂ => (Gamma z)⁻¹ * (Gamma (z + 1 / 2))⁻¹) univ := by
    refine DifferentiableOn.analyticOnNhd ?_ isOpen_univ
    refine (differentiable_one_div_Gamma.mul ?_).differentiableOn
    exact differentiable_one_div_Gamma.comp (differentiable_id.add (differentiable_const _))
  have h2 : AnalyticOnNhd ℂ
      (fun z => (Gamma (2 * z))⁻¹ * (2 : ℂ) ^ (2 * z - 1) / ↑(√π)) univ := by
    refine DifferentiableOn.analyticOnNhd ?_ isOpen_univ
    refine (Differentiable.mul ?_ (differentiable_const _)).differentiableOn
    apply Differentiable.mul
    · exact differentiable_one_div_Gamma.comp (differentiable_id.const_mul _)
    · refine fun t => DifferentiableAt.const_cpow ?_ (Or.inl two_ne_zero)

steps.text: Beta–Gamma. For real s>0, B(s,s)=Γ(s)²/Γ(2s) and B(s,1/2)=Γ(s)Γ(1/2)/Γ(s+1/2).
Value of Γ(1/2). Put s=1/2 in step 1 with both parameters equal to 1/2: Γ(1/2)²=B(1/2,1/2)Γ(1)=∫₀¹du/√(u(1−u)). With u=sin²θ this integral is ∫₀^{π/2}2dθ=π. So Γ(1/2)=√π.
Fold the integral. The function u(1−u) is symmetric about u=1/2. So B(s,s)=∫₀¹(u(1−u))^{s−1}du=2∫₀^{1/2}(u(1−u))^{s−1}du.
Substitute v=4u(1−u). On [0,1/2] this is increasing from 0 to 1. We have dv=4(1−2u)du and (1−2u)²=1−v. So du=dv/(4√(1−v)), and u(1−u)=v/4.
Apply step 1 on both sides: Γ(s)²/Γ(2s)=2^{1−2s}Γ(s)√π/Γ(s+1/2). Cancel Γ(s)>0 and rearrange: Γ(s)Γ(s+1/2)=2^{1−2s}√π Γ(2s) for real s>0.

Extend. Let U=ℂ∖{s: 2s∈{0,−1,−2,…}}. It is open and connected. Both sides of the formula are holomorphic on U, because the poles of Γ(s), Γ(s+1/2) and Γ(2s) all lie in the excluded set. They agree on (0,∞), which has accumulation points in U. By the identity theorem they agree on U.
Poles. At s=−m (m≥0) Γ(s)=0 in the Lean convention. At s=−m−1/2 we have Γ(s+1/2)=0. In both cases Γ(2s)=0 too. So the formula holds for all s as a statement about values with that convention.
Half integer values. Put s=n≥1 and use Γ(n)=(n−1)! and Γ(2n)=(2n−1)!. Then Γ(n+1/2)=2^{1−2n}√π(2n−1)!/(n−1)!=(2n)!√π/(4ⁿ n!), because (2n−1)!=(2n)!/(2n) and (n−1)!=n!/n. The case n=0 is Γ(1/2)=√π.

steps.text: Fourier transform of the Gaussian. For a>0, ∫e^{−ax²−2πixξ}dx=√(π/a)e^{−π²ξ²/a}, by completing the square. With a=πt this gives f̂(ξ)=t^{−1/2}e^{−πξ²/t}.
Periodize. Put F(x)=∑_{n∈ℤ}f(x+n). The series and the series of derivatives converge uniformly on [0,1] by the Gaussian decay. So F is C¹ and 1-periodic.

Fourier coefficients of F. For m∈ℤ, ∫₀¹F(x)e^{−2πimx}dx=∑_n∫₀¹f(x+n)e^{−2πimx}dx=∑_n∫_n^{n+1}f(y)e^{−2πimy}dy=f̂(m). Here e^{−2πim(y−n)}=e^{−2πimy}. The interchange of sum and integral is allowed by uniform convergence.

Pointwise convergence. A C¹ periodic function equals its Fourier series at every point, and here the series converges absolutely because the coefficients f̂(m) have Gaussian decay. At x=0 this gives F(0)=∑_m f̂(m).
Read off both sides. F(0)=∑_n e^{−πtn²}=θ(t). Also ∑_m f̂(m)=t^{−1/2}∑_m e^{−πm²/t}=t^{−1/2}θ(1/t). So θ(t)=t^{−1/2}θ(1/t), that is, θ(1/t)=√t θ(t).

Complex form. Both sides of ∑e^{πin²τ}=(−iτ)^{−1/2}∑e^{−πin²/τ} are holomorphic in τ on the upper half plane. They agree for τ=it with t>0 by step 5, which is a set with accumulation points. The identity theorem gives equality for all Im τ>0.

steps.text: Mellin transform of ψ. For Re s>1 and n≥1, the substitution u=πn²t gives ∫₀^∞e^{−πn²t}t^{s/2−1}dt=π^{−s/2}Γ(s/2)n^{−s}. Sum over n. The interchange of sum and integral is allowed because ∑∫|e^{−πn²t}t^{s/2−1}|dt=π^{−σ/2}Γ(σ/2)ζ(σ)<∞ with σ=Re s. So Λ(s)=∫₀^∞ψ(t)t^{s/2−1}dt for Re s>1.
Theta inversion. For t>0, θ(1/t)=√tθ(t). With θ=1+2ψ this reads ψ(1/t)=√tψ(t)+(√t−1)/2.
Split the integral at t=1. Write Λ(s)=∫₁^∞ψ(t)t^{s/2−1}dt+∫₀¹ψ(t)t^{s/2−1}dt. In the second integral put t→1/t. It becomes ∫₁^∞ψ(1/t)t^{−s/2−1}dt.

Continuation. Since ψ(t)≤2e^{−πt} for t≥1, the integral converges locally uniformly in s∈ℂ and is entire. So the right side of step 5 is meromorphic on ℂ with simple poles at s=1 (residue 1) and s=0 (residue −1). This is the continuation of Λ.
Symmetry. The right side of step 5 is unchanged under s→1−s. The terms 1/(s−1)−1/s become 1/(−s)−1/(1−s)=1/(s−1)−1/s. The integrand t^{s/2−1}+t^{(1−s)/2−1} swaps its two terms. So Λ(1−s)=Λ(s) on ℂ.

steps.text: Functional equation. For s∉{1,0,−1,…}, ζ(1−s)=2(2π)^{−s}Γ(s)cos(πs/2)ζ(s). Put s=m+1 for an integer m≥1. Then 1−s=−m, and s is not a pole of Γ.

Even m. If m is even, then s=m+1 is odd and cos(π(m+1)/2)=0. Since Γ(s) and ζ(s) are finite (s≥3), ζ(−m)=0. For m=2k this gives the trivial zeros. It also matches the claim, because B_{m+1}=0 for odd index m+1≥3.
Odd m. Let m=2k−1 with k≥1, so s=2k. Then cos(πk)=(−1)^k, Γ(2k)=(2k−1)!, and ζ(1−2k)=2(2π)^{−2k}(2k−1)!(−1)^kζ(2k).

Insert the even values. ζ(2k)=(−1)^{k+1}(2π)^{2k}B_{2k}/(2(2k)!). The product is 2·(2k−1)!·(−1)^k·(−1)^{k+1}B_{2k}/(2·(2k)!)=−B_{2k}/(2k). So ζ(1−2k)=−B_{2k}/(2k). This agrees with (−1)^{n}B_{n+1}/(n+1) for n=2k−1, because (−1)^n=−1.

The case n=0. Here s=1 is the pole of ζ and step 1 does not apply. Use the limit s→1. We have ζ(s)=1/(s−1)+O(1), so (s−1)ζ(s)→1. Also cos(πs/2)=−sin(π(s−1)/2)=−(π/2)(s−1)+O((s−1)³). So cos(πs/2)ζ(s)→−π/2. Then ζ(1−s)→2(2π)^{−1}Γ(1)(−π/2)=−1/2. Since ζ is continuous at 0, ζ(0)=−1/2. This equals B₁·(−1)⁰/1 with B₁=−1/2.
Combine. The cases of steps 2, 4 and 5 cover every n≥0. In each case ζ(−n)=(−1)ⁿB_{n+1}/(n+1).

/-- The function `ζ s - 1 / (s - 1)` tends to `γ` as `s → 1`. -/
theorem _root_.tendsto_riemannZeta_sub_one_div :
    Tendsto (fun s : ℂ ↦ riemannZeta s - 1 / (s - 1)) (𝓝[≠] 1) (𝓝 γ) := by
  -- We use the removable-singularity theorem to show that *some* limit over `𝓝[≠] (1 : ℂ)` exists,
  -- and then use the previous result to deduce that this limit must be `γ`.
  let f (s : ℂ) := riemannZeta s - 1 / (s - 1)
  suffices ∃ C, Tendsto f (𝓝[≠] 1) (𝓝 C) by
    obtain ⟨C, hC⟩ := this
    suffices Tendsto (fun s : ℝ ↦ f s) _ _
      from (tendsto_nhds_unique this tendsto_riemannZeta_sub_one_div_nhds_right) ▸ hC
    refine hC.comp (tendsto_nhdsWithin_of_tendsto_nhds_of_eventually_within _ ?_ ?_)
    · exact (Complex.continuous_ofReal.tendsto 1).mono_left (nhdsWithin_le_nhds ..)
    · filter_upwards [self_mem_nhdsWithin] with a ha
      rw [mem_compl_singleton_iff, ← Complex.ofReal_one, Ne, Complex.ofReal_inj]
      exact ne_of_gt ha
  refine ⟨_, Complex.tendsto_limUnder_of_differentiable_on_punctured_nhds_of_isLittleO ?_ ?_⟩
  · filter_upwards [self_mem_nhdsWithin] with s hs
    refine (differentiableAt_riemannZeta hs).sub ((differentiableAt_const _).div ?_ ?_)
    · fun_prop
    · rwa [mem_compl_singleton_iff, ← sub_ne_zero] at hs
  · refine Asymptotics.isLittleO_of_tendsto' ?_ ?_
    · filter_upwards [self_mem_nhdsWithin] with t ht ht'
      rw [inv_eq_zero, sub_eq_zero] at ht'

steps.text: Apply Abel summation with a_n=1, so A(t)=⌊t⌋, and f(t)=t^{−s}. For Re s>1 and integer N, ∑_{n≤N}n^{−s}=N·N^{−s}+s∫₁^N⌊t⌋t^{−s−1}dt.
Let N→∞. Since Re s>1, N^{1−s}→0 and the integral converges absolutely. So ζ(s)=s∫₁^∞⌊t⌋t^{−s−1}dt.
Split ⌊t⌋=t−{t}. Then s∫₁^∞t·t^{−s−1}dt=s∫₁^∞t^{−s}dt=s/(s−1). So ζ(s)=s/(s−1)−s∫₁^∞{t}t^{−s−1}dt.

Continuation. The function J(s)=∫₁^∞{t}t^{−s−1}dt satisfies |{t}t^{−s−1}|≤t^{−Re s−1}, which is integrable when Re s>0. The integral is holomorphic there, by dominated convergence and Morera. So the right side of step 3 is holomorphic on Re s>0 except at s=1, and it agrees with ζ for Re s>1. It is the continuation of ζ.
Pole and constant. s/(s−1)=1+1/(s−1). So ζ(s)−1/(s−1)=1−sJ(s), which is holomorphic at s=1. Its value at s=1 is 1−J(1)=1−∫₁^∞{t}t⁻²dt.

Identify J(1). Abel summation with f(t)=1/t and an integer N gives H_N=1+∫₁^N⌊t⌋t⁻²dt=1+ln N−∫₁^N{t}t⁻²dt. So H_N−ln N=1−∫₁^N{t}t⁻²dt. The right side tends to 1−J(1) as N→∞. The left side tends to γ by definition.
Conclusion. lim_{s→1}(ζ(s)−1/(s−1))=1−J(1)=γ. So the Laurent expansion at s=1 is ζ(s)=1/(s−1)+γ+O(s−1).

steps.text: Write the product as a double series. L(f,s)L(g,s)=∑_{a≥1}∑_{b≥1}f(a)a^{−s}g(b)b^{−s}=∑_{a,b}f(a)g(b)(ab)^{−s}.
Absolute convergence. ∑_{a,b}|f(a)||g(b)|(ab)^{−σ}=(∑|f(a)|a^{−σ})(∑|g(b)|b^{−σ})<∞ with σ=Re s. So we may sum the terms in any order.
Group by the product n=ab. Each n≥1 collects the terms with ab=n. The sum over these terms is ∑_{ab=n}f(a)g(b)n^{−s}=(f∗g)(n)n^{−s}.
Result. L(f,s)L(g,s)=∑_{n≥1}(f∗g)(n)n^{−s}=L(f∗g,s). The same grouping applied to |f|,|g| shows absolute convergence of L(f∗g,s), since |f∗g|≤|f|∗|g|.

The Möbius inverse. Let 1 be the constant function 1. The Möbius property ∑_{d|n}μ(d)=[n=1] says μ∗1=δ, where δ(1)=1 and δ(n)=0 otherwise. Apply step 4 with f=μ and g=1: L(μ,s)ζ(s)=L(δ,s)=1 for Re s>1. So 1/ζ(s)=∑μ(n)n^{−s}.
Coprime pairs. For a,b∈[1,N], [gcd(a,b)=1]=∑_{k|gcd(a,b)}μ(k). Sum over a and b. The number of multiples of k in [1,N] is ⌊N/k⌋. So C(N)=#{coprime pairs}=∑_{k≤N}μ(k)⌊N/k⌋².
Limit. ⌊N/k⌋²=N²/k²+O(N/k). So C(N)/N²=∑_{k≤N}μ(k)/k²+O(ln N/N). The first sum tends to L(μ,2)=1/ζ(2)=6/π². So C(N)/N²→6/π².

results.name: Galois connection, closure operator and the polarity of closed elements
results.statement: Let P and Q be posets and let l:P→Q and u:Q→P be maps with l(a)≤b if and only if a≤u(b), for all a in P and b in Q. Then: (1) a≤u(l(a)) and l(u(b))≤b. (2) l and u are monotone. (3) l∘u∘l=l and u∘l∘u=u. (4) cl=u∘l is a closure operator on P: it is extensive, monotone and idempotent, and cl(a) is the least element of the form u(q) above a. (5) Let P_c be the set of a with a=u(l(a)) and Q_k the set of b with b=l(u(b)). Then l restricts to an order isomorphism P_c→Q_k, with inverse u. (6) If a subset S of P has a join, then l sends it to the join of l(S). Dually, u sends every existing meet in Q to a meet in P.
hypotheses: P and Q are partially ordered sets. Preorders also work for parts (1) and (2).
The pair (l,u) satisfies the equivalence l(a)≤b⇔a≤u(b) for all a and b. This is called a Galois connection.
Part (6) holds for each join, or meet, that exists. No completeness of P or Q is needed.

definitions.name: Galois connection
definitions.text: A pair of maps l:P→Q and u:Q→P with l(a)≤b if and only if a≤u(b). The map l is the lower adjoint. The map u is the upper adjoint.

definitions.name: closure operator
definitions.text: A map cl:P→P with a≤cl(a), cl monotone, and cl(cl(a))=cl(a). The elements with cl(a)=a are the closed elements.

definitions.name: derivation operators of a formal context
definitions.text: A formal context is a set G of objects, a set M of attributes and a relation I⊆G×M. For A⊆G put A′ for the set of attributes shared by all objects in A. For B⊆M put B′ for the set of objects that have all attributes in B. The two maps A↦A′ and B↦B′ reverse inclusion. They form a Galois connection when M is ordered by reverse inclusion.

steps.text: Part 1. Put b=l(a) in the equivalence. Because l(a)≤l(a), we get a≤u(l(a)). Put a=u(b). Because u(b)≤u(b), we get l(u(b))≤b.

Part 2. Let a≤a′ in P. By part 1, a≤a′≤u(l(a′)). The equivalence with b=l(a′) turns a≤u(l(a′)) into l(a)≤l(a′). So l is monotone. Let b≤b′ in Q. Then l(u(b))≤b≤b′ by part 1. The equivalence turns this into u(b)≤u(b′). So u is monotone.

Part 3. Apply part 1 to a to get a≤u(l(a)). The map l is monotone, so l(a)≤l(u(l(a))). Apply part 1 to b=l(a) to get l(u(l(a)))≤l(a). By antisymmetry l(u(l(a)))=l(a). The identity u∘l∘u=u follows by the dual argument: u(b)≥u(l(u(b))) by monotonicity of u and l(u(b))≤b, and u(b)≤u(l(u(b))) by part 1 with a=u(b).

Part 4. Extensive is part 1. Monotone holds because cl is a composite of monotone maps. Idempotent: cl(cl(a))=u(l(u(l(a))))=u(l(a)) by part 3 applied to the inner l(u(l(a))). Now let a≤c with c=u(q) for some q. Then l(a)≤q by the equivalence. Apply the monotone map u: cl(a)=u(l(a))≤u(q)=c. So cl(a) is the least such element above a.

Part 5. If a is in P_c, then l(u(l(a)))=l(a) by part 3. So l(a) is in Q_k. If b is in Q_k, then u(l(u(b)))=u(b) by part 3, so u(b) is in P_c. For a in P_c, u(l(a))=a by definition. For b in Q_k, l(u(b))=b by definition. So l and u are inverse bijections between P_c and Q_k. Both are monotone by part 2, so both are order isomorphisms.

Part 6. Let j be the join of S in P. Because l is monotone, l(j) is an upper bound of l(S). Let b be any upper bound of l(S). For each x in S, l(x)≤b, so x≤u(b) by the equivalence. So u(b) is an upper bound of S, and j≤u(b). The equivalence gives l(j)≤b. So l(j) is the least upper bound of l(S). The statement for meets and u is the same argument with the order reversed.

Remark for the polarity form. If the pair is antitone, as for the derivation operators of a formal context, replace the order on Q by its reverse. The proof above then applies, and the lower adjoint turns unions into intersections.

worked_application.title: The closed sets of a small formal context
worked_application.goal: Take five objects 1 to 5 and four attributes a,b,c,d. Object 1 has a,b. Object 2 has b,c. Object 3 has a,b,d. Object 4 has c,d. Object 5 has b,c,d. Find all closed sets of objects and check the polarity.
hypotheses: Let A↦A′ send objects to the attributes common to all of them. Let B↦B′ send attributes to the objects that have all of them. The empty set of objects has A′=M.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The two derivation operators form a Galois connection, once M is ordered by reverse inclusion. So the theorem gives the closure A↦A′′ and an order isomorphism of closed object sets with closed attribute sets.

steps.text: Compute the closure of {1,2}. The common attributes are {b}, because object 1 has a,b and object 2 has b,c. Then {b}′ is {1,2,3,5}. So the closure of {1,2} is {1,2,3,5}. It is larger than {1,2}, as the closure must be.
Check idempotence. {1,2,3,5}′={b}, and {b}′={1,2,3,5}. The closure of {1,2,3,5} is itself.

List all closed object sets. They are ∅, {3}, {5}, {1,3}, {2,5}, {3,5}, {4,5}, {2,4,5}, {3,4,5}, {1,2,3,5} and {1,2,3,4,5}. That is 11 sets. The matching attribute sets A′ are abcd, abd, bcd, ab, bc, bd, cd, c, d, b and the empty set.

Count the closed attribute sets directly. The sets B with B′′=B are abcd, abd, bcd, ab, bc, bd, cd, c, d, b and the empty set. That is also 11 sets. This agrees with part 5: the two closed families have the same size.

Check part 6 for joins. Take A={1,3} and B={2,5}. Then A′={a,b} and B′={b,c}. The union A∪B={1,2,3,5} has (A∪B)′={b}, which equals {a,b}∩{b,c}. In the reversed order on attribute sets, the join of A′ and B′ is their intersection. So the lower adjoint turns a union into a join.

Part 4 predicts that {1,3} is the smallest closed set that contains {1,3}. It is closed, since {1,3}′={a,b} and {a,b}′={1,3}. The set {1,2} is not closed, and the smallest closed superset is {1,2,3,5}. No other closed set from the list is a superset of {1,2} and smaller.

worked_application.result: The context has 11 closed object sets and 11 closed attribute sets. The map A↦A′ is an order isomorphism between them when the attribute sets are ordered by reverse inclusion. The closure of {1,2} is {1,2,3,5}.
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: The pair must satisfy the full equivalence. A monotone pair with only a≤u(l(a)) and l(u(b))≤b is enough, and it is equivalent to the equivalence. A pair of monotone maps with only one of the two inequalities is not enough.
Part 6 does not say that l preserves meets. The lower adjoint need not preserve meets. It does so only in special cases, such as a distributive lattice of closed sets.
The closed elements form a complete lattice when P is a complete lattice. A concept lattice from a finite context is always complete, but it can be much bigger than the context.

results.name: Yoneda lemma and the full faithfulness of the Yoneda embedding
results.statement: Let C be a locally small category and F:C^op→Set a functor. For every object X, the map Φ:Nat(Hom(−,X),F)→F(X), Φ(η)=η_X(id_X), is a bijection. Its inverse sends x in F(X) to the transformation η^x with (η^x)_Y(f)=F(f)(x) for f:Y→X. The bijection is natural in X and in F. Dually, for a functor G:C→Set, Nat(Hom(X,−),G)≅G(X), by η↦η_X(id_X). Consequences: (a) the Yoneda embedding X↦Hom(−,X) is fully faithful. (b) Hom(−,X)≅Hom(−,Y) as functors if and only if X≅Y.
hypotheses: C is locally small: each Hom(X,Y) is a set.
F is a functor from C^op to the category of sets. The covariant statement uses a functor from C to sets.
Natural transformations are taken between functors C^op→Set, so Nat(Hom(−,X),F) is a set.

definitions.name: representable functor
definitions.text: A functor C^op→Set that is naturally isomorphic to Hom(−,X) for some object X. The object X represents the functor.

definitions.name: Yoneda embedding
definitions.text: The functor C→Fun(C^op,Set) that sends X to Hom(−,X) and a morphism g:X→Y to the transformation g∘−.

definitions.name: natural transformation
definitions.text: A family η_Y:F(Y)→G(Y) with G(f)∘η_Y=η_Z∘F(f) for each f:Z→Y.

source.excerpt:
/-- We have a type-level equivalence between natural transformations from the yoneda embedding
and elements of `F.obj X`, without any universe switching.
-/
@[implicit_reducible]
def yonedaEquiv {X : C} {F : Cᵒᵖ ⥤ Type v₁} : (yoneda.obj X ⟶ F) ≃ F.obj (op X) where
  toFun η := η.app (op X) (𝟙 X)
  invFun ξ := { app _ := ↾fun f ↦ F.map f.op ξ }
  left_inv := by
    intro η
    ext Y f
    simp [← NatTrans.naturality_apply]
  right_inv := by intro ξ; simp

steps.text: Write y(X)=Hom(−,X). For f:Y→X, F(f):F(X)→F(Y) because F is contravariant. The functor y(X) sends g:Z→Y to the map h↦h∘g from Hom(Y,X) to Hom(Z,X).

Φ and Ψ are maps. Define Ψ(x)_Y(f)=F(f)(x). We check that Ψ(x) is natural. Let g:Z→Y and f:Y→X. Then Ψ(x)_Z(f∘g)=F(f∘g)(x)=F(g)(F(f)(x))=F(g)(Ψ(x)_Y(f)). This is the square for g, so Ψ(x) is a natural transformation.
Φ(Ψ(x))=Ψ(x)_X(id_X)=F(id_X)(x)=x, because F preserves identities.

Ψ(Φ(η))=η. Let η be natural and f:Y→X. The naturality square of η for the morphism f says η_Y(h∘f)=F(f)(η_X(h)) for each h in Hom(X,X). Take h=id_X. Then η_Y(f)=F(f)(η_X(id_X))=Ψ(Φ(η))_Y(f). So η=Ψ(Φ(η)). Steps 3 and 4 show that Φ is a bijection with inverse Ψ.
Naturality in F. Let θ:F→G be a natural transformation. Then Φ(θ∘η)=θ_X(η_X(id_X))=θ_X(Φ(η)). So Φ commutes with the maps induced by θ.

Naturality in X. Let h:X′→X. Then the induced map on Nat(y(X),F) sends η to η∘y(h). We get Φ(η∘y(h))=η_{X′}(h∘id_{X′})=η_{X′}(id_X∘h)=F(h)(η_X(id_X))=F(h)(Φ(η)), by the naturality square of η for h. This is the naturality in X.

Consequence (a). Take F=y(Y). Then Φ:Nat(y(X),y(Y))→Hom(X,Y). For g:X→Y, the transformation y(g) has Φ(y(g))=g∘id_X=g. So the composite g↦y(g)↦Φ(y(g)) is the identity on Hom(X,Y). Since Φ is a bijection, the map g↦y(g) is also a bijection from Hom(X,Y) onto Nat(y(X),y(Y)). So y is fully faithful.

Consequence (b). If X≅Y, then y(X)≅y(Y) because a functor preserves isomorphisms. Conversely let η:y(X)→y(Y) be an isomorphism with inverse η′. By (a), η=y(g) and η′=y(h) for unique g and h. Then y(h∘g)=y(h)∘y(g)=id=y(id_X). Since y is faithful, h∘g=id_X. In the same way g∘h=id_Y.
Covariant form. Apply the result to C^op. The category of functors C^op→Set for C^op is the category of functors C→Set, so Nat(Hom(X,−),G)≅G(X) by η↦η_X(id_X).

worked_application.title: Natural power operations on groups are powers
worked_application.goal: On the category of groups, let T_m(G)={x in G: x^m=1}. Find all natural transformations T_12→T_8. Natural means that the map commutes with every group homomorphism.
hypotheses: The category is the category of all groups, with all homomorphisms.
T_m is a functor to sets. A homomorphism f sends T_m(G) into T_m(H).
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: T_m is represented by the cyclic group Z/m. A homomorphism from Z/m to G is determined by the image of the generator, and this image can be any x with x^m=1. This gives a natural isomorphism Hom(Z/m,G)≅T_m(G). The covariant Yoneda lemma then applies.

steps.text: By the covariant Yoneda lemma, Nat(T_12,T_8)≅Nat(Hom(Z/12,−),T_8)≅T_8(Z/12). Write Z/12 additively with generator 1.

T_8(Z/12) is the set of k in Z/12 with 8k≡0 (mod 12). Solve: 8k is a multiple of 12 if and only if 2k is a multiple of 3, i.e. k is a multiple of 3. So k is in {0,3,6,9}. This set has gcd(12,8)=4 elements.

The Yoneda inverse of the element k in T_8(Z/12) is the transformation η^k. Its component at G sends x in T_12(G) to the image of k under the homomorphism φ_x:Z/12→G that sends 1 to x. This image is x^k. So η^k is x↦x^k.
Check that x↦x^k really maps T_12(G) into T_8(G) for k=3. We have (x^3)^8=x^24=(x^12)^2=1. The same holds for k=0,6,9 because 8k is a multiple of 12 in each case.

No other natural operation exists. For example, x↦x^{−1} would need k=11, but 8·11=88 is not a multiple of 12. Test it in Z/12 with x=1: x is in T_12, but the image −8≡4 (mod 12) is not zero, so it is not in T_8. So the inverse map is not a natural transformation into T_8.
In general Nat(T_m,T_n) has exactly gcd(m,n) elements, which are the maps x↦x^k with k a multiple of m/gcd(m,n).

worked_application.result: There are exactly 4 natural transformations T_12→T_8. They are x↦x^0, x↦x^3, x↦x^6 and x↦x^9.
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: The lemma needs local smallness. Without it, Nat(y(X),F) may fail to be a set.
The bijection is not a statement about the objects only: representing objects are unique up to unique isomorphism, but one must give the universal element.
Yoneda is for Set valued functors. For enriched categories one needs the enriched form.

results.name: Left adjoints preserve colimits, right adjoints preserve limits
results.statement: Let L:C→D and R:D→C be functors with a bijection Hom_D(LX,Y)≅Hom_C(X,RY) natural in X and Y. Let K:J→C be a diagram and let (c,ι) be a colimit cocone of K. Then (Lc,Lι) is a colimit cocone of L∘K. Dually, if (d,π) is a limit cone of a diagram H:J→D, then (Rd,Rπ) is a limit cone of R∘H. In particular L preserves initial objects, coproducts, coequalizers and cokernels, and R preserves terminal objects, products, equalizers and kernels.
hypotheses: L is left adjoint to R. The bijection is natural in both variables.
The colimit or limit is assumed to exist in the source category. The theorem says it is preserved. It does not say colimits exist.
The index category J is arbitrary, so the result covers all shapes at the same time.
results.empty_prerequisites_reason: The proof uses only the naturality of the adjunction bijection and the universal property. No catalog theorem is cited.

definitions.name: adjunction
definitions.text: Functors L and R with a bijection a_{X,Y}:Hom_D(LX,Y)→Hom_C(X,RY) natural in X and Y. Naturality in X says a(h∘Lf)=a(h)∘f for f:X′→X.

definitions.name: cocone and colimit
definitions.text: A cocone over K with vertex Y is a family g_j:K(j)→Y with g_k∘K(u)=g_j for each u:j→k. A colimit is a cocone (c,ι) such that each cocone factors through it in exactly one way: g_j=h∘ι_j for a unique h:c→Y.

definitions.name: cokernel
definitions.text: The cokernel of f:A→B in a category with zero maps is the colimit of the parallel pair f,0:A→B.

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: We prove the colimit part. The limit part is the same argument in the opposite categories, where R becomes a left adjoint.
Fix Y in D. Write a for the adjunction bijection. Naturality in the first variable says a(h∘L(f))=a(h)∘f for h:LX→Y and f:X′→X.

Cocones correspond. Let g_j:L(K(j))→Y be a family of maps. Let g_j′=a(g_j):K(j)→RY. For u:j→k in J, naturality gives a(g_k∘L(K(u)))=a(g_k)∘K(u). Since a is a bijection, g_k∘L(K(u))=g_j holds if and only if g_k′∘K(u)=g_j′. So (g_j) is a cocone over L∘K with vertex Y if and only if (g_j′) is a cocone over K with vertex RY. The assignment is a bijection between these two sets of cocones.
Use the colimit property of (c,ι). The cocones over K with vertex RY are in bijection with the morphisms f:c→RY, by f↦(f∘ι_j). This is the universal property.
Morphisms correspond. The bijection a sends h:Lc→Y to f=a(h):c→RY. Naturality gives a(h∘L(ι_j))=a(h)∘ι_j=f∘ι_j. So the family (h∘L(ι_j)) corresponds, under step 3, to the cocone (f∘ι_j).

Combine. The map h↦(h∘L(ι_j))_j from Hom(Lc,Y) to the set of cocones over L∘K with vertex Y is the composite of three bijections: a, then f↦(f∘ι_j), then the inverse of the correspondence in step 3. So it is a bijection. This says that for every cocone (g_j) over L∘K with vertex Y there is exactly one h with g_j=h∘L(ι_j). So (Lc,Lι) is a colimit.
Special cases. The empty diagram gives the initial object. A discrete diagram gives coproducts. The parallel pair f,0 gives cokernels. Dually R preserves terminal objects, products and kernels.

worked_application.title: Z/12 ⊗ Z/18 by preserving a cokernel
worked_application.goal: For an abelian group M, the functor M⊗− is left adjoint to Hom(M,−). Use the theorem to compute Z/12 ⊗ Z/18 and then check that tensoring does not preserve kernels.
hypotheses: Work in abelian groups.
The adjunction is the tensor-hom adjunction: Hom(M⊗A,B)≅Hom(A,Hom(M,B)), natural in A and B.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: M⊗− is a left adjoint, so it preserves all colimits that exist. The group Z/n is the cokernel of the map n:Z→Z, which is a colimit of the parallel pair (n,0).

steps.text: Write Z/18 as the cokernel of multiplication by 18 on Z. The theorem says that M⊗Z/18 is the cokernel of M⊗(18):M⊗Z→M⊗Z. Since M⊗Z≅M, this is the cokernel of multiplication by 18 on M. So M⊗Z/18≅M/18M.
Take M=Z/12. The subgroup 18M is generated by 18 mod 12, i.e. by 6. It has 2 elements, namely 0 and 6. So M/18M has 12/2=6 elements and is cyclic. Hence Z/12⊗Z/18≅Z/6, which is Z/gcd(12,18).
Check with a presentation. Z/12⊗Z/18 is generated by one element e⊗f with relations 12(e⊗f)=0 and 18(e⊗f)=0. The relations generate gcd(12,18)=6 times the generator. So the group is Z/6. This agrees.
Use preservation of coproducts. Z/12⊗(Z/18⊕Z/5)≅(Z/12⊗Z/18)⊕(Z/12⊗Z/5). The second term is Z/gcd(12,5)=Z/1=0, so the total is Z/6.

Kernels are not preserved. The map 2:Z→Z has trivial kernel. Apply Z/2⊗−. We get the map 2:Z/2→Z/2, which is zero, with kernel Z/2. A left adjoint is not required to preserve limits, and here it fails to.

In contrast, the right adjoint Hom(Z/2,−) preserves kernels. The map 2:Z/4→Z/4 has kernel {0,2}≅Z/2. Now Hom(Z/2,Z/4)≅Z/2 by sending a homomorphism to the image of 1, which lies in {0,2}. The induced map 2 on it is zero, so its kernel is Z/2. This equals Hom(Z/2,{0,2})≅Z/2, as the theorem predicts.

worked_application.result: Z/12⊗Z/18≅Z/6, and Z/12⊗(Z/18⊕Z/5)≅Z/6. The functor Z/2⊗− does not preserve the kernel of 2:Z→Z.

limitations: Left adjoints do not preserve limits and right adjoints do not preserve colimits in general. The kernel example shows this.
The theorem needs the existence of the original colimit. A left adjoint need not create colimits.
Right exactness of a tensor functor is a special case. Left exactness needs flatness.

results.name: Snake lemma and the connecting homomorphism
results.statement: Let R be a ring. Consider a commutative diagram of R-modules with exact rows A→B→C→0 (maps f,g) and 0→A′→B′→C′ (maps f′,g′), and vertical maps a:A→A′, b:B→B′, c:C→C′, so that b∘f=f′∘a and c∘g=g′∘b. Then there is a homomorphism δ:ker c→coker a such that the sequence ker a→ker b→ker c→δ coker a→coker b→coker c is exact. The maps other than δ are induced by f, g, f′ and g′. The map δ is computed as follows. For z in ker c, pick y in B with g(y)=z. Then b(y) lies in the image of f′, say b(y)=f′(x′) for a unique x′. Then δ(z)=x′ mod a(A). If f is injective, then ker a→ker b is injective. If g′ is surjective, then coker b→coker c is surjective.
hypotheses: The rows are exact where stated: f(A)=ker g, g is surjective, f′ is injective, and f′(A′)=ker g′.
Both squares commute.
The proof is by diagram chase in modules. The same result holds in every abelian category.

definitions.name: connecting homomorphism

source.excerpt:
/--
**Snake Lemma**
Suppose we have an exact commutative diagram
```
                K₃
                |
                ι₃
                ↓
M₁ -f₁→ M₂ -f₂→ M₃
|       |       |
i₁      i₂      i₃
↓       ↓       ↓
N₁ -g₁→ N₂ -g₂→ N₃
|
π₁
↓
C₁

```
such that `f₂` is surjective with a (set-theoretic) section `σ`, `g₁` is injective with a
(set-theoretic) retraction `ρ`,
then the map `π₁ ∘ ρ ∘ i₂ ∘ σ ∘ ι₃` is a linear map from `K₃` to `C₁`.

Also see `SnakeLemma.δ'` for a noncomputable version
that does not require an explicit section and retraction.
-/
def SnakeLemma.δ : K₃ →ₗ[R] C₁ :=
  haveI H₁ : ∀ x, f₂ (σ x) = x := congr_fun hσ
  haveI H₂ := δ_aux i₂ i₃ f₂ g₁ g₂ hg h₂ σ hσ ρ hρ ι₃ hι₃
  { toFun := fun x ↦ π₁ (ρ (i₂ (σ (ι₃ x))))
    map_add' := fun x y ↦ by
      rw [← map_add]
      exact eq_of_eq i₁ i₂ f₁ f₂ hf g₁ h₁ ρ hρ ι₃ π₁ hπ₁ (x + y) _ (H₁ _) _ (H₂ _)
        (σ (ι₃ x) + σ (ι₃ y)) (by simp only [map_add, H₁]) _ (by simp only [map_add, H₂])
    map_smul' := fun r x ↦ by
      simp only [← map_smul, RingHom.id_apply]
      apply eq_of_eq i₁ i₂ f₁ f₂ hf g₁ h₁ ρ hρ ι₃ π₁ hπ₁ (r • x) _ (H₁ _) _ (H₂ _)
        (r • σ (ι₃ x)) (by simp only [map_smul, H₁]) _ (by simp only [map_smul, H₂]) }

/--
Suppose we have an exact commutative diagram
```
                K₃
                |
                ι₃
                ↓
M₁ -f₁→ M₂ -f₂→ M₃
|       |       |
i₁      i₂      i₃
↓       ↓       ↓
N₁ -g₁→ N₂ -g₂→ N₃
|       |
π₁      π₂
↓       ↓
C₁ -G-→ C₂

```
such that `f₂` is surjective with a (set-theoretic) section `σ`, `g₁` is injective with a
(set-theoretic) retraction `ρ`, and `π₁` is surjective, then `K₃ -δ→ C₁ -G→ C₂` is exact.
-/
lemma SnakeLemma.exact_δ_left (G : C₁ →ₗ[R] C₂) (hF : G.comp π₁ = π₂.comp g₁) (h : Surjective π₁) :
    Exact (δ i₁ i₂ i₃ f₁ f₂ hf g₁ g₂ hg h₁ h₂ σ hσ ρ hρ ι₃ hι₃ π₁ hπ₁) G := by
  have H₂ := δ_aux i₂ i₃ f₂ g₁ g₂ hg h₂ σ hσ ρ hρ ι₃ hι₃
  intro x
  constructor
  · intro H
    obtain ⟨x, rfl⟩ := h x
    obtain ⟨y, hy⟩ := (hπ₂ (g₁ x)).mp (by simpa only [← LinearMap.comp_apply, hF] using H)
    obtain ⟨z, hz⟩ : f₂ y ∈ range ι₃ := (hι₃ (f₂ y)).mp (by rw [← i₃.comp_apply, ← h₂,
      g₂.comp_apply, hy, hg.apply_apply_eq_zero])
    exact ⟨z, δ_eq i₁ i₂ i₃ f₁ f₂ hf g₁ g₂ hg h₁ h₂ σ hσ ρ hρ ι₃ hι₃ π₁ hπ₁ _ _ hz.symm _ hy.symm⟩
  · rintro ⟨x, rfl⟩
    simp only [δ, coe_mk, AddHom.coe_mk]
    rw [← G.comp_apply, hF, π₂.comp_apply, H₂, hπ₂.apply_apply_eq_zero]

Suppose we have an exact commutative diagram
```
        K₂ -F-→ K₃
        |       |
        ι₂      ι₃
        ↓       ↓
M₁ -f₁→ M₂ -f₂→ M₃
|       |       |
i₁      i₂      i₃
↓       ↓       ↓
N₁ -g₁→ N₂ -g₂→ N₃
|
π₁
↓
C₁

```
such that `f₂` is surjective with a (set-theoretic) section `σ`, `g₁` is injective with a
(set-theoretic) retraction `ρ`, and `ι₃` is injective, then `K₂ -F→ K₃ -δ→ C₁` is exact.
-/
lemma SnakeLemma.exact_δ_right (F : K₂ →ₗ[R] K₃) (hF : f₂.comp ι₂ = ι₃.comp F)
    (h : Injective ι₃) :
    Exact F (δ i₁ i₂ i₃ f₁ f₂ hf g₁ g₂ hg h₁ h₂ σ hσ ρ hρ ι₃ hι₃ π₁ hπ₁) := by
  have H₁ : ∀ x, f₂ (σ x) = x := congr_fun hσ
  have H₂ := δ_aux i₂ i₃ f₂ g₁ g₂ hg h₂ σ hσ ρ hρ ι₃ hι₃
  intro x
  constructor
  · intro H
    obtain ⟨y, hy⟩ := (hπ₁ _).mp H
    obtain ⟨k, hk⟩ : σ (ι₃ x) - f₁ y ∈ Set.range ι₂ := by
      rw [← hι₂, map_sub, ← H₂, ← hy, sub_eq_zero]; congrm $h₁ y
    refine ⟨k, h ?_⟩
    rw [← ι₃.comp_apply, ← hF, f₂.comp_apply, hk, map_sub, H₁, hf.apply_apply_eq_zero, sub_zero]
  · rintro ⟨y, rfl⟩
    exact (δ_eq i₁ i₂ i₃ f₁ f₂ hf g₁ g₂ hg h₁ h₂ σ hσ ρ hρ ι₃ hι₃ π₁ hπ₁ _ (ι₂ y) congr($hF y)
      _ (by rw [map_zero, hι₂.apply_apply_eq_zero])).trans π₁.map_zero

steps.text: Induced maps. If a(x)=0, then b(f(x))=f′(a(x))=0, so f sends ker a into ker b. If b(y)=0, then c(g(y))=g′(b(y))=0, so g sends ker b into ker c. For the cokernels, f′(a(A))=b(f(A))⊆b(B), so f′ induces coker a→coker b. In the same way g′ induces coker b→coker c.

The map δ is well defined. Let z be in ker c. Choose y in B with g(y)=z, which exists because g is surjective. Then g′(b(y))=c(g(y))=c(z)=0, so b(y) is in ker g′=f′(A′). Because f′ is injective, there is a unique x′ with f′(x′)=b(y). Take another y₂ with g(y₂)=z. Then g(y₂−y)=0, so y₂−y=f(x) for some x in A. Then b(y₂)=b(y)+b(f(x))=b(y)+f′(a(x)). So the new element is x′+a(x), which has the same class in coker a. The map δ is additive and R-linear, since sums and multiples of lifts are lifts.

Exactness at ker b. The composite g∘f is zero, so the image of ker a lies in ker g. Conversely let y be in ker b with g(y)=0. Then y=f(x) for some x in A. We have f′(a(x))=b(f(x))=b(y)=0. Because f′ is injective, a(x)=0. So y=f(x) with x in ker a.

Exactness at ker c. Let y be in ker b and z=g(y). Use this y in the definition of δ. Then b(y)=0=f′(0), so δ(z)=0. So the image of ker b is in ker δ. Conversely let z in ker c have δ(z)=0. Take a lift y of z, and x′ with f′(x′)=b(y). Because the class of x′ is zero, x′=a(x) for some x in A. Then b(y)=f′(a(x))=b(f(x)), so y−f(x) is in ker b. Also g(y−f(x))=g(y)=z because g∘f=0. So z is in g(ker b).

Exactness at coker a. Let z be in ker c, and let x′ represent δ(z) as above. Its image in coker b is the class of f′(x′)=b(y), which is zero because b(y) is in b(B). So the composite is zero. Conversely let x′ in A′ have class mapping to zero in coker b. Then f′(x′)=b(y) for some y in B. Now c(g(y))=g′(b(y))=g′(f′(x′))=0. So z=g(y) is in ker c. This y is a valid lift of z, and the pullback of b(y) is x′. So δ(z) is the class of x′.

Exactness at coker b. The composite coker a→coker b→coker c is induced by g′∘f′=0, so it is zero. Conversely let y′ in B′ have a class that maps to zero in coker c. Then g′(y′)=c(z) for some z in C. Choose y in B with g(y)=z. Then g′(y′−b(y))=c(z)−c(g(y))=0. So y′−b(y)=f′(x′) for some x′ in A′. Thus the class of y′ equals the class of f′(x′), which is in the image of coker a.
The two extra claims are direct. If f is injective, its restriction to ker a is injective. If g′ is surjective, then every element of C′ lifts to B′, so the induced map on cokernels is surjective.

worked_application.title: Kernels of multiplication on Z/12 and Z/18
worked_application.goal: Use the snake lemma on the multiplication-by-m map applied to the sequence Z→Z→Z/n→0. Take n=12 and m=18. Compute the connecting map.
hypotheses: The top row is Z --12--> Z --π--> Z/12 → 0, with f=12 and g=π. The bottom row is 0→Z --12--> Z --π--> Z/12.
All three vertical maps are multiplication by 18. They commute with the rows since all maps are linear over Z.
The top row is exact. The bottom row is exact because multiplication by 12 is injective.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: Both rows are exact and the squares commute, so the snake lemma applies.

steps.text: Compute the kernels. Multiplication by 18 is injective on Z, so ker a=ker b=0. On Z/12, multiplication by 18 has kernel {x: 18x≡0 mod 12}={0,2,4,6,8,10}. So ker c has 6 elements.
Compute the cokernels. coker a=Z/18Z=Z/18, and coker b=Z/18. The map coker a→coker b is induced by f′=12, so it is multiplication by 12 on Z/18. Also coker c=(Z/12)/18(Z/12)=(Z/12)/{0,6}≅Z/6.

The snake sequence reads 0→0→ker c→δ Z/18 --12--> Z/18→Z/6→0. The last zero holds because g′ is surjective. Exactness at ker c says δ is injective. Exactness at coker a says the image of δ is the kernel of multiplication by 12 on Z/18.
The kernel of 12 on Z/18 is {y: 12y≡0 mod 18}={y: 2y≡0 mod 3}={0,3,6,9,12,15}. It has 6 elements, equal to the size of ker c. So δ is an isomorphism ker(18 on Z/12)≅ker(12 on Z/18).

Compute δ explicitly. Take z=2 in ker c. Lift to y=2 in Z. Then b(y)=18·2=36=12·3, so x′=3. Therefore δ(2)=3 mod 18. In general δ(x)=18x/12=3x/2 mod 18. For x=0,2,4,6,8,10 this gives 0,3,6,9,12,15. That is exactly the kernel of 12 on Z/18, as computed.
The rest of the sequence also checks. Z/18 --12--> Z/18 has cokernel Z/gcd(18,12)=Z/6, and this is coker c, which we computed directly. So the sequence is exact at coker b.

worked_application.result: The connecting map sends x in {0,2,4,6,8,10} to 3x/2 mod 18 and gives an isomorphism of order 6 groups. The same sequence shows coker(12 on Z/18)≅Z/6.

The map δ depends on the diagram, not only on the six objects. A different pair of rows gives a different δ.
The lemma gives a six-term sequence. To extend it to the left (with 0 on the left) one needs f injective, and to the right one needs g′ surjective.

results.name: Long exact homology sequence of a short exact sequence of complexes
results.statement: Let 0→A→B→C→0 be a short exact sequence of chain complexes of R-modules, with chain maps f:A→B and g:B→C, exact in each degree. Then there is a long exact sequence … → H_n(A) → H_n(B) → H_n(C) →∂ H_{n−1}(A) → H_{n−1}(B) → … in homology. The maps H_n(A)→H_n(B) and H_n(B)→H_n(C) are induced by f and g. The connecting map is ∂[z]=[x], where z is a cycle of C_n, y in B_n is any lift of z, the element d(y) in B_{n−1} lies in f(A_{n−1}), and x in A_{n−1} is the unique element with f(x)=d(y). The map ∂ is natural for maps of short exact sequences.
hypotheses: The sequence 0→A_n→B_n→C_n→0 is exact for every n.
f and g commute with the differentials.
The ring R is arbitrary. The same holds in any abelian category.

/-- Exactness of `S.X₁.homology i ⟶ S.X₂.homology i ⟶ S.X₃.homology i`. -/
lemma homology_exact₂ : (ShortComplex.mk (HomologicalComplex.homologyMap S.f i)
    (HomologicalComplex.homologyMap S.g i) (by rw [← HomologicalComplex.homologyMap_comp,
      S.zero, HomologicalComplex.homologyMap_zero])).Exact := by
  by_cases h : c.Rel i (c.next i)
  · exact (snakeInput hS i _ h).L₀_exact
  · have := hS.epi_g
    have : ∀ (K : HomologicalComplex C c), IsIso (K.homologyι i) :=
      fun K => ShortComplex.isIso_homologyι (K.sc i) (K.shape _ _ h)
    have e : S.map (HomologicalComplex.homologyFunctor C c i) ≅
        S.map (HomologicalComplex.opcyclesFunctor C c i) :=
      ShortComplex.isoMk (asIso (S.X₁.homologyι i))
        (asIso (S.X₂.homologyι i)) (asIso (S.X₃.homologyι i)) (by simp) (by simp)
    exact ShortComplex.exact_of_iso e.symm (opcycles_right_exact S hS.exact i)

steps.text: Set up the snake diagram for each n. Let the top row be A_n/dA_{n+1} → B_n/dB_{n+1} → C_n/dC_{n+1} → 0, with the maps induced by f and g. Let the bottom row be 0 → Z_{n−1}(A) → Z_{n−1}(B) → Z_{n−1}(C), with the same maps. Let the vertical maps be d̄:[y]↦d(y). This is well defined, since d(dw)=0, and d(y) is a cycle.

The top row is exact. The map on C is surjective because g is surjective. The composite is zero since g∘f=0. Let y be in B_n with g(y)=d(w) for some w in C_{n+1}. Choose v in B_{n+1} with g(v)=w. Then g(y−d(v))=g(y)−d(g(v))=0. So y−d(v)=f(x) for some x in A_n, and [y]=[f(x)] in B_n/dB_{n+1}.

The bottom row is exact. The maps are injective on the left because f is. Let y be a cycle of B_{n−1} with g(y)=0. Then y=f(x) for some x. We have f(d(x))=d(f(x))=d(y)=0, so d(x)=0 because f is injective. So y comes from a cycle of A.

The squares commute because f, g and d commute. So the snake lemma applies. The kernel of d̄ on B_n/dB_{n+1} is Z_n(B)/B_n(B)=H_n(B). The cokernel of d̄ is Z_{n−1}(B)/dB_n=H_{n−1}(B). The same holds for A and C.

The snake lemma gives the exact six-term sequence H_n(A)→H_n(B)→H_n(C)→∂ H_{n−1}(A)→H_{n−1}(B)→H_{n−1}(C), and the formula for ∂ in the snake lemma is the formula in the statement: lift z to y, apply d, pull back along f.

Join the sequences. The snake lemma gives exactness at the inner four terms of the six-term sequence. The term H_m(A) is the fourth term of the sequence for n=m+1. The term H_m(B) is the second term of the sequence for n=m. The term H_m(C) is the third term of the sequence for n=m. Every term of the long sequence is an inner term of some six-term sequence. The maps agree between neighbouring pieces, so the long sequence is exact.
Naturality of ∂. Take a map of short exact sequences. The lifts and pull-backs in the formula for ∂ are preserved by the maps, so the formula gives a commuting square.

worked_application.title: Bockstein sequence for a complex that models the real projective plane
worked_application.goal: Take the complex K with K_2=K_1=K_0=Z, d_2=2 and d_1=0. It is the cellular chain complex of the real projective plane. Use the sequence 0→K --2--> K → K/2 → 0 to find H_*(K;Z/2) from H_*(K;Z) and compute the Bockstein.
hypotheses: K_n=0 for n outside 0,1,2. The differential d_2 is multiplication by 2. The differential d_1 is 0.
Multiplication by 2 is injective on free abelian groups, so the sequence 0→K→K→K/2→0 is exact in each degree.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The sequence is a short exact sequence of chain complexes. The long exact sequence applies, with A=B=K and C=K/2=K⊗Z/2.

steps.text: Compute H_*(K). H_2=ker(2)=0. H_1=ker(0)/im(2)=Z/2Z=Z/2. H_0=Z/im(0)=Z. All other groups are 0.
Compute H_*(K/2). The complex is Z/2 --0--> Z/2 --0--> Z/2 in degrees 2,1,0, because 2=0 mod 2. All differentials vanish. So H_n(K/2)=Z/2 for n=0,1,2.

Check exactness without extra computation. Multiplication by 2 on H_1(K)=Z/2 is zero. So ∂:Z/2→Z/2 in degree 2 has kernel 0 (from the left zero) and image all of Z/2 (the kernel of the zero map). Thus it is an isomorphism.

Then H_1(K)→H_1(K/2) is injective, since the previous map 2 is zero, and its image is the kernel of ∂:H_1(K/2)→Z. The kernel of 2 on Z is 0, so ∂=0 and the map is onto. It is an isomorphism Z/2→Z/2. Finally coker(2 on Z)=Z/2=H_0(K/2), as found.

Compute the Bockstein ∂ in degree 2 by the formula. Let z be the generator 1 of H_2(K/2)=Z/2. Lift to y=1 in K_2. Then d(y)=2 in K_1. This equals 2·1, so it comes from x=1 under multiplication by 2. So ∂(z)=[1]∈H_1(K)=Z/2Z, the nonzero class.
This computes the mod 2 homology from integer homology, and it shows how a torsion class in H_1(K) produces classes in both H_1(K;Z/2) and H_2(K;Z/2).

worked_application.result: H_*(K;Z)=(Z, Z/2, 0) in degrees (0,1,2). H_*(K;Z/2)=(Z/2, Z/2, Z/2). The Bockstein ∂:H_2(K;Z/2)→H_1(K;Z) is an isomorphism Z/2→Z/2.

results.name: Infinite sets satisfy |X×X|=|X|, by Zorn's lemma
results.statement: Assume the axiom of choice. Let X be an infinite set. Then there is a bijection X×X→X, so κ·κ=κ for every infinite cardinal κ. Consequently: (a) if κ is infinite and 1≤λ≤κ, then κ+λ=κ·λ=κ, i.e. κ+λ=κ·λ=max(κ,λ). (b) The set X^{<ω} of finite sequences in X, and the set of finite subsets of X, have the same cardinality as X. (c) If K is an infinite field, then K[x] has cardinality |K|.
hypotheses: The axiom of choice holds. It is used through Zorn's lemma and through the comparability of cardinals.
X is infinite, i.e. it has a countably infinite subset.
The consequences (a) to (c) use the first statement for the infinite cardinal or set named there.

/-- If `α` is an infinite type, then `α × α` and `α` have the same cardinality. -/
theorem mul_eq_self {c : Cardinal} (hc : ℵ₀ ≤ c) : c * c = c := by
  -- The only nontrivial part is `c * c ≤ c`. We prove it inductively.
  induction c using WellFoundedLT.induction with | ind c IH
  refine le_antisymm ?_ (by simpa using mul_le_mul_right (one_le_aleph0.trans hc) c)
  -- Consider the minimal well-order on `α` (a type with cardinality `c`).
  induction c using Cardinal.inductionOn with | mk α
  obtain ⟨_, _, hα⟩ := exists_ord_eq_type_lt α
  have : NoMaxOrder α := by
    rw [← isSuccPrelimit_type_lt_iff, ← hα]
    exact (isSuccLimit_ord hc).isSuccPrelimit
  -- We embed `α × α` into `α ×ₗ α ×ₗ α` by sending `(x, y)` to `(max x y, x, y)`.
  -- Every initial segment of the embedding is contained in `β × β` for some `#β < c`.

steps.text: Let S be the set of pairs (A,f) with A an infinite subset of X and f:A×A→A a bijection. Order S by (A,f)≤(A′,f′) if A⊆A′ and f′ restricted to A×A is f. S is not empty. Take a countably infinite A₀⊆X. The Cantor pairing (a,b)↦(a+b)(a+b+1)/2+b is a bijection ℕ×ℕ→ℕ, so A₀ has such an f₀.

Every chain in S has an upper bound. Let ((A_i,f_i)) be a nonempty chain. Put A=∪A_i and f=∪f_i. Any two points a,b of A lie in a common A_i, because the A_i are linearly ordered. So f is defined on all of A×A and is a single-valued function. It is injective, since two pairs lie in a common A_i×A_i and f_i is injective. It is onto A, since each a in A lies in some A_i and f_i is onto A_i. So (A,f) is in S and is an upper bound. Zorn's lemma gives a maximal element (A,f) of S.

Claim: |X∖A|<|A|. Suppose not. By comparability of cardinals, |A|≤|X∖A|. So there is B⊆X∖A with |B|=|A|. The set (A∪B)×(A∪B) is the disjoint union of A×A, and D=(A×B)∪(B×A)∪(B×B). The three pieces of D have cardinality |A|·|A|=|A| each, using f and |B|=|A|.

Now |D|=3|A|. We have |A|≤3|A|. Also 3|A|≤|A|·|A|=|A|: choose three distinct elements e₀,e₁,e₂ in A, and map (i,a) to (e_i,a). This is an injection {0,1,2}×A→A×A. So |D|=|A|=|B|, and there is a bijection h:D→B.

Define A′=A∪B and f′=f∪h. Since f maps A×A onto A and h maps D onto B, and the union of the two domains is A′×A′ and the union of the images is A′, the map f′ is a bijection A′×A′→A′. The set A′ is infinite. So (A′,f′) is in S and is strictly above (A,f) because B is not empty. This contradicts maximality. So |X∖A|<|A|.

Now |A|≤|X|=|A|+|X∖A|≤|A|+|A|=2|A|≤3|A|=|A|, using |X∖A|<|A| and step 4. By the Schröder–Bernstein theorem |X|=|A|. So X×X has the same size as A×A, which has the same size as A by f, which has the same size as X. This proves |X×X|=|X|.
Consequence (a). Let κ be infinite and 1≤λ≤κ. Then κ≤κ·λ≤κ·κ=κ and κ≤κ+λ≤κ+κ≤κ·κ=κ. Here κ+κ=2κ≤κ·κ by the injection of step 4.

Consequence (b). By induction on n≥1, |X^n|=|X|, since X^{n+1}=X^n×X and |X|·|X|=|X|. So |X^{<ω}|=|⋃_n X^n|≤ℵ₀·|X|=|X| by (a), and |X|≤|X^{<ω}|. A finite subset of X is a finite sequence without order, so choose a listing of each. This gives an injection from finite subsets to X^{<ω}. Singletons give an injection from X, so the finite subsets also have cardinality |X|.
Consequence (c). A polynomial over K is a finite sequence of coefficients, so |K[x]|≤|K^{<ω}|=|K| by (b), and K is a subset of K[x].

worked_application.title: Counting algebraic and transcendental reals, and cardinalities of function spaces
worked_application.goal: Let c=2^{ℵ₀} be the cardinality of ℝ. Show that ℝ^n, ℝ^ℕ and the continuous functions on ℝ all have cardinality c, and that the transcendental real numbers have cardinality c.
hypotheses: Use ℵ₀<c (Cantor) and the theorem for infinite cardinals.
The continuous functions are determined by their values on ℚ.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: Each cardinal that occurs is infinite. The theorem gives κ·κ=κ for these cardinals, and the product rule gives sums and products by max.

steps.text: ℝ^n for n≥1. Induction: |ℝ^{n+1}|=|ℝ^n|·|ℝ|=c·c=c. So |ℝ^n|=c. This also gives |ℂ|=|ℝ²|=c.
ℝ^ℕ. We have |ℝ^ℕ|=c^{ℵ₀}=(2^{ℵ₀})^{ℵ₀}=2^{ℵ₀·ℵ₀}=2^{ℵ₀}=c, using ℵ₀·ℵ₀=ℵ₀, the theorem for ℵ₀.

Continuous functions. A continuous f:ℝ→ℝ is determined by its restriction to ℚ. So there is an injection into ℝ^ℚ, which has cardinality c^{ℵ₀}=c. The constants give an injection from ℝ. So the cardinality is c.

Algebraic numbers. A real algebraic number is a root of a nonzero polynomial with integer coefficients. The polynomials are finite sequences of integers, so by consequence (b) for the infinite set ℤ there are ℵ₀ of them. Each polynomial has at most finitely many roots. So the algebraic reals are a countable union of finite sets, hence countable.

Transcendental numbers. We have c=|ℝ|=|alg|+|trans|. If |trans| were at most ℵ₀, then c≤ℵ₀+ℵ₀=ℵ₀, which contradicts Cantor's ℵ₀<c. So |trans| is infinite, and c=ℵ₀+|trans|=max(ℵ₀,|trans|) by consequence (a). Because ℵ₀<c, the max is |trans|. So |trans|=c.

Check the pairing numerically. The pairing π(a,b)=(a+b)(a+b+1)/2+b sends (3,5) to 36+5=41. A computer check shows that π takes each value 0 to 999 exactly once on pairs with π(a,b)<1000. So it is a bijection on that range, as expected.

worked_application.result: ℝ^n, ℝ^ℕ and C(ℝ,ℝ) all have cardinality c. The transcendental reals have cardinality c, while the algebraic reals are countable.

limitations: The theorem needs choice. The statement for all infinite sets is known to imply the axiom of choice.
The result is about products and sums. Powers of infinite cardinals are not determined by it: 2^{ℵ₀} can be ℵ₁ or larger.
Infinite sequences and countable products of a set have larger cardinality. The set X^ℕ has cardinality |X|^{ℵ₀}, which can be bigger than |X|.
