results.name: Ax-Grothendieck: injective polynomial maps of K^n are surjective, by finite fields and compactness
results.statement: Let K be an algebraically closed field and n≥1. If f=(f₁,…,f_n) with f_i in K[x₁,…,x_n] is a polynomial map K^n→K^n that is injective, then f is surjective. More generally, the same holds on any zero set of an ideal of K[x₁,…,x_n] that f maps into itself. The proof has two parts. (I) If K is an algebraic extension of a finite field, every injective polynomial map of K^n is surjective. (II) A first-order sentence σ_{n,d} states the claim for all n-variable maps of degree at most d. It holds in all algebraically closed fields of every prime characteristic, so it holds in characteristic 0 as well.
hypotheses: K is algebraically closed. The claim fails for fields that are not algebraically closed.
The map is given by polynomials in K[x₁,…,x_n]. Regular functions in other forms (power series, analytic maps) are not allowed.
The domain and codomain are both K^n, with the same n.

definitions.name: complete theory
definitions.text: A consistent theory T such that for every sentence σ, either T proves σ or T proves ¬σ.

/-- Any injective polynomial map over an algebraic extension of a finite field is surjective. -/
theorem ax_grothendieck_of_locally_finite {ι K R : Type*} [Field K] [Finite K] [CommRing R]
    [Finite ι] [Algebra K R] [alg : Algebra.IsAlgebraic K R] (ps : ι → MvPolynomial ι R)
    (S : Set (ι → R))
    (hm : S.MapsTo (fun v i => eval v (ps i)) S)
    (hinj : S.InjOn (fun v i => eval v (ps i))) :
    S.SurjOn (fun v i => eval v (ps i)) S := by
  have is_int : ∀ x : R, IsIntegral K x := fun x => isAlgebraic_iff_isIntegral.1
    (alg.isAlgebraic x)
  classical
  intro v hvS
  cases nonempty_fintype ι
  /- `s` is the set of all coefficients of the polynomial, as well as all of
    the coordinates of `v`, the point I am trying to find the preimage of. -/
  let s : Finset R :=
    (Finset.biUnion (univ : Finset ι) fun i => (ps i).support.image fun x => (ps i).coeff x) ∪
      (univ : Finset ι).image v
  have hv : ∀ i, v i ∈ Algebra.adjoin K (s : Set R) := fun j =>
    Algebra.subset_adjoin (mem_union_right _ (mem_image.2 ⟨j, mem_univ _, rfl⟩))
  have hs₁ : ∀ (i : ι) (k : ι →₀ ℕ),
      k ∈ (ps i).support → (ps i).coeff k ∈ Algebra.adjoin K (s : Set R) :=
    fun i k hk => Algebra.subset_adjoin
      (mem_union_left _ (mem_biUnion.2 ⟨i, mem_univ _, mem_image_of_mem _ hk⟩))
  have := isNoetherian_adjoin_finset s fun x _ => is_int x
  have : Finite (Algebra.adjoin K (s : Set R)) := Module.finite_of_finite K
  -- The restriction of the polynomial map, `ps`, to the subalgebra generated by `s`
  let S' : Set (ι → Algebra.adjoin K (s : Set R)) :=
    (fun v => Subtype.val ∘ v) ⁻¹' S
  let res : S' → S' := fun x => ⟨fun i =>
    ⟨eval (fun j : ι => (x.1 j : R)) (ps i), eval_mem (hs₁ _) fun i => (x.1 i).2⟩,
      hm x.2⟩
  have hres_surj : Function.Surjective res := by
    rw [← Finite.injective_iff_surjective]
    intro x y hxy
    ext i
    simp only [Subtype.ext_iff, funext_iff] at hxy
    congrm $(hinj x.2 y.2 (funext hxy)) i
  rcases hres_surj ⟨fun i => ⟨v i, hv i⟩, hvS⟩ with ⟨⟨w, hwS'⟩, hw⟩
  refine ⟨fun i => w i, hwS', ?_⟩
  simpa [Subtype.ext_iff, funext_iff] using hw

end

/-- The **Ax-Grothendieck** theorem

If `K` is an algebraically closed field, and `S : Set (ι → K)` is the `zeroLocus` of an ideal
of the multivariable polynomial ring, then any injective polynomial map `S → S`  is also
surjective on `S`. -/

    (I : Ideal (MvPolynomial ι K))
    (p : ι → MvPolynomial ι K) :
    let S := zeroLocus K I
    S.MapsTo (fun v i => eval v (p i)) S →
    S.InjOn (fun v i => eval v (p i)) →
    S.SurjOn (fun v i => eval v (p i)) S := by

  intro S
  obtain ⟨s, rfl⟩ : I.FG := IsNoetherian.noetherian I

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Part I, finite fields. Let F be a finite set and g:F→F injective. Then g is surjective, because the image has |F| elements. Now let K be an algebraic extension of a finite field k, f an injective polynomial map K^n→K^n, and b a point of K^n. Let L be the subring of K generated over k by the coefficients of f₁,…,f_n and the coordinates of b. Each generator is algebraic over k, so L is a finite-dimensional k-algebra, hence a finite set.

The map f sends L^n into L^n because its coefficients lie in L. It is injective on L^n because it is injective on K^n. By step 1 it is surjective on L^n. So b has a preimage in L^n, which is in K^n. This proves Part I. In particular it holds for the algebraic closure of F_p.

Part II, completeness of ACF_p. For p prime or 0, ACF_p has no finite models. Take an uncountable cardinal κ. An algebraically closed field of characteristic p and cardinality κ has transcendence degree κ over the prime field, since the algebraic closure of a set of fewer than κ transcendentals has fewer than κ elements. By Steinitz's theorem two such fields are isomorphic. So ACF_p is categorical in κ. The Łoś–Vaught test shows ACF_p is complete.

Fix n and d. There are finitely many monomials of degree at most d in n variables. Let c be the tuple of their coefficients for f₁,…,f_n. The statement "if f_c is injective, then it is surjective" is the sentence σ_{n,d}, with the coefficients quantified universally. Injective is "∀x∀y (f_c(x)=f_c(y) → x=y)". Surjective is "∀y∃x f_c(x)=y". All are first-order in the language of rings.

For a prime p, the field F̄_p, the algebraic closure of F_p, is a model of ACF_p. By Part I it satisfies σ_{n,d}. Since ACF_p is complete, ACF_p proves σ_{n,d}. So every algebraically closed field of characteristic p satisfies σ_{n,d}.

Characteristic 0. ACF_0 is complete by step 3. Suppose ACF_0 did not prove σ_{n,d}. Then ACF_0 proves ¬σ_{n,d}. By the compactness theorem a finite part of ACF_0 proves ¬σ_{n,d}. This finite part uses only the axioms for algebraically closed fields and finitely many sentences "m≠0". So there is N such that every algebraically closed field of characteristic larger than N satisfies ¬σ_{n,d}. This contradicts step 5 for a prime p>N. So ACF_0 proves σ_{n,d}. This is the Lefschetz principle: a sentence holds in ACF_0 if and only if it holds in ACF_p for infinitely many primes p.

Conclusion. Let K be any algebraically closed field and f an injective polynomial map K^n→K^n of degree at most d. The field K has some characteristic p, prime or 0. K satisfies ACF_p, so it satisfies σ_{n,d} by steps 5 and 6. Taking the coefficients of f for c, we get that f is surjective.

Zero sets. If S is the zero set of an ideal I and f maps S into S and is injective on S, then S is described by finitely many polynomials, because K[x] is Noetherian. The statement "f maps S to S, is injective on S, and is onto S" is also a first-order sentence in the coefficients of f and of the generators of I. The same transfer argument proves it.

worked_application.goal: In characteristic 2, take f(x,y)=(x²,x+y). Show that it is injective on the algebraic closure of F₂ and trace the proof of Part I for the target b=(ω,1), where ω²+ω+1=0. Then show that the hypotheses cannot be dropped.
hypotheses: K is the algebraic closure of F₂, and n=2. The element ω is a generator of F₄ with ω²=ω+1.
The coefficients of f lie in F₂, and the coordinates of b lie in F₄. So L=F₄ works in step 1 of the proof.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: K is algebraically closed of characteristic 2 and is an algebraic extension of F₂. The map f has polynomial entries. So Part I applies directly.

steps.text: Injective on K². Suppose (x²,x+y)=(x′²,x′+y′). In characteristic 2, x²=x′² gives (x−x′)²=0, so x=x′. Then y=y′. So f is injective.

Take L=F₄={0,1,ω,ω²}. It is generated over F₂ by ω, which is the only non-trivial coordinate of b=(ω,1). The set L² has 16 points. A computer check of all 16 images shows that f maps L² to 16 distinct points. This agrees with step 2: an injective map of a finite set is onto it.
Find the preimage of b. We need x²=ω. Since ω⁴=ω, x=ω² works: (ω²)²=ω⁴=ω. Then x+y=1 gives y=1+ω²=ω, using ω²+ω+1=0. Check: f(ω²,ω)=(ω,ω²+ω)=(ω,1). So b has a preimage in F₄².

The map f has no polynomial inverse. Its set-theoretic inverse is (u,v)↦(√u, v+√u), and the square root is not a polynomial. So f is bijective without being an automorphism of the polynomial ring. The theorem gives surjectivity without constructing an inverse.

The field must be algebraically closed. Over ℚ, the map x↦x³ is injective, but 2 is not a cube in ℚ, so it is not surjective. The map must be a polynomial map of K^n to itself. Over ℤ, the map x↦2x is injective but not surjective, and ℤ is not a field.

results.name: Circumcenter of an affinely independent point set, by a Gram linear system
results.statement: Let p₀,…,p_n be affinely independent points of a Euclidean space. Then exactly one point c in their affine span has the same distance to all p_i. This point is the circumcenter. Its common distance r is the circumradius. In coordinates, write c=p₀+Σλ_j v_j with v_j=p_j−p₀. Then λ is the unique solution of G λ = b, where G_{ij}=⟨v_i,v_j⟩ and b_i=|v_i|²/2. The matrix G is invertible. Any point of the whole space that has equal distance to all p_i is the circumcenter plus a vector orthogonal to the span.
hypotheses: The ambient space is a real inner product space (or a Euclidean affine space).
The points p₀,…,p_n are affinely independent. Equivalently, the vectors v₁,…,v_n are linearly independent.
The point c must lie in the affine span. Without this, c is not unique when n is smaller than the dimension.

definitions.name: circumsphere

definitions.name: affine span
definitions.text: The set of all points p₀+Σλ_j v_j with real λ_j. It is the smallest affine subspace that contains all p_i.

/-- Given a finite nonempty affinely independent family of points,
there is a unique (circumcenter, circumradius) pair for those points
in the affine subspace they span. -/
theorem _root_.AffineIndependent.existsUnique_dist_eq {ι : Type*} [hne : Nonempty ι] [Finite ι]
    {p : ι → P} (ha : AffineIndependent ℝ p) :
    ∃! cs : Sphere P, cs.center ∈ affineSpan ℝ (Set.range p) ∧ Set.range p ⊆ (cs : Set P) := by
  cases nonempty_fintype ι
  induction hn : Fintype.card ι generalizing ι with
  | zero =>
    exfalso
    have h := Fintype.card_pos_iff.2 hne
    lia
  | succ m hm =>
    rcases m with - | m
    · rw [Fintype.card_eq_one_iff] at hn
      obtain ⟨i, hi⟩ := hn
      have : Unique ι := ⟨⟨i⟩, hi⟩
      use ⟨p i, 0⟩
      simp only [Set.range_unique, AffineSubspace.mem_affineSpan_singleton]
      constructor
      · simp_rw [hi default, Set.singleton_subset_iff]
        exact ⟨⟨⟩, by simp only [Metric.sphere_zero, Set.mem_singleton_iff]⟩
      · rintro ⟨cc, cr⟩
        rintro ⟨rfl, hdist⟩

steps.text: Reduce to a linear condition. Take c=p₀+u with u in the linear span of v₁,…,v_n. For i≥1 we have c−p_i=u−v_i. So |c−p_i|²=|c−p₀|² means |u−v_i|²=|u|². This is |v_i|²−2⟨u,v_i⟩=0, that is ⟨u,v_i⟩=|v_i|²/2.

The conditions for i=1,…,n imply the condition for all i, since the case i=0 is trivial. Write u=Σλ_j v_j. Then ⟨u,v_i⟩=Σ_j G_{ij}λ_j. So c has equal distance to all p_i if and only if Gλ=b with b_i=|v_i|²/2.
The matrix G is invertible. Take x in ℝ^n with Gx=0. Then xᵀGx=0, so |Σx_j v_j|²=0, so Σx_j v_j=0. The v_j are linearly independent, so x=0. Thus G has trivial kernel and is invertible.

Existence and uniqueness. Since G is invertible, Gλ=b has exactly one solution λ. So exactly one c in the affine span has equal distance to all p_i. Its distance r=|u| is the circumradius. The sphere with center c and radius r contains every p_i.

Points outside the span. Let q be any point with equal distance to all p_i. Let c′ be the orthogonal projection of q on the affine span. For each i, |q−p_i|²=|q−c′|²+|c′−p_i|² by Pythagoras, because q−c′ is orthogonal to the span. So c′ has equal distance to all p_i. By step 4, c′=c. Hence q=c+w with w orthogonal to the span.

Dependence on the hypothesis. If the points are not affinely independent, G is singular. The system can then have no solution or many. Three distinct collinear points have no equidistant point in their span. Hence the hypothesis is needed.

results.name: Cantor normal form: every ordinal has a unique base-b expansion with decreasing exponents
results.statement: Let b>1 be an ordinal. Every ordinal o>0 can be written in exactly one way as o = b^{e₁}·c₁ + b^{e₂}·c₂ + … + b^{e_k}·c_k, where e₁>e₂>…>e_k are ordinals, k≥1, and each coefficient c_i is an ordinal with 0<c_i<b. The leading exponent e₁ is the logarithm log_b(o), which is the largest e with b^e ≤ o. The list is called CNF_b(o), and the case o=0 gives the empty list. For b=ω, the coefficients are positive natural numbers. This is the Cantor normal form. For an integer b≥2, it is the base-b expansion with the digits written as (exponent, digit) pairs.
hypotheses: b is an ordinal with b>1. For b≤1 the expansion fails, because the powers of b do not grow.
The exponents are strictly decreasing, and the coefficients satisfy 0<c_i<b.
The coefficient c_i stands on the right of the power b^{e_i}. Ordinal multiplication is not commutative, so b^e·c and c·b^e differ.
results.empty_prerequisites_reason: The proof uses only ordinal division and the monotonicity of ordinal powers.

definitions.name: ordinal power and logarithm
definitions.text: For b>1 the map e↦b^e is strictly increasing and continuous. For o>0 the logarithm log_b(o) is the unique e with b^e ≤ o < b^{e+1}.

definitions.name: ordinal division
definitions.text: For d>0 and any ordinal o there are unique ordinals q and r with o = d·q + r and r<d.

definitions.name: base-b value
definitions.text: For a decreasing list of pairs (e_i,c_i), the value is b^{e₁}c₁ + … + b^{e_k}c_k, summed from left to right.

/-- Evaluating the Cantor normal form of an ordinal returns the ordinal. -/
protected theorem foldr (b o : Ordinal) : (CNF b o).foldr (fun p r ↦ b ^ p.1 * p.2 + r) 0 = o := by
  refine CNF.rec b ?_ ?_ o
  · rw [zero_right, foldr_nil]
  · intro o ho IH
    rw [CNF.ne_zero ho, foldr_cons, IH, div_add_mod]

protected theorem sortedGT (b o : Ordinal) : ((CNF b o).map Prod.fst).SortedGT := by
  simp_rw [sortedGT_iff_pairwise]
  refine CNF.rec b ?_ (fun o ho IH ↦ ?_) o
  · rw [zero_right]
    exact .nil
  · rcases le_or_gt b 1 with hb | hb
    · rw [CNF.of_le_one hb ho]
      exact pairwise_singleton _ _
    · obtain hob | hbo := lt_or_ge o b
      · rw [CNF.of_lt ho hob]
        exact pairwise_singleton _ _
      · rw [CNF.ne_zero ho, map_cons, pairwise_cons]
        refine ⟨fun a H ↦ ?_, IH⟩
        rw [mem_map] at H
        rcases H with ⟨⟨a, a'⟩, H, rfl⟩
        exact (fst_le_log H).trans_lt (log_mod_opow_log_lt_log_self hb hbo)

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Two facts on ordinal arithmetic. (F1) Left multiplication distributes over sum: d(x+y)=dx+dy, and in particular d(c+1)=dc+d. (F2) For b>1 the map e↦b^e is strictly increasing, so e<e′ implies b^{e+1} ≤ b^{e′}.

Bound lemma. Let o be the value of a decreasing list with 0<c_i<b. Then b^{e₁} ≤ o < b^{e₁+1}. Proof by induction on the length k. Write o = b^{e₁}c₁ + t, where t is the value of the tail. We have b^{e₁} ≤ b^{e₁}c₁ ≤ o because c₁≥1. For k=1, t=0 and o = b^{e₁}c₁ < b^{e₁}·b = b^{e₁+1}, because c₁<b.

Bound lemma, case k>1. By induction t < b^{e₂+1}. Since e₂<e₁, F2 gives b^{e₂+1} ≤ b^{e₁}. So t<b^{e₁}. Then o = b^{e₁}c₁ + t < b^{e₁}c₁ + b^{e₁} = b^{e₁}(c₁+1) ≤ b^{e₁}·b = b^{e₁+1}, by F1 and c₁+1 ≤ b. This proves the lemma. In particular e₁ = log_b(o).

Existence, by strong induction on o>0. Let e=log_b(o), so b^e ≤ o < b^{e+1}. The logarithm exists because e↦b^e is continuous and unbounded: take the supremum of all x with b^x ≤ o. Divide: o = b^e·c + r with r<b^e. Since b^e ≤ o, c≥1. If c≥b, then o ≥ b^e·c ≥ b^e·b = b^{e+1}, a contradiction. So 0<c<b.

Existence, end of the induction. If r=0, then o=b^e·c is a one-term list. If r>0, then r<b^e ≤ o, so the induction hypothesis gives a list for r. Its leading exponent is log_b(r). Because r<b^e, log_b(r)<e. Put (e,c) in front of this list. The result is a decreasing list with value b^e·c + r = o.

Uniqueness, by strong induction on o. Take any list for o as in the statement, with leading pair (e₁,c₁) and tail value t. By the bound lemma, b^{e₁} ≤ o < b^{e₁+1}, so e₁ = log_b(o). Step 3 shows t<b^{e₁} (or t=0). So o = b^{e₁}c₁ + t with t<b^{e₁}. This is the division of o by b^{e₁}, and the quotient and the remainder are unique. Hence c₁ and t are determined by o.

Uniqueness, end. The tail is a list for t, with leading exponent less than e₁. If t=0 the tail is empty. Otherwise t<o, because t<b^{e₁} ≤ o. By the induction hypothesis the tail is the unique list of t. So the whole list is determined by o.

Comparison. Two ordinals in normal form compare in lexicographic order of their lists. If e₁<e₁′ then the bound lemma gives o<b^{e₁+1} ≤ b^{e₁′} ≤ o′. If e₁=e₁′ and c₁<c₁′, then o<b^{e₁}(c₁+1) ≤ o′ as before. If both are equal, compare the tails.

worked_application.title: Ordinal arithmetic below ω^ω in normal form, and the base-10 case
worked_application.goal: Let α=ω²·3+ω·2+1 and β=ω+5. Compute α+β, β+α, α·β and β·α in Cantor normal form. Then write the integer 2026 in base 10 as a normal form.
hypotheses: The base is b=ω. The exponents of α and β are natural numbers.
For the integer case take b=10, so the coefficients are digits 1 to 9.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: Each result is an ordinal below ω^ω, so it has a unique normal form with base ω. The computation uses the rules (a) terms of the left sum that have an exponent below the leading exponent of the right summand are absorbed, and (b) α·ω^f = ω^{a+f} for f>0 and leading exponent a of α.

steps.text: Sum α+β. The leading exponent of β is 1. The term 1 (exponent 0) of α is below it, so it is absorbed. The terms ω²·3 and ω·2 stay, and ω·2 merges with ω to give ω·3. The result is α+β = ω²·3 + ω·3 + 5.
Sum β+α. The leading exponent of α is 2. Both terms of β have exponent below 2, so β is absorbed. The result is β+α = α = ω²·3 + ω·2 + 1. So addition is not commutative.
Product α·β. By F1, α·(ω+5)=α·ω+α·5. Here α·ω=ω^{2+1}=ω³, because the lower terms of α do not matter. Also α·5 = ω²·15 + ω·2 + 1. So α·β = ω³ + ω²·15 + ω·2 + 1.

Product β·α. Use α = ω²·3+ω·2+1. We get β·ω²·3 = ω³·3, β·ω·2 = ω²·2, and β·1 = ω+5. So β·α = ω³·3 + ω²·2 + ω + 5. A Python implementation of these rules for lists (exponent, coefficient) gives the same four results, and confirms α·5 = α+α+α+α+α and α·(β+ω)=α·β+α·ω.
Order. The lists of β·α and α·β start with exponent 3 and coefficients 3 and 1. So α·β < β·α by the lexicographic comparison of the theorem.

Base 10. The integer 2026 satisfies 10³ ≤ 2026 < 10⁴, so log₁₀(2026)=3. Division gives 2026 = 10³·2 + 26. Next, log₁₀(26)=1 and 26 = 10·2 + 6. Then 6 = 10⁰·6. So CNF₁₀(2026) = [(3,2),(1,2),(0,6)]. A computer check agrees and gives the value 2026.

worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: The theorem needs b>1. The Mathlib definition returns the one-term list [(0,o)] for b≤1.
The normal form does not give an easy formula for sum and product when the coefficients are large. Absorption rules are needed.

For b=ω an exponent can be as large as the ordinal itself. If ε=ω^ε, then the normal form of ε is ω^ε·1. So the exponents do not always get smaller than the number, and the normal form does not give a finite notation for all countable ordinals.

results.name: Stone-Cech compactification of a set: ultrafilters extend every map to a compact Hausdorff space
results.statement: Let X be a set and let βX be the set of ultrafilters on X. Give βX the topology with basis O_s={U : s∈U} for s⊆X. Then: (1) βX is compact and Hausdorff, and every O_s is open and closed. (2) The map pure:X→βX, a↦(principal ultrafilter at a), has dense image. (3) For every map f:X→K into a compact Hausdorff space K there is exactly one continuous map f̃:βX→K with f̃∘pure=f. It is given by f̃(U)=lim_{f_*U} id, the unique limit of the ultrafilter f_*U={W : f^{-1}(W)∈U} on K.
hypotheses: X is an arbitrary set. It carries the discrete topology, so every map f from X is continuous.
The target K is compact and Hausdorff. Both are needed: compactness gives the limit, and the Hausdorff property gives its uniqueness and the uniqueness of f̃.
The existence of nonprincipal points of βX for infinite X uses the ultrafilter lemma.

prerequisites.reason: The proof of the remark uses the ultrafilter lemma to show that nonprincipal ultrafilters exist.

definitions.name: ultrafilter
definitions.text: A filter U on X that is maximal. Equivalently, for each s⊆X exactly one of s and X∖s belongs to U.

definitions.name: push-forward
definitions.text: For f:X→K and an ultrafilter U on X, f_*U={W⊆K : f^{-1}(W)∈U}. It is an ultrafilter on K.

definitions.name: limit of an ultrafilter
definitions.text: An ultrafilter V on K converges to y if every neighborhood of y belongs to V. In a compact space every ultrafilter converges. In a Hausdorff space the limit is unique.

/-- Every ultrafilter `u` on `Ultrafilter α` converges to a unique
  point of `Ultrafilter α`, namely `joinM u`. -/
theorem ultrafilter_converges_iff {u : Ultrafilter (Ultrafilter α)} {x : Ultrafilter α} :
    ↑u ≤ 𝓝 x ↔ x = joinM u := by
  rw [eq_comm, ← Ultrafilter.coe_le_coe]
  change ↑u ≤ 𝓝 x ↔ ∀ s ∈ x, { v : Ultrafilter α | s ∈ v } ∈ u
  simp only [TopologicalSpace.nhds_generateFrom, le_iInf_iff, ultrafilterBasis, le_principal_iff,
    mem_ofPred_eq]
  constructor
  · intro h a ha
    exact h _ ⟨ha, a, rfl⟩
  · rintro h a ⟨xi, a, rfl⟩
    exact h _ xi

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: The topology. We have O_s∩O_t=O_{s∩t} and O_X=βX, so the sets O_s form a basis. For each ultrafilter U exactly one of s and X∖s is in U, so βX is the disjoint union of O_s and O_{X∖s}. Hence each O_s is open and closed.

Hausdorff. Let U≠V be ultrafilters. Neither contains the other, because both are maximal. So there is s in U that is not in V. Then X∖s is in V. The sets O_s and O_{X∖s} are disjoint open neighborhoods of U and V.

Compact. A space is compact if every ultrafilter on it converges. Let 𝔘 be an ultrafilter on βX. Put x={s⊆X : O_s∈𝔘}. Then x is a filter: ∅∉x because O_∅=∅, x is closed under intersection because O_{s∩t}=O_s∩O_t, and it is upward closed because s⊆t gives O_s⊆O_t. For each s the union O_s∪O_{X∖s} is βX, which is in 𝔘. An ultrafilter that contains a union of two sets contains one of them. So s∈x or X∖s∈x, and x is an ultrafilter. Each basic neighborhood O_s of x has s∈x, so O_s∈𝔘. Thus 𝔘 converges to x.
Density. A non-empty basic open set O_s has s non-empty. For a in s the principal ultrafilter at a contains s. So O_s meets the image of pure. Thus the image is dense.

Existence of f̃. Let f:X→K as stated, and let U be in βX. The push-forward f_*U is an ultrafilter on K, so it converges since K is compact. The limit is unique since K is Hausdorff. Define f̃(U) as this limit. For the principal ultrafilter at a, f_*U is the principal ultrafilter at f(a), and its limit is f(a). So f̃∘pure=f.

Continuity of f̃. Let U be in βX and let V be an open neighborhood of f̃(U) in K. A compact Hausdorff space is regular, so there is an open W with f̃(U)∈W and closure(W)⊆V. Since f_*U converges to f̃(U), W∈f_*U. This means s=f^{-1}(W)∈U, so U∈O_s. Let U′ be in O_s. Then W∈f_*U′. The limit of an ultrafilter that contains W lies in closure(W), since otherwise K∖closure(W) would be a neighborhood of the limit that is disjoint from W. So f̃(U′)∈closure(W)⊆V. Hence O_s⊆f̃^{-1}(V), and f̃ is continuous at U.

Uniqueness. If g is another continuous map with g∘pure=f, then g and f̃ agree on the image of pure. The set where two continuous maps into a Hausdorff space agree is closed. It contains a dense set, so it is all of βX. Hence g=f̃.

Remark on points outside the image of pure. If X is infinite, the cofinite sets form a proper filter. By the ultrafilter lemma it extends to an ultrafilter U. This U contains no finite set, so it is not principal. So pure is not onto, and βX has extra points. The extension f̃ gives these points their value as an ultralimit.

worked_application.title: Ultralimits of sequences along a nonprincipal ultrafilter
worked_application.goal: Let U be a nonprincipal ultrafilter on ℕ. Define a_n=(-1)^n·(1+1/n) for n≥1. Compute the ultralimit L(a)=lim_U a_n in [-2,2]. Then compute L(a²) and compare with L(a)².
hypotheses: X=ℕ and K=[-2,2]. The map n↦a_n is a map ℕ→K.
U contains no finite set, since it is nonprincipal.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: K=[-2,2] is compact and Hausdorff, so the theorem gives a continuous map βℕ→K with value L(a)=lim_U a_n at U.

steps.text: Cluster values. The even terms are 1+1/n and tend to 1. The odd terms are -(1+1/n) and tend to -1. A computer check for n between 1000 and 100000 shows that every term lies within 0.001 of 1 or of -1.
The set E of even numbers and the set O of odd numbers split ℕ. Exactly one of them is in U.
Case E∈U. Take ε>0. The set of even n with |a_n-1|<ε is E without a finite set. Since U contains E and no finite set, it contains this set. So every neighborhood of 1 is in a_*U. Hence L(a)=1.
Case O∈U. The same argument with odd n gives L(a)=-1. So L(a) is 1 or -1, and in both cases it is a cluster value of the sequence.

The squares are a_n²=(1+1/n)², which tend to 1. For a nonprincipal ultrafilter, a limit in the ordinary sense is also the ultralimit, because each neighborhood of the limit contains a cofinite set. So L(a²)=1.

Compare: L(a)²=(±1)²=1=L(a²). This agrees with the multiplicativity of the ultralimit, which follows from the continuity of the product on K×K and of f̃. The ultralimit is a linear and multiplicative functional on bounded sequences.

worked_application.result: L(a)=1 if the even numbers are in U, and L(a)=-1 if the odd numbers are in U. In both cases L(a²)=L(a)²=1.

limitations: The space βX is not metrizable and has no explicit description for infinite X. Its points outside X cannot be written down. They need the ultrafilter lemma.
The theorem is for a set X with the discrete topology. For a general space the Stone-Cech compactification is a quotient of βX and it may not contain X as a subspace.
The ultralimit depends on U. Different nonprincipal ultrafilters can give different limits for the same sequence.

results.name: Path and homotopy lifting for covering maps, and the fundamental group of the circle
results.statement: Let p:E→X be a covering map. (1) Path lifting: for every path γ:[0,1]→X and every e in E with p(e)=γ(0) there is exactly one path Γ:[0,1]→E with p∘Γ=γ and Γ(0)=e. (2) Homotopy lifting: for every homotopy H(s,t) on [0,1]×[0,1] with values in X, and every lift f of the map s↦H(s,0), there is exactly one lift H̃ of H with H̃(s,0)=f(s). (3) If two paths γ₀,γ₁ with the same end points are homotopic relative to their end points, then their lifts that start at the same point also end at the same point. (4) For the covering p:ℝ→S¹=ℝ/ℤ, the number w(γ)=Γ(1)−Γ(0) of a loop γ at p(x₀) is an integer. It defines a group isomorphism π₁(S¹,p(x₀))→ℤ. The loop t↦p(x₀+nt) has winding number n.
hypotheses: p is a covering map: each point of X has an open neighborhood U such that p⁻¹(U) is a disjoint union of open sets (sheets), and p maps each sheet homeomorphically onto U.
The domain of paths is the interval [0,1], which is compact and connected. Lifting along other spaces needs more hypotheses.
Part (4) uses the covering ℝ→ℝ/ℤ and the fact that ℝ is contractible.

prerequisites.reason: Existence of lifts splits the interval by a Lebesgue number.

definitions.name: sheet
definitions.text: An open subset of p⁻¹(U) that p maps homeomorphically onto the evenly covered open set U.

definitions.name: homotopy relative to end points
definitions.text: Paths γ₀,γ₁ from x to y are homotopic relative to end points if there is a continuous H(s,t) with H(0,·)=γ₀, H(1,·)=γ₁, H(s,0)=x and H(s,1)=y.

definitions.name: winding number
definitions.text: For a loop γ in S¹=ℝ/ℤ with lift Γ, the winding number is Γ(1)−Γ(0). It is an integer because p(Γ(1))=p(Γ(0)).

/-- The path lifting property (existence) for covering maps. -/
theorem exists_path_lifts : ∃ Γ : C(I, E), p ∘ Γ = γ ∧ Γ 0 = e := by
  let U x := (cov x).2.choose
  choose mem_base U_open _ H _ using fun x ↦ (cov x).2.choose_spec
  obtain ⟨t, t_0, t_mono, ⟨n_max, h_max⟩, t_sub⟩ :=
    exists_monotone_Icc_subset_open_cover_unitInterval
    (fun x ↦ (U_open x).preimage γ.continuous) fun t _ ↦ Set.mem_iUnion.2 ⟨γ t, mem_base _⟩
  suffices ∀ n, ∃ Γ : I → E, ContinuousOn Γ (Set.Icc 0 (t n)) ∧
      (Set.Icc 0 (t n)).EqOn (p ∘ Γ) γ ∧ Γ 0 = e by
    obtain ⟨Γ, cont, eqOn, Γ_0⟩ := this n_max
    rw [h_max _ le_rfl] at cont eqOn
    exact ⟨⟨Γ, continuousOn_univ.mp
      (by convert cont; rw [eq_comm, Set.eq_univ_iff_forall]; exact fun t ↦ ⟨bot_le, le_top⟩)⟩,
      funext fun _ ↦ eqOn ⟨bot_le, le_top⟩, Γ_0⟩
  intro n
  induction n with
  | zero =>
    refine ⟨fun _ ↦ e, continuous_const.continuousOn, fun t ht ↦ ?_, rfl⟩
    rw [t_0, Set.Icc_self, Set.mem_singleton_iff] at ht; subst ht; exact γ_0.symm
  | succ n ih => ?_
  obtain ⟨Γ, cont, eqOn, Γ_0⟩ := ih
  obtain ⟨x, t_sub⟩ := t_sub n
  have pΓtn : p (Γ (t n)) = γ (t n) := eqOn ⟨t_0 ▸ t_mono n.zero_le, le_rfl⟩
  have : Nonempty (p ⁻¹' {x}) :=
    ⟨(H x ⟨Γ (t n), Set.mem_preimage.mpr (pΓtn ▸ t_sub ⟨le_rfl, t_mono n.le_succ⟩)⟩).2⟩
  let q := (cov x).toTrivialization
  refine ⟨fun s ↦ if s ≤ t n then Γ s else q.invFun (γ s, (q (Γ (t n))).2),
    .if (fun s hs ↦ ?_) (cont.mono fun _ h ↦ ?_) ?_, fun s hs ↦ ?_, ?_⟩
  · cases frontier_Iic_subset _ hs.2
    rw [← pΓtn]
    refine (q.symm_apply_mk_proj ?_).symm
    rw [q.mem_source, pΓtn]
    exact t_sub ⟨le_rfl, t_mono n.le_succ⟩
  · rw [closure_le_eq continuous_id' continuous_const] at h; exact ⟨h.1.1, h.2⟩
  · apply q.continuousOn_invFun.comp ((Continuous.prodMk_left _).comp γ.2).continuousOn
    simp_rw [not_le, q.target_eq]; intro s h
    exact ⟨t_sub ⟨closure_lt_subset_le continuous_const continuous_subtype_val h.2, h.1.2⟩, ⟨⟩⟩
  · rw [Function.comp_apply]; split_ifs with h
    exacts [eqOn ⟨hs.1, h⟩, q.proj_symm_apply' (t_sub ⟨le_of_not_ge h, hs.2⟩)]
  · dsimp only; rwa [ite_eq_left (t_0 ▸ t_mono n.zero_le)]

/-- The existence of `liftHomotopy` satisfying `liftHomotopy_lifts` and `liftHomotopy_zero` is
  the homotopy lifting property for covering maps.
  In other words, a covering map is a Hurewicz fibration.
  Proposition 1.30 of [hatcher02]. -/
@[simps] def liftHomotopy : C(I × A, E) where
  toFun ta := cov.liftPath (H.comp <| (ContinuousMap.id I).prodMk <| .const I ta.2)
    (f ta.2) (H_0 ta.2) ta.1
  continuous_toFun := cov.isLocalHomeomorph.continuous_lift cov.isSeparatedMap H
    (by ext ⟨t, a⟩; exact congr_fun (cov.liftPath_lifts ..) t)
    (by convert! f.continuous with a; exact cov.liftPath_zero ..)
    fun a ↦ by dsimp only; exact (cov.liftPath (γ_0 := by simp [*])).2

/-- The winding number of a loop in `AddCircle p` is `(f 1 - f 0) / p`, for any continuous lift
`f` of the loop to `ℝ`. -/
theorem windingNumber_eq_div {x : AddCircle p} (γ : Path x x) (f : C(I, ℝ)) (hf : (↑) ∘ f = γ) :
    (windingNumber (.mk γ) : ℝ) = (f 1 - f 0) / p := by
  have h0 : (f 0 : AddCircle p) = x := congr($hf 0).trans γ.source
  obtain ⟨n, hn⟩ : ∃ n : ℤ, n • p = f 1 - f 0 :=
    AddSubgroup.mem_zmultiples_iff.mp <| QuotientAddGroup.eq_iff_sub_mem.mp <|
      congr($hf 1).trans <| γ.target.trans h0.symm
  have h : (isAddQuotientCoveringMap_coe p).fundamentalGroupEquiv (x := x) ⟨f 0, h0⟩ (.mk γ) =
      .op (.ofAdd ⟨n • p, n, rfl⟩) :=
    (isAddQuotientCoveringMap_coe p).fundamentalGroupToMulOpposite_apply_mk_eq hf rfl (by simp [hn])
  simp [windingNumber, windingNumberIso, AddSubgroup.zmultiplesEquivInt_apply_zsmul hp.out.ne' n,
    (isAddQuotientCoveringMap_coe p).fundamentalGroupEquiv_eq _ ⟨f 0, h0⟩, h,
    eq_div_iff hp.out.ne', ← zsmul_eq_mul, ← hn]

steps.text: Uniqueness in (1). Let Γ and Γ′ be two lifts of γ with Γ(0)=Γ′(0). Let Z be the set of t with Γ(t)=Γ′(t). Z is closed: if Γ(t)≠Γ′(t), the two points lie over the same point γ(t) of an evenly covered set U. They are different, and p is injective on each sheet, so they lie in different sheets. Disjoint sheets are open, so Γ(t′) and Γ′(t′) lie in different sheets for t′ near t. Hence Γ(t′)≠Γ′(t′) near t. Z is open: if Γ(t)=Γ′(t) lies in a sheet S, then Γ and Γ′ stay in S near t. On S the map p is injective, and p∘Γ=p∘Γ′, so Γ=Γ′ near t. The interval [0,1] is connected, Z contains 0, so Z=[0,1].

Existence in (1). Cover X by evenly covered open sets U_α. The sets γ⁻¹(U_α) form an open cover of the compact interval [0,1]. By the Lebesgue number lemma there is a partition 0=t₀<t₁<…<t_n=1 such that γ([t_{i−1},t_i]) lies in one set U_i of the cover, for each i.

Existence in (1), the induction. Suppose Γ is defined and continuous on [0,t_{i−1}] with p∘Γ=γ there. The point Γ(t_{i−1}) lies over γ(t_{i−1}) in U_i, so it lies in exactly one sheet S of p⁻¹(U_i). Define Γ on [t_{i−1},t_i] by (p|S)⁻¹∘γ. This is continuous, it lifts γ, and it agrees with the old Γ at t_{i−1}. By the pasting lemma Γ is continuous on [0,t_i]. For i=n the lift is complete.

Homotopy lifting (2). Let H(s,t) on [0,1]² and a lift f of s↦H(s,0) be given. For each s let H̃(s,·) be the lift of H(s,·) from steps 2 and 3 that starts at f(s). Fix s₀. Apply steps 2 and 3 to the path H(s₀,·). It gives a partition 0=t₀<…<t_n=1 and evenly covered sets U_i with H({s₀}×[t_{i−1},t_i])⊆U_i. By the tube lemma (compactness of [t_{i−1},t_i]) there is an open neighborhood N of s₀ with H(N×[t_{i−1},t_i])⊆U_i for all i.

Continuity of H̃ near s₀. By induction on i, shrink N so that H̃ is continuous on N×[0,t_{i−1}] and H̃(N×{t_{i−1}}) lies in one sheet S_i over U_i. This holds for i=1 by the continuity of f, after shrinking N. Then H̃(s,t)=(p|S_i)⁻¹(H(s,t)) for t in [t_{i−1},t_i] and s in N, by the uniqueness in step 1. So H̃ is continuous on N×[t_{i−1},t_i]. The point H̃(s₀,t_i) lies in one sheet over U_{i+1}, so a smaller N keeps H̃(N×{t_i}) in the next sheet. After n steps H̃ is continuous on N×[0,1]. Uniqueness of H̃ follows from step 1 for each fixed s.

End points (3). Let H be a homotopy relative to end points from γ₀ to γ₁, and e the common starting point. Take f(s)=e for all s, a lift of H(·,0)=x constant. By steps 4 and 5, H̃ exists and is a lift of H. The path s↦H̃(s,1) lifts the constant path at y, so it maps into the fiber p⁻¹(y). The fiber is discrete, and [0,1] is connected, so this path is constant. By uniqueness in step 1, H̃(0,·) is the lift of γ₀ from e and H̃(1,·) is the lift of γ₁ from e. They end at H̃(0,1)=H̃(1,1).

The circle (4), well defined. Let p:ℝ→ℝ/ℤ and let γ be a loop at p(x₀). Its lift Γ from x₀ has p(Γ(1))=p(Γ(0)), so Γ(1)−Γ(0) is an integer. By step 6 it depends only on the class of γ in π₁(S¹,p(x₀)), so w is a map on π₁.

The circle (4), homomorphism. For loops γ and δ, let Γ lift γ from x₀, and let Δ lift δ from x₀. The translate Δ+w(γ) by an integer also lifts δ, since p(y+n)=p(y). It starts at x₀+w(γ)=Γ(1). So Γ followed by Δ+w(γ) lifts the concatenation γ·δ. It ends at x₀+w(γ)+w(δ). So w(γ·δ)=w(γ)+w(δ).
The circle (4), onto. For n in ℤ the path t↦x₀+nt lifts the loop t↦p(x₀+nt), and it has w=n. So w is onto.

The circle (4), injective. Let w(γ)=0. Then the lift Γ is a loop in ℝ at x₀. The map H(s,t)=(1−s)Γ(t)+s·x₀ is a homotopy in ℝ relative to end points from Γ to the constant path. The map p∘H is a homotopy relative to end points from γ to the constant loop. So the class of γ is trivial, and w is injective. Hence π₁(S¹)≅ℤ.

worked_application.title: Winding numbers of polynomial loops and a root count
worked_application.goal: Let q(z)=z³+2z+1. For radius R, let γ_R be the loop t↦q(Re^{2πit})/|q(Re^{2πit})| in the unit circle S¹⊂ℂ. Compute the winding number of γ_R for R=0.3, 1 and 3. Then use the homotopy invariance to show that q has a root in |z|<3.
hypotheses: The winding number is w(γ_R) as in part (4), with S¹=ℝ/ℤ identified with the unit circle by x↦e^{2πix}.
The loop is defined only if q has no root on |z|=R.
The roots of q are one real root near −0.4534 and a complex pair of modulus about 1.4851.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: Each γ_R is a loop in S¹, so the theorem gives an integer winding number that is invariant under homotopy of loops in S¹ relative to the base point.

steps.text: Numerical lift. For each R, take 20000 equal steps in t. At each step add the principal argument of the ratio of consecutive values of q(Re^{2πit}), then divide the total by 2π. The largest single step is about 0.0011 radians for R=3, which is well below π. So the sum is the true lift.

The results are w(γ_{0.3})=0, w(γ_1)=1 and w(γ_3)=3, up to errors of order 10⁻¹⁴. They are integers, as the theorem requires. They also equal the number of roots of q inside the circle, because 0.4534<1<1.4851, in agreement with the argument principle.

Homotopy for R=3. Put q_s(z)=z³+s(2z+1) for s in [0,1]. On |z|=3 we have |z³|=27 and |2z+1|≤7, so q_s has no root on the circle. A computer check of 6300 sample points confirms that the margin 27−|2z+1| is at least 20. So the loops γ^{(s)}(t)=q_s(3e^{2πit})/|q_s(3e^{2πit})| form a homotopy in S¹ from the loop of z³ to γ_3. The base point moves. This is still fine: by steps 4 and 5 the homotopy lifts, and s↦H̃(s,1)−H̃(s,0) is continuous and integer valued, so it is constant. Hence the winding number is the same for all s. For q_0 the loop is t↦e^{6πit}, with winding number 3. This agrees with the computed value.

Root in |z|<3. Suppose q had no root with |z|≤3. Then H(s,t)=q(3s·e^{2πit})/|q(3s·e^{2πit})| is a homotopy of loops from the constant loop at q(0)/|q(0)| to γ_3. The winding number is constant along it by the argument of step 3, so w(γ_3)=0. This contradicts w(γ_3)=3. So q has a root with |z|≤3.

The argument does not find the root. It shows only that one exists. For a monic polynomial of degree n, the same homotopy to zⁿ on a large circle gives winding number n, hence a root. This is a proof of the fundamental theorem of algebra.

worked_application.result: The winding numbers of γ_R for R=0.3, 1, 3 are 0, 1, 3. The value 3 for R=3 forces a root of z³+2z+1 inside |z|≤3.

limitations: A lift depends on the choice of the starting point. A loop in the base need not lift to a loop in the cover.
The statement is for paths and homotopies of the interval. For a map from a general space A, lifting needs A to be simply connected and locally path connected.
The method gives the fundamental group of the circle only. For other spaces one needs a simply connected covering space and its deck group.

results.name: Characteristic functions decide independence
results.statement: Let X and Y be random vectors in ℝᵈ on a probability space (Ω,F,P). Write φ_Z(t)=E e^{i⟨t,Z⟩}. (a) If two finite Borel measures μ and ν on ℝⁿ satisfy φ_μ=φ_ν, then μ=ν. (b) X and Y are independent if and only if E exp(i⟨s,X⟩+i⟨t,Y⟩)=φ_X(s)φ_Y(t) for all s,t in ℝᵈ.
hypotheses: The measures in (a) are finite and Borel. The space is ℝⁿ with the usual inner product.
In (b) the vectors X and Y are measurable. They take values in the same space ℝᵈ, but the argument also works for different dimensions.
The factorization in (b) must hold for every pair (s,t). One pair is not enough.

Dominated convergence to remove the smoothing and to approximate closed sets.

definitions.name: characteristic function
definitions.text: For a finite measure μ on ℝⁿ, φ_μ(t)=∫e^{i⟨t,x⟩}dμ(x). For a random vector Z, φ_Z is the characteristic function of its law.

definitions.name: independence of random vectors
definitions.text: X and Y are independent when the law of the pair (X,Y) is the product of the laws of X and Y.

definitions.name: Gaussian smoothing
definitions.text: The convolution of a measure μ with the centered normal law N(0,σ²I). It has a bounded continuous density.

/-- Two random variables are independent if and only if their joint characteristic function is equal
to the product of the characteristic functions. This is the version for Hilbert spaces, see
`indepFun_iff_charFunDual_prod` for the Banach space version. -/
lemma indepFun_iff_charFun_prod [CompleteSpace E] (hX : AEMeasurable X P) (hY : AEMeasurable Y P) :
    X ⟂ᵢ[P] Y ↔ ∀ t, charFun (P.map (fun ω ↦ toLp 2 (X ω, Y ω))) t =
      charFun (P.map X) t.ofLp.1 * charFun (P.map Y) t.ofLp.2 := by
  rw [indepFun_iff_map_prod_eq_prod_map_map hX hY, ← charFun_eq_prod_iff,
    AEMeasurable.map_map_of_aemeasurable (by fun_prop) (by fun_prop), Function.comp_def]

a complete second-countable inner product space coincide, then `μ = ν`. -/
theorem Measure.ext_of_charFun [CompleteSpace E]
    [IsFiniteMeasure μ] [IsFiniteMeasure ν] (h : charFun μ = charFun ν) :
    μ = ν := by
  simp_rw [funext_iff, charFun_eq_integral_innerProbChar] at h
  refine ext_of_integral_char_eq continuous_probChar probChar_ne_one (L := innerₗ E)
    ?_ ?_ h
  · exact fun v hv ↦ DFunLike.ne_iff.mpr ⟨v, inner_self_ne_zero.mpr hv⟩
  · exact continuous_inner

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Normal characteristic function. Let g(x)=e^{−x²/2}/√(2π) and φ(t)=∫e^{itx}g(x)dx. The factor |x|e^{−x²/2} is integrable, so differentiation under the integral is allowed. Then φ′(t)=∫ix e^{itx}g(x)dx. Integration by parts gives φ′(t)=−tφ(t). Also φ(0)=1. So φ(t)=e^{−t²/2}.

Gaussian inversion formula. The scaling x↦x/σ gives ∫e^{itu}e^{−σ²t²/2}dt=(√(2π)/σ)e^{−u²/(2σ²)} for σ>0. Take the product over d coordinates. With g_σ(u)=(2πσ²)^{−d/2}e^{−|u|²/(2σ²)} we get g_σ(u)=(2π)^{−d}∫e^{i⟨t,u⟩}e^{−σ²|t|²/2}dt. The d-dimensional integrals split into products by the Fubini theorem.

Smoothed density from the characteristic function. Let μ be a finite measure and h_σ(x)=∫g_σ(x−z)dμ(z). Insert the formula of step 2. The integrand is bounded by e^{−σ²|t|²/2}, which is integrable for dt⊗dμ. So Fubini gives h_σ(x)=(2π)^{−d}∫e^{i⟨t,x⟩}e^{−σ²|t|²/2}φ_μ(−t)dt. Thus h_σ depends on μ only through φ_μ.

Equal smoothings. If φ_μ=φ_ν, then h_σ is the same function for μ and ν, for each σ>0. So the measures h_σ(x)dx coincide. Let f be bounded and continuous. Then ∫f(x)h_σ(x)dx=∫E f(z+σN)dμ(z), where N is a standard normal vector. The same holds for ν.

Remove the smoothing. As σ→0, f(z+σN)→f(z) for each z. The integrand is bounded by sup|f|, and μ is finite. So the dominated convergence theorem gives ∫E f(z+σN)dμ(z)→∫f dμ. The same holds for ν. Hence ∫f dμ=∫f dν for every bounded continuous f.

Equal measures. Let F be a closed set and f_k(x)=max(0,1−k·dist(x,F)). Each f_k is bounded and continuous, and f_k↓1_F. By dominated convergence μ(F)=ν(F). Closed sets form a π-system that generates the Borel σ-algebra, and μ(ℝⁿ)=ν(ℝⁿ). So μ=ν by the π-λ uniqueness theorem. This proves (a).
Proof of (b), forward direction. If X and Y are independent, the law of (X,Y) is μ_X⊗μ_Y. The Fubini theorem gives E exp(i⟨s,X⟩+i⟨t,Y⟩)=∫e^{i⟨s,x⟩}dμ_X ∫e^{i⟨t,y⟩}dμ_Y=φ_X(s)φ_Y(t).

Proof of (b), reverse direction. The product measure μ_X⊗μ_Y has characteristic function φ_X(s)φ_Y(t) by the same Fubini computation. This equals the characteristic function of the law of (X,Y) by hypothesis. By part (a) with n=2d, the law of (X,Y) equals μ_X⊗μ_Y. This is independence.

worked_application.title: Uncorrelated variables that are not independent
worked_application.goal: Use the joint characteristic function to show that a pair is dependent, and to show that a pair of normal combinations is independent.
hypotheses: Case 1: (X,Y) is uniform on the three points (0,0), (1,1) and (−1,1).
Case 2: X and Z are independent N(0,1) variables. The pair is (U,V)=(X+Z,X−Z).
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: Part (b) says independence is equivalent to the factorization for every (s,t). So one failing pair (s,t) proves dependence, and a general identity proves independence.

steps.text: Case 1 marginals. X takes the values 0, 1, −1 with probability 1/3 each. So φ_X(s)=(1+2cos s)/3. Y takes the value 0 with probability 1/3 and 1 with probability 2/3. So φ_Y(t)=(1+2e^{it})/3.

Case 1 joint function. φ_{(X,Y)}(s,t)=(1+e^{i(s+t)}+e^{i(−s+t)})/3. At (s,t)=(π,π) both exponentials equal 1, so the value is 1. The product is φ_X(π)φ_Y(π)=(−1/3)(−1/3)=1/9. Since 1≠1/9, the factorization fails and X,Y are dependent.

Case 1 is uncorrelated. E X=0 and E[XY]=(0+1−1)/3=0. So Cov(X,Y)=0. Covariance zero does not give independence. A second test point (s,t)=(1,0.5) gives the joint value 0.6494+0.1727i and the product 0.6369+0.2217i. They differ again.
Case 2 joint function. E exp(is(X+Z)+it(X−Z))=E exp(i(s+t)X)E exp(i(s−t)Z)=exp(−((s+t)²+(s−t)²)/2)=exp(−(s²+t²)).

Case 2 marginals. U=X+Z and V=X−Z are N(0,2). So φ_U(s)=e^{−s²} and φ_V(t)=e^{−t²}. The product is e^{−(s²+t²)}. It equals the joint function for all (s,t). At (s,t)=(0.7,−1.3) both sides equal e^{−2.18}=0.113042. By part (b), U and V are independent.

worked_application.result: Case 1: the pair is dependent although Cov(X,Y)=0, because φ_{(X,Y)}(π,π)=1 and φ_X(π)φ_Y(π)=1/9. Case 2: X+Z and X−Z are independent.
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: Part (a) needs finite measures. For infinite measures the characteristic function may not exist.
The factorization must hold for all arguments. Testing a finite set of (s,t) cannot prove independence.
The proof of (a) shown here is for ℝⁿ. Infinite-dimensional spaces need a different argument. The source declaration covers Hilbert spaces.
This entry says nothing about convergence of laws. That is the Lévy continuity theorem.

results.name: Jointly Gaussian and uncorrelated implies independent
results.statement: Let (X,Y) be a jointly Gaussian pair of real random variables. This means every real combination aX+bY has a normal law, possibly with variance 0. If Cov(X,Y)=0, then X and Y are independent. Hence for i.i.d. normal X₁,…,Xₙ the sample mean X̄ is independent of every residual Xᵢ−X̄ and of the sample variance.
hypotheses: The pair must be jointly Gaussian. Two normal marginals are not enough.
All second moments are finite, because a normal law has all moments.
Degenerate normal laws are allowed. A constant is a normal law with variance 0.

prerequisites.reason: The independence criterion that turns the factorization into independence.

definitions.name: jointly Gaussian
definitions.text: A random vector is jointly Gaussian when every real linear functional of it has a normal law.

definitions.name: covariance

definitions.name: sample variance
definitions.text: S²=(1/(n−1))Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)². It is a function of the residuals Xᵢ−X̄.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Reduce to a characteristic function. For real s,t let W=sX+tY. By assumption W is normal with mean m_W=sEX+tEY and variance v_W. Hence E e^{iW}=exp(i m_W−v_W/2). The normal characteristic function is derived in the entry on characteristic functions.
Compute the variance. v_W=s²Var X+2s t Cov(X,Y)+t²Var Y. With Cov(X,Y)=0 this is s²Var X+t²Var Y.
Factor the joint function. E e^{i(sX+tY)}=exp(i sEX−s²Var X/2)·exp(i tEY−t²Var Y/2).

Identify the factors. Take (s,t)=(s,0) and (0,t) in step 1. Then X is normal with mean EX and variance Var X, and Y is normal with mean EY and variance Var Y. So the two factors are φ_X(s) and φ_Y(t).
Conclude. The joint characteristic function equals φ_X(s)φ_Y(t) for all (s,t). By the characteristic-function criterion for independence, X and Y are independent.

Sample mean and residuals. Let X₁,…,Xₙ be i.i.d. N(μ,σ²). The vector (X̄, X₁−X̄,…,Xₙ−X̄) is a linear image of the Gaussian vector (X₁,…,Xₙ), so it is jointly Gaussian. Cov(X̄,Xᵢ)=σ²/n and Var X̄=σ²/n. So Cov(X̄,Xᵢ−X̄)=0. Every pair (X̄,Xᵢ−X̄) is jointly Gaussian and uncorrelated, so it is independent. Now let R=(X₁−X̄,…,Xₙ−X̄). For real s and a vector t, the combination sX̄+⟨t,R⟩ is normal with variance s²Var X̄+Var⟨t,R⟩, because Cov(X̄,⟨t,R⟩)=0. So the joint characteristic function factorizes, as in steps 1 to 4. By the criterion, X̄ is independent of R. Then X̄ is independent of S², which is a function of R.

worked_application.title: Sample mean against residuals, and a counterexample
worked_application.goal: Check that Cov(X̄,Xᵢ−X̄)=0 for n=5 and σ²=2. Then build a pair with normal marginals and zero covariance that is not independent.
hypotheses: n=5, Xᵢ i.i.d. N(μ,2).
Counterexample: X is N(0,1), S is an independent fair sign ±1, and Y=S·X.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: In the first case the vector is a linear image of a Gaussian vector, so the theorem applies. In the second case the pair is not jointly Gaussian, so the theorem does not apply.

steps.text: Variance of the mean. Var X̄=σ²/n=2/5. Also Cov(X̄,Xᵢ)=σ²/n=2/5 for each i.
Residual covariance. Cov(X̄,Xᵢ−X̄)=2/5−2/5=0 for i=1,…,5. The pair (X̄,Xᵢ−X̄) is jointly Gaussian, so X̄ is independent of Xᵢ−X̄.
Counterexample marginals. Y=S·X is N(0,1) because S is independent of X and symmetric. Cov(X,Y)=E[S]E[X²]=0, since E S=0.
Counterexample dependence. |Y|=|X| always. So P(|X|>1,|Y|≤1)=0. But P(|X|>1)=0.317311 and P(|Y|≤1)=0.682689, whose product is 0.216625. The two numbers differ, so X and Y are dependent.
Why the theorem does not apply. If (X,Y) were jointly Gaussian, then X+Y would be normal. But X+Y=(1+S)X is 0 with probability 1/2 and 2X with probability 1/2. This is not a normal law.

worked_application.result: Cov(X̄,Xᵢ−X̄)=0 gives independence in the Gaussian case. The pair (X,SX) has normal marginals and zero covariance but is dependent, with P(|X|>1,|Y|≤1)=0 against a product of 0.216625.
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: The result needs joint Gaussianity. The counterexample in the application shows that normal marginals and zero covariance are not enough.
Independence of the vector (X̄,residuals) from S² needs the block form. It follows from the same characteristic-function factorization for a block covariance that is zero.
The theorem is special to Gaussian laws. For other laws, zero covariance is weaker than independence.

results.name: The boundary of a convex set has Lebesgue measure zero
results.statement: Let C⊂ℝᵈ be convex. Then the Lebesgue measure of the boundary ∂C is 0. Hence C is Lebesgue measurable. If C is also bounded, the outer approximations by grid cubes meeting C and the inner approximations by grid cubes inside C have areas that differ by a quantity that tends to 0 with the mesh.
hypotheses: C need not be open, closed or bounded.
The measure is Lebesgue measure on ℝᵈ. Any Haar measure on a finite-dimensional real space gives the same result.
The grid statement is for bounded C. It uses cubes of side h in the lattice hℤᵈ.
results.empty_prerequisites_reason: The proof uses only scaling of Lebesgue measure and elementary convexity. No catalog theorem is cited.

/-- Haar measure of the frontier of a convex set is zero. -/
theorem addHaar_frontier (hs : Convex ℝ s) : μ (frontier s) = 0 := by
  /- If `s` is included in a hyperplane, then `frontier s ⊆ closure s` is included in the same
    hyperplane, hence it has measure zero. -/
  rcases ne_or_eq (affineSpan ℝ s) ⊤ with hspan | hspan
  · refine measure_mono_null ?_ (addHaar_affineSubspace _ _ hspan)
    exact frontier_subset_closure.trans
      (closure_minimal (subset_affineSpan _ _) (affineSpan ℝ s).closed_of_finiteDimensional)
  rw [← hs.interior_nonempty_iff_affineSpan_eq_top] at hspan
  rcases hspan with ⟨x, hx⟩
  /- Without loss of generality, `s` is bounded. Indeed, `∂s ⊆ ⋃ n, ∂(s ∩ ball x (n + 1))`, hence it
    suffices to prove that `∀ n, μ (s ∩ ball x (n + 1)) = 0`; the latter set is bounded.
    -/
  suffices H : ∀ t : Set E, Convex ℝ t → x ∈ interior t → IsBounded t → μ (frontier t) = 0 by
    let B : ℕ → Set E := fun n => ball x (n + 1)
    have : μ (⋃ n : ℕ, frontier (s ∩ B n)) = 0 := by
      refine measure_iUnion_null fun n =>
        H _ (hs.inter (convex_ball _ _)) ?_ (isBounded_ball.subset inter_subset_right)
      rw [interior_inter, isOpen_ball.interior_eq]
      exact ⟨hx, mem_ball_self (add_pos_of_nonneg_of_pos n.cast_nonneg zero_lt_one)⟩
    refine measure_mono_null (fun y hy => ?_) this; clear this
    set N : ℕ := ⌊dist y x⌋₊
    refine mem_iUnion.2 ⟨N, ?_⟩
    have hN : y ∈ B N := by simp [B, N, Nat.lt_floor_add_one]
    suffices y ∈ frontier (s ∩ B N) ∩ B N from this.1
    rw [frontier_inter_open_inter isOpen_ball]
    exact ⟨hy, hN⟩
  intro s hs hx hb
  /- Since `s` is bounded, we have `μ (interior s) ≠ ∞`, hence it suffices to prove
    `μ (closure s) ≤ μ (interior s)`. -/
  replace hb : μ (interior s) ≠ ∞ := (hb.subset interior_subset).measure_lt_top.ne
  suffices μ (closure s) ≤ μ (interior s) by
    rwa [frontier, measure_sdiff interior_subset_closure isOpen_interior.nullMeasurableSet hb,
      tsub_eq_zero_iff_le]
  /- Due to `Convex.closure_subset_image_homothety_interior_of_one_lt`, for any `r > 1` we have
    `closure s ⊆ homothety x r '' interior s`, hence `μ (closure s) ≤ r ^ d * μ (interior s)`,
    where `d = finrank ℝ E`. -/
  set d : ℕ := Module.finrank ℝ E
  have : ∀ r : ℝ≥0, 1 < r → μ (closure s) ≤ ↑(r ^ d) * μ (interior s) := fun r hr ↦ by
    refine (measure_mono <|
      hs.closure_subset_image_homothety_interior_of_one_lt hx r hr).trans_eq ?_
    rw [addHaar_image_homothety, ← NNReal.coe_pow, NNReal.abs_eq, ENNReal.ofReal_coe_nnreal]
  have : ∀ᶠ (r : ℝ≥0) in 𝓝[>] 1, μ (closure s) ≤ ↑(r ^ d) * μ (interior s) :=
    mem_of_superset self_mem_nhdsWithin this
  -- Taking the limit as `r → 1`, we get `μ (closure s) ≤ μ (interior s)`.
  refine ge_of_tendsto ?_ this
  refine (((ENNReal.continuous_mul_const hb).comp
    (ENNReal.continuous_coe.comp (continuous_pow d))).tendsto' _ _ ?_).mono_left nhdsWithin_le_nhds
  simp

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Low-dimensional case. If the affine hull of C is a proper subspace, it lies in a hyperplane. So C̄ lies in the same hyperplane, which has measure 0. Then ∂C⊂C̄ has measure 0.

Reduction to bounded sets. Assume C has an interior point. Translate so that it is 0 and pick r>0 with the ball B_r⊂C. Let C_n=C∩B(0,n) for n>r. The frontier is local, so ∂C⊂⋃_n ∂C_n. Each C_n is convex and bounded and contains B_r. A countable union of null sets is null. So it is enough to treat bounded C with B_r⊂C.

Shrinking lemma. Let K=C̄ and 0<t<1. Fix k∈K. Pick c∈C with |k−c|<δ, where δ=r(1−t)/(2t). For b with |b|<r/2 put b′=b+t(k−c)/(1−t). Then |b′|<r/2+r/2=r, so b′∈B_r⊂C. Now t k+(1−t)b=t c+(1−t)b′ is a convex combination of c and b′, which are in C. So t k+(1−t)B_{r/2}⊂C, and t k∈int C.
Boundary inclusion. By step 3, tK⊂int C. Hence ∂C=K∖int C⊂K∖tK for every t<1.
Measure of the shell. K is bounded, so Leb(K)<∞. The map x↦t x scales Lebesgue measure by tᵈ. So Leb(K∖tK)=Leb(K)−tᵈLeb(K)=(1−tᵈ)Leb(K). Let t→1. Then Leb(∂C)=0.
Measurability. C=int C ∪ (C∩∂C). The set int C is open, and C∩∂C is a subset of a null set. So C is Lebesgue measurable.

Grid statement. Let C be bounded and F=∂C. F is closed and bounded. A closed cube Q that meets both C and its complement contains a segment from a point of C to a point outside C. That segment contains a point of F. So the cubes that are not inside C but meet C all meet F. Let Q_k be the union of the closed dyadic cubes of side 2⁻ᵏ that meet F. These sets are nested, bounded and decreasing. Their intersection is F, because F is closed. So Leb(Q_k)→Leb(F)=0. The difference between the outer and inner sums is at most Leb(Q_k).

worked_application.title: Area of the unit disk by grid cubes
worked_application.goal: Bound the area of the quarter unit disk by cubes of side 1/m, and watch the boundary layer shrink.
hypotheses: Quarter disk D={x,y≥0, x²+y²≤1}, convex and compact.
Cubes [i/m,(i+1)/m]×[j/m,(j+1)/m] with 0≤i,j<m.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: D is convex. So its boundary has measure zero. The cubes that touch the boundary but are not inside D have total area that tends to 0.

steps.text: Count the inner cubes. A cube is inside D when (i+1)²+(j+1)²≤m². For m=10, 50, 200, 1000 the counts are 69, 1911, 31207 and 784387.
Count the boundary cubes. A cube is a boundary cube when it is not inside D and i²+j²<m². The counts are 17, 95, 395 and 1993.

Area bounds. Inner area = count/m² and outer area = (inner+boundary)/m². The bounds are 0.69 to 0.86 for m=10, 0.7644 to 0.8024 for m=50, 0.780175 to 0.79005 for m=200, and 0.784387 to 0.78638 for m=1000.
Multiply by 4. The bounds on π are 2.76 to 3.44, 3.0576 to 3.2096, 3.1207 to 3.1602 and 3.137548 to 3.14552. All intervals contain π=3.14159.
Boundary layer. The area gap equals 0.17, 0.038, 0.009875 and 0.001993. The gap times m is 1.7, 1.9, 1.975 and 1.993. So the gap shrinks like 2/m in this example.

worked_application.result: The inner and outer grid areas squeeze π/4 with a gap that goes to 0, as the theorem predicts for a convex set.
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: The result is about convex sets. A bounded open set can have a boundary of positive measure, as in the complement of a fat Cantor set.

The rate 2/m in the application is an observation for the disk. The theorem gives only convergence to 0. For general convex bodies the gap is O(h) in a fixed dimension, but that rate is not proved here.
Infinite-dimensional spaces have no Lebesgue measure.

results.statement: Let E be a real normed space, x₀∈E, r>0 and f convex on the open ball B(x₀,r). Assume |f|≤M on B(x₀,r). Then for every ε>0, f is Lipschitz on B(x₀,r−ε) with constant 2M/ε.

ε>0. If ε≥r the inner ball is empty and the claim is empty.
E can be infinite-dimensional. The bound does not depend on the dimension.

lemma ConvexOn.lipschitzOnWith_of_abs_le (hf : ConvexOn ℝ (ball x₀ r) f) (hε : 0 < ε)
    (hM : ∀ a, dist a x₀ < r → |f a| ≤ M) :
    LipschitzOnWith (2 * M / ε).toNNReal f (ball x₀ (r - ε)) := by
  set K := 2 * M / ε with hK
  have oneside {x y : E} (hx : x ∈ ball x₀ (r - ε)) (hy : y ∈ ball x₀ (r - ε)) :
      f x - f y ≤ K * ‖x - y‖ := by
    obtain rfl | hxy := eq_or_ne x y
    · simp
    have hx₀r : ball x₀ (r - ε) ⊆ ball x₀ r := ball_subset_ball <| by linarith
    have hx' : x ∈ ball x₀ r := hx₀r hx
    have hy' : y ∈ ball x₀ r := hx₀r hy
    let z := x + (ε / ‖x - y‖) • (x - y)
    replace hxy : 0 < ‖x - y‖ := by rwa [norm_sub_pos_iff]
    have hz : z ∈ ball x₀ r := mem_ball_iff_norm.2 <| by
      calc
        _ = ‖(x - x₀) + (ε / ‖x - y‖) • (x - y)‖ := by simp only [z, add_sub_right_comm]
        _ ≤ ‖x - x₀‖ + ‖(ε / ‖x - y‖) • (x - y)‖ := norm_add_le ..
        _ < r - ε + ε :=
          add_lt_add_of_lt_of_le (mem_ball_iff_norm.1 hx) <| by
            simp [norm_smul, abs_of_nonneg, hε.le, hxy.ne']
        _ = r := by simp
    let a := ε / (ε + ‖x - y‖)
    let b := ‖x - y‖ / (ε + ‖x - y‖)
    have hab : a + b = 1 := by simp [field, a, b]
    have hxyz : x = a • y + b • z := by
      calc
        x = a • x + b • x := by rw [Convex.combo_self hab]
        _ = a • y + b • z := by simp [z, a, b, smul_smul, hxy.ne', smul_sub]; abel
    rw [hK, mul_comm, ← mul_div_assoc, le_div_iff₀' hε]
    calc

steps.text: Setup. Let x,y be distinct points of B(x₀,r−ε) and d=‖x−y‖>0. Define z=x+(ε/d)(x−y).
The point z is in the ball. ‖z−x₀‖≤‖x−x₀‖+ε<(r−ε)+ε=r. So z∈B(x₀,r), and |f(z)|≤M.
Convex combination. Put a=ε/(ε+d) and b=d/(ε+d). Then a+b=1, and a y+b z=x. Check: a y+b z=(ε y+d x+ε(x−y))/(ε+d)=((ε+d)x)/(ε+d)=x.
Apply convexity. f(x)≤a f(y)+b f(z). Since a=1−b, this gives f(x)−f(y)≤b(f(z)−f(y)).
Bound the right side. |f(z)−f(y)|≤2M because both points are in the ball. So f(x)−f(y)≤2M·d/(ε+d)≤2Md/ε.
Symmetry. Exchange x and y. The argument gives f(y)−f(x)≤(2M/ε)‖x−y‖. Together, |f(x)−f(y)|≤(2M/ε)‖x−y‖ on B(x₀,r−ε).

worked_application.title: Log-sum-exp on a disk
worked_application.goal: Find a Lipschitz constant for f(x,y)=ln(eˣ+eʸ) on a small disk from a bound on a large disk, and compare with the true constant.
hypotheses: f is convex on ℝ². Take x₀=0 and r=2.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: f is convex, and |f| is bounded on the open disk of radius 2. So the theorem applies with M equal to that bound.

steps.text: Bound on the large disk. The maximum of |f| over the circle of radius 2 is 2.15045. The convex function f attains its sup on the boundary circle. The minimum of f on the disk is ln2−√2=−0.72107, which is smaller in absolute value. Use M=2.1505.
Constants from the theorem. K=2M/ε equals 4.3010 on B(0,1) for ε=1. It equals 8.6020 on B(0,1.5) for ε=0.5. It equals 17.2040 on B(0,1.75) for ε=0.25.
True constant on B(0,1). The gradient of f is (p,1−p) with p=1/(1+e^{y−x}). So |∇f|²=p²+(1−p)². On the unit disk |x−y|≤√2, so p lies in [0.19570, 0.80430]. The maximum of |∇f| is 0.8278.
Check by sampling. Among 200000 random pairs in the unit disk, the largest ratio |f(x)−f(y)|/‖x−y‖ is 0.8174. It stays below 0.8278 and below 4.3010.
Comparison. The theorem bound 4.3010 is about 5.2 times the true constant 0.8278. The bound is safe but not sharp.

results.name: Exponential tilting and the Chernoff bound
results.statement: Let X be a real random variable. Put M(t)=E e^{tX} and Λ(t)=ln M(t). Assume M is finite on an open interval I. For t in I define the tilted law P_t by dP_t/dP=e^{tX−Λ(t)}. Then (a) P_t is a probability law equivalent to P, and P(A)=E_t[e^{−tX+Λ(t)}1_A] for every event A. (b) E_t X=Λ′(t) and Var_t X=Λ″(t)≥0, so Λ is convex on I. (c) For t≥0 in I, P(X≥a)≤exp(−(ta−Λ(t))). (d) If X₁,…,Xₙ are i.i.d. copies of X and Sₙ=ΣXᵢ, then P(Sₙ≥na)≤exp(−n(ta−Λ(t))). If a=Λ′(t*) with t*>0 in I, then P(Sₙ≥na)=e^{−nI}E_{t*}[e^{−t*(Sₙ−na)}1_{Sₙ≥na}]≤e^{−nI}, where I=t*a−Λ(t*).
hypotheses: M(t) is finite on an open interval I. This gives all moments under every tilt.
In (c) and (d) the point t is in I and t≥0.
For the exact identity in (d), the tilt t* satisfies Λ′(t*)=a. Then t* gives the best exponent.

steps.text: Tilted law. The density e^{tX−Λ(t)} is positive and has mean M(t)e^{−Λ(t)}=1. So P_t is a probability law, and P and P_t have the same null sets. Dividing by the density gives P(A)=E_t[e^{−tX+Λ(t)}1_A]. This proves (a).
Domination. Fix t in I and δ>0 with [t−δ,t+δ]⊂I. For |s−t|≤δ/2 and k≥0, |x|ᵏe^{sx}≤|x|ᵏe^{δ|x|/2}e^{tx}≤C_k(e^{(t+δ)x}+e^{(t−δ)x}), with C_k=sup_x|x|ᵏe^{−δ|x|/2}. The right side is integrable.
Differentiation under the integral. By step 2 and the dominated convergence theorem, M is smooth on I and M^{(k)}(t)=E[Xᵏe^{tX}].
Cumulants. Λ′=M′/M=E[Xe^{tX}]/M=E_t X. Next Λ″=M″/M−(M′/M)²=E_t[X²]−(E_t X)²=Var_t X. A variance is nonnegative, so Λ″≥0 and Λ is convex. This proves (b).
Chernoff bound. For t≥0 the event {X≥a} is the event {e^{tX}≥e^{ta}}. The Markov inequality gives P(X≥a)≤e^{−ta}M(t)=exp(−(ta−Λ(t))). This proves (c).
Independent sums. For independent Xᵢ, E e^{tSₙ}=∏E e^{tXᵢ}=M(t)ⁿ. So Λ_{Sₙ}=nΛ. Apply step 5 to Sₙ and the level na. This gives P(Sₙ≥na)≤exp(−n(ta−Λ(t))).

Exact identity. The tilt of the product law P^{⊗n} by t has density e^{tSₙ−nΛ(t)}. By step 1 for the product law, P(Sₙ≥na)=E_{t*}[e^{−t*Sₙ+nΛ(t*)}1_{Sₙ≥na}]. Since nΛ(t*)−t*na=−nI, this equals e^{−nI}E_{t*}[e^{−t*(Sₙ−na)}1_{Sₙ≥na}]. On the event the exponent is at most 0 and t*>0. So the expectation is at most 1. Under P_{t*} the mean of X is Λ′(t*)=a, so the tilted walk is centered at the level na.

worked_application.title: Fair coin tosses reaching 70 heads in 100
worked_application.goal: Compute the Chernoff bound and the exact tail for 100 fair tosses, and show the tilted law.
hypotheses: Xᵢ are i.i.d. Bernoulli(1/2), n=100, a=0.7, so the target is Sₙ≥70.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The mgf is finite for all t. Part (d) applies with the tilt t* that solves Λ′(t*)=0.7.

steps.text: Find the tilt. Λ′(t)=eᵗ/(1+eᵗ). Setting it to 0.7 gives eᵗ=7/3, so t*=ln(7/3)=0.847298.

Cumulant values. Λ(t*)=ln((1+7/3)/2)=ln(5/3)=0.510826. A central difference check gives Λ′=0.700000 and Λ″=0.210000. The theorem predicts Λ″=0.7·0.3=0.21, the variance of Bernoulli(0.7). So the tilted law of each toss is Bernoulli(0.7).
Exact tail. P(S₁₀₀≥70)=Σ_{j≥70}C(100,j)/2¹⁰⁰=3.925×10⁻⁵. It is below the bound 2.670×10⁻⁴, as the theorem says.

worked_application.result: P(S₁₀₀≥70)=3.925×10⁻⁵ against the Chernoff bound 2.670×10⁻⁴. The bound is loose by the factor 0.14701, which is the tilted expectation.

limitations: The bound is an upper bound only. Cramér theorem on large deviations gives the matching lower bound on the exponent, which this entry does not prove.
The mgf must be finite near t. For heavy tails such as the Cauchy law there is no such t, and the method fails.

/-- **Chebyshev's inequality**: one can control the deviation probability of a real random variable
from its expectation in terms of the variance. -/
theorem meas_ge_le_variance_div_sq [IsFiniteMeasure μ] {X : Ω → ℝ} (hX : MemLp X 2 μ) {c : ℝ}
    (hc : 0 < c) : μ {ω | c ≤ |X ω - μ[X]|} ≤ ENNReal.ofReal (variance X μ / c ^ 2) := by
  rw [ENNReal.ofReal_div_of_pos (sq_pos_of_ne_zero hc.ne.symm), hX.ofReal_variance_eq]
  convert @meas_ge_le_evariance_div_sq _ _ _ _ hX.aestronglyMeasurable c.toNNReal
    (by simp [hc]) using 1
  · simp
  · rw [ENNReal.ofReal_pow hc.le]
    rfl

steps.text: Variance of a sum. Var(ΣYᵢ)=ΣᵢΣⱼCov(Yᵢ,Yⱼ), by bilinearity of the covariance.
Indicators. Cov(1_{Aᵢ},1_{Aᵢ})=pᵢ(1−pᵢ), and Cov(1_{Aᵢ},1_{Aⱼ})=P(Aᵢ∩Aⱼ)−pᵢpⱼ. Combined with step 1 this proves (d).
Chebyshev route. If X=0 then |X−μ|=μ. So {X=0}⊂{|X−μ|≥μ}. The Chebyshev inequality gives P(X=0)≤Var X/μ². This proves (b).

Cauchy-Schwarz route. If P(X>0)=0, then X=0 almost surely and μ=0, which is false. So q=P(X>0)>0. For every real λ, 0≤E[(X−λ1_{X>0})²]=E[X²]−2λE[X1_{X>0}]+λ²q. Because X≥0, X1_{X>0}=X, so the middle term is −2λμ.
Optimize λ. Take λ=μ/q. Then 0≤E[X²]−μ²/q. Rearranging, q≥μ²/E[X²]. This proves (a).
Compare. Put u=Var X/μ². Then E[X²]=μ²(1+u), so μ²/E[X²]=1/(1+u). Also 1/(1+u)≥1−u, because (1+u)(1−u)=1−u²≤1. This proves (c).
Use in a sequence. If a family Xₙ has Var Xₙ/(E Xₙ)²→0, part (b) gives P(Xₙ=0)→0. If the ratio tends to a finite limit u, part (a) gives liminf P(Xₙ>0)≥1/(1+u).

worked_application.title: Triangles in a random graph
worked_application.goal: Bound the chance that G(n,p) contains a triangle, for three choices of (n,p).
hypotheses: G(n,p) has n vertices, and each edge is present independently with probability p.
X is the number of triangles. N=C(n,3) triples, and Aₜ is the event that triple T is a triangle.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: X is a sum of indicators with P(Aₜ)=p³. Two distinct triples that share one vertex or none use disjoint edge sets, so their indicators are independent. Two triples that share two vertices share one edge, and P(Aₜ∩A_{T′})=p⁵.

steps.text: Moments. E X=Np³. The number of ordered pairs of distinct triples with two common vertices is 3N(n−3). So Var X=N(p³−p⁶)+3N(n−3)(p⁵−p⁶).

Exact check, n=6 and p=2/5. Here N=20. The formula gives E X=32/25 and Var X=288/125=2.304. A full enumeration of all 2¹⁵ graphs with exact fractions gives the same E X=32/25 and E[X²]=2464/625. So the formula is correct.
Small case. P(X=0)=0.386586 exactly. Part (b) gives Var X/μ²=1.40625, which is trivial. Part (a) gives P(X>0)≥μ²/E[X²]=0.415584. The true value is 0.613414. So (a) is useful here and (b) is not.
Dense case, n=1000 and p=0.01. E X=166.167 and Var X=215.370. The ratio is 0.0078. So P(no triangle)≤0.0078 by part (b), and a triangle appears with probability at least 0.9922.

Sparse case, n=1000 and p=0.001. E X=0.166167 and the ratio Var X/μ² is 6.036. Part (b) is trivial. Part (a) gives P(X>0)≥1/(1+6.036)=0.1421. The Markov inequality gives P(X>0)≤E X=0.1662. So the true value lies in [0.1421,0.1662].

worked_application.result: A triangle exists with probability at least 0.415584 for (6,2/5), at least 0.9922 for (1000,0.01) and at least 0.1421 for (1000,0.001).

limitations: The method only shows P(X>0)>0. It does not give a construction.
If Var X/μ² does not tend to 0, part (b) is empty. Part (a) still gives a constant lower bound.
The pair counts in the application are for triangles. Other subgraphs need their own overlap counts.

results.name: Wald identity and gambler ruin from optional stopping
results.statement: Let ξ₁,ξ₂,… be i.i.d. integrable real variables with mean μ. Put Sₙ=ξ₁+…+ξₙ and Fₙ=σ(ξ₁,…,ξₙ). Let T be a stopping time with E T<∞. Then E S_T=μ E T. For the simple symmetric walk started at a in {0,…,N}, with T the first time at 0 or N, one has P(S_T=N)=a/N and E T=a(N−a).

/-- **The optional stopping theorem** (fair game theorem): a strongly adapted integrable process `f`
is a submartingale if and only if for all bounded stopping times `τ` and `π` such that `τ ≤ π`, the
stopped value of `f` at `τ` has expectation smaller than its stopped value at `π`. -/
theorem submartingale_iff_expected_stoppedValue_mono [SigmaFiniteFiltration μ 𝒢]
    (hadp : StronglyAdapted 𝒢 f) (hint : ∀ i, Integrable (f i) μ) :
    Submartingale f 𝒢 μ ↔ ∀ τ π : Ω → WithTop ℕ, IsStoppingTime 𝒢 τ → IsStoppingTime 𝒢 π →
      τ ≤ π → (∃ N : ℕ, ∀ x, π x ≤ N) → μ[stoppedValue f τ] ≤ μ[stoppedValue f π] :=
  ⟨fun hf _ _ hτ hπ hle ⟨_, hN⟩ => hf.expected_stoppedValue_mono hτ hπ hle hN,
    submartingale_of_expected_stoppedValue_mono hadp hint⟩

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Martingale. M_n=Sₙ−nμ is a martingale for (Fₙ), because E[ξ_{n+1}|Fₙ]=μ. The stopping time T∧n is bounded by n.
Bounded optional stopping. Apply optional stopping to M and to −M, with the times 0 and T∧n. This gives E M_{T∧n}=E M₀=0. So E S_{T∧n}=μ E[T∧n].
Domination. Put m=E|ξ₁| and Y=Σ_{i≤T}|ξᵢ|. Step 2 for the variables |ξᵢ| gives E Σ_{i≤T∧n}|ξᵢ|=m E[T∧n]. The left side increases with n. By the monotone convergence theorem E Y=m E T<∞.

Limit. T<∞ almost surely, so S_{T∧n}→S_T almost surely. Also |S_{T∧n}|≤Y with Y integrable. The dominated convergence theorem gives E S_{T∧n}→E S_T. The monotone convergence theorem gives E[T∧n]→E T. Step 2 now gives E S_T=μ E T.

Finite stopping time in the ruin problem. In any N consecutive steps, N up-steps in a row take the walk to N, so T≤N after such a block. Thus P(T>kN)≤(1−2^{−N})ᵏ. The tail sum Σ_j P(T>j) is finite, so E T<∞.
Hitting probability. Apply the identity with μ=0 to the walk Sₙ−a. It gives E S_T=a. Since S_T∈{0,N}, N·P(S_T=N)=a, so P(S_T=N)=a/N.

Expected duration. Sₙ²−n is a martingale, because E[(Sₙ+ξ)²|Fₙ]=Sₙ²+1. Bounded optional stopping gives E S²_{T∧n}=a²+E[T∧n]. Let n→∞. The left side tends to E S_T²=N²·a/N=aN by dominated convergence, since S²≤N². The right side tends to a²+E T. So E T=aN−a²=a(N−a).

results.name: Borel-Cantelli dichotomy for the growth of i.i.d. maxima
results.statement: Let X₁,X₂,… be i.i.d. with P(X₁>x)=e^{−x} for x≥0. Put Mₙ=max_{k≤n}X_k. Then, almost surely, limsup Xₙ/ln n=1 and lim Mₙ/ln n=1. More precisely, for c>1 one has Xₙ≤c ln n for all large n, and for c≤1 one has Xₙ>c ln n for infinitely many n.
hypotheses: The variables are independent. Independence is used in the second Borel-Cantelli lemma and in P(Mₙ≤x)=P(X₁≤x)ⁿ.
The tail is exactly exponential. The same method works for any law with P(X>x)≈e^{−x}.
Almost sure statements hold outside a null set.

/-- **The second Borel-Cantelli lemma**: Given a sequence of independent sets `(sₙ)` such that
`∑ n, μ sₙ = ∞`, `limsup sₙ` has measure 1. -/
theorem measure_limsup_eq_one {s : ℕ → Set Ω} (hsm : ∀ n, MeasurableSet (s n)) (hs : iIndepSet s μ)
    (hs' : (∑' n, μ (s n)) = ∞) : μ (limsup s atTop) = 1 := by
  have : IsProbabilityMeasure μ := hs.isProbabilityMeasure
  rw [measure_congr (eventuallyEqSet_iff.2 (ae_mem_limsup_atTop_iff μ <|
    measurableSet_filtrationOfSet' hsm) : limsup s atTop =ᵐ[μ]
      {ω | Tendsto (fun n => ∑ k ∈ Finset.range n,
        (μ[(s (k + 1)).indicator (1 : Ω → ℝ)|filtrationOfSet hsm k]) ω) atTop atTop})]
  suffices {ω | Tendsto (fun n => ∑ k ∈ Finset.range n,
      (μ[(s (k + 1)).indicator (1 : Ω → ℝ)|filtrationOfSet hsm k]) ω) atTop atTop} =ᵐ[μ] Set.univ by
    rw [measure_congr this, measure_univ]
  have : ∀ᵐ ω ∂μ, ∀ n, (μ[(s (n + 1)).indicator (1 : Ω → ℝ) | filtrationOfSet hsm n]) ω = _ :=
    ae_all_iff.2 fun n => hs.condExp_indicator_filtrationOfSet_ae_eq hsm n.lt_succ_self
  filter_upwards [this] with ω hω
  refine eq_true (?_ : Tendsto _ _ _)
  simp_rw [hω]
  have htends : Tendsto (fun n => ∑ k ∈ Finset.range n, μ (s (k + 1))) atTop (𝓝 ∞) := by
    rw [← ENNReal.tsum_add_one_eq_top hs' (measure_ne_top _ _)]
    exact ENNReal.tendsto_nat_tsum _
  rw [ENNReal.tendsto_nhds_top_iff_nnreal] at htends
  refine tendsto_atTop_atTop_of_monotone' ?_ ?_
  · refine monotone_nat_of_le_succ fun n => ?_
    rw [← sub_nonneg, Finset.sum_range_succ_sub_sum]
    exact ENNReal.toReal_nonneg
  · rintro ⟨B, hB⟩
    refine not_eventually.2 (Frequently.of_forall fun n => ?_) (htends B.toNNReal)
    rw [mem_upperBounds] at hB
    specialize hB (∑ k ∈ Finset.range n, μ (s (k + 1))).toReal _
    · refine ⟨n, ?_⟩
      rw [ENNReal.toReal_sum (by finiteness)]
      rfl
    · rwa [not_lt, ENNReal.ofNNReal_toNNReal, ENNReal.le_ofReal_iff_toReal_le]
      · simp
      · exact le_trans (by positivity) hB

source_references.excerpt:
/-- One direction of the **Borel-Cantelli lemma**
(sometimes called the "*first* Borel-Cantelli lemma"):
if `(s i)` is a sequence of sets such that `∑' i, μ (s i)` is finite,
then the limit superior of the `s i` along the `atTop` filter is a null set.

Note: for the *second* Borel-Cantelli lemma (applying to independent sets in a probability space),
see `ProbabilityTheory.measure_limsup_eq_one`. -/
theorem measure_limsup_atTop_eq_zero {s : ℕ → Set α} (hs : ∑' i, μ (s i) ≠ ∞) :
    μ (limsup s atTop) = 0 := by
  rw [← Nat.cofinite_eq_atTop, measure_limsup_cofinite_eq_zero hs]

steps.text: Tail probabilities. For n≥2 and c>0, P(Xₙ>c ln n)=e^{−c ln n}=n^{−c}.

Upper bound for the limsup. Let c>1. Then Σn^{−c}<∞. The first Borel-Cantelli lemma shows that Xₙ>c ln n happens only finitely often almost surely. Use c=1+1/j for j=1,2,… and intersect countably many almost sure events. So limsup Xₙ/ln n≤1 almost surely.

Lower bound for the limsup. The events {Xₙ>ln n} are independent and ΣP=Σ1/n=∞. The second Borel-Cantelli lemma shows that they occur infinitely often almost surely. So limsup Xₙ/ln n≥1 almost surely. Combined with step 2, limsup Xₙ/ln n=1.
Upper bound for the maximum. Let c>1 and take ω outside the null set of step 2. There is K=K(ω) with X_k≤c ln k for k≥K. For n≥K, Mₙ≤max(M_K,c ln n). So limsup Mₙ/ln n≤c. Let c↓1 along 1+1/j.

Lower bound for the maximum. Let 0<c<1. By independence P(Mₙ≤c ln n)=(1−n^{−c})ⁿ≤exp(−n^{1−c}), using 1−u≤e^{−u}. For large n, n^{1−c}≥2 ln n, so the bound is at most n^{−2}. The series converges, so the first Borel-Cantelli lemma shows Mₙ>c ln n for all large n almost surely. So liminf Mₙ/ln n≥c. Let c↑1 along 1−1/j.

Conclusion. Steps 4 and 5 give lim Mₙ/ln n=1 almost surely. Step 2 and step 3 give limsup Xₙ/ln n=1. The single terms Xₙ do not satisfy lim Xₙ/ln n=1, since the events {Xₙ<1} are independent with probability 1−e⁻¹ each. The second lemma shows they occur infinitely often, so the liminf of the ratio is 0.

worked_application.title: Counting exceedances of ln n by exponential variables
worked_application.goal: Compare the expected number of exceedances Σn^{−c} with one simulated run of 10⁶ variables, and check the lower bound for the maximum.
hypotheses: Xₙ i.i.d. Exp(1) for n=2,…,10⁶, drawn with Python random.seed(20261011) and random.expovariate(1.0).
Thresholds c=1, 1.5 and 2.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The tail P(Xₙ>c ln n)=n^{−c} has a divergent sum for c=1 and a convergent sum for c=1.5 and 2.

steps.text: Expected counts. For N=10⁶, Σ_{n=2}^N n^{−1}=13.3927, Σ n^{−1.5}=1.6104 and Σ n^{−2}=0.6449. The first sum grows like ln N−0.4228, so it diverges but very slowly.
Partial sums for c=1. The sums up to 10³, 10⁴, 10⁵ and 10⁶ are 6.4855, 8.7876, 11.0901 and 13.3927. Each step of ×10 adds ln10=2.3026.

One simulated run. The counts of exceedances are 7 for c=1, 1 for c=1.5 and 0 for c=2. The last exceedance indices are 486096 for c=1 and 729 for c=1.5. This one run is below the expected count 13.39 for c=1, which is allowed because the count has a spread of about √13.
Maximum. In the same run M=13.3873 and ln N=13.8155. The ratio is 0.9690, close to 1.
Lower-bound probability. For n=10⁶ and c=0.75, P(Mₙ≤0.75 ln n)=(1−n^{−0.75})ⁿ=1.8458×10⁻¹⁴. The bound exp(−n^{0.25}) equals 1.8467×10⁻¹⁴. The two agree and show how fast the lower tail dies.

The sharp description is Gumbel: Mₙ−ln n converges in law. That is not proved here.

results.name: Projection onto a convex set: variational inequality and fixed-point test
results.statement: Let K be a nonempty closed convex subset of a real Hilbert space H, and let u be in H. (a) A point v in K satisfies ‖u−v‖=dist(u,K) if and only if ⟨u−v,w−v⟩≤0 for all w in K. Such a point exists and is unique. Call it P_K u. (b) ‖P_K u−P_K u′‖²≤⟨P_K u−P_K u′,u−u′⟩, hence ‖P_K u−P_K u′‖≤‖u−u′‖. (c) Let f be convex and differentiable on H with gradient ∇f, and let η>0. A point v in K minimizes f over K if and only if v=P_K(v−η∇f(v)).
hypotheses: K is closed, convex and nonempty. The space is a real Hilbert space.
In (c) the function f is convex and differentiable. Convexity is used for the direction from the condition to the minimum.
The number η>0 is arbitrary. The fixed-point test does not depend on it.
